My home office already has a dual monitor setup with docking station so that's easy, however, there are times my husband also works from home and we fight over the monitor setup, so this might just save our marriage. ;) Joking aside, I wish we had this thing during the pandemic shutdown because it would have made working from home so much easier.

I've had this one in my cart for quite some time, and then noticed around Black Friday/ Cyber Monday, it was an extra 15 off or so, and I decided to leap. In deciding which monitor to get, there were mostly positive reviews, though some more critical. I wasn't entirely sure what to expect, but have thus far been absolutely blown away!

My favorite features:
--It is quite thin and lightweight, in a nice and portable way rather than "this is a cheap piece of... " way
--The quality is phenomenal. Very crisp and clear and plenty bright without being blinding. There are settings to mess with too, though I found it perfect right out of the box
--It comes with multiple connectors so should work for a variety of purposes and with different computer or other device configurations
--It was pretty much plug and play straight out of the box. It turned on with 0 issues. My PC laptop always defaults second monitors to duplicate screens rather than extending screens, so I wasn't surprised when this was the same. It was a simple, quick fix by going to my display settings and changing the monitor to extend rather than duplicate. I had to switch my monitors around in settings so this monitor would work with dragging things from my laptop monitor to the right, rather than to the left due to my preferences. It might be tricky if you've never done it, but it's old hat for me. Long story short, play around with your display settings until all is configured the way you want. I find when I plug it in again, it automatically defaults to this setup unless I have changed the settings for a different monitor setup at work or home, and then I might need to reset again. I could see where a duplicate screen could actually be handy in a meeting, however, at a meeting where multiple people around a table need to see the same thing, so I could have my laptop facing one direction, and the other screen facing another. I see so many possibilities with this one, actually, for work purposes and I'm grateful to have it.
--It comes with a felt carrying case which is perfect for keeping the screen scratch-free and keeping the cables and such together. The velcro doesn't fasten if you have the stand connected, but it still all fits in the case just the same.
--I've looked at many different portable monitors, but ultimately loved this one for coming with multiple adaptors/ cords and the adjustable monitor stand, saving me time and money. The stand is very easy to install and uninstall -- just two simple screws and it's fairly adjustable so you can line it up with your laptop screen if that's your preference, or change the angle. It works very well for my needs, but if you have super specific needs or need to raise it up or down quite a bit, you may want to look at a different monitor stand with more adjustments. I found this one to be just right, however.

My only criticism so far, but the pros far outweigh the cons!
--As mentioned, the carrying case won't fasten if you have the monitor stand attached. It's pretty minor, but do wish the velcro had a couple different fastening settings so everything could close up with or without the stand. Yes, I could technically remove the stand easily but would prefer to have everything set up and ready to go for quick access.

Long story short, run, don't walk, and grab this monitor! Whether you need it for work purposes or for gaming capability (per many of the other reviews), this monitor is fire! I highly recommend!

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
What I needed:
I needed a computer for my electronics lab. It didn't need to be immensely powerful, but I wanted something that would be easy to expand as needed. This PC met my needs almost perfectly, and at a very economical price. I purchased this 6 months ago (almost to the day), so this is not an "out of the box" impression, but one based on months of experience. It has been powered on (or sleeping) continuously, so I can remote access it when needed.

My uses are primarily centered around my lab work: Electronic Design, PCB Layout, and 3D Rendering of PCBs, along with Design of small enclosures and modest software development. I also have several PC connected pieces of bench equipment: Digital Scope, Power Supplies, Function Generator, and whatever thing I'm creating. Most of these connect via USB, and one via RS-232.

This PC:
You can see in the pictures that the front panel has 4 USB ports - 2 are SuperSpeed. These have already proven valuable for quick attachments.

The rear panel is loaded up with 6 more USB ports (2 of which are SuperSpeed), and I've used most of them. If I had to, I could easily dig out an old PS2 Keyboard to free up another USB port - but with 4 empty ports on the front I'm ok for now.

As noted above, I needed RS-232, and this PC had one - which is a bonus. Of course, I could have plugged in a USB to RS-232 adapter. Beneath the back-panel RS-232 port (the gray plug in the picture) is a VGA connector, which I don't expect to use. To the left of those are a couple of Display Ports - one connected to my big screen (3440 x 1440). The specs say that each can support a 4K monitor, but my bench doesn't have space (and the screen resolution works for my eyeballs and needs).

The host processor in the unit I purchased is an i5-4590 quad core running at 3.3 GHz. The motherboard memory slots are full, loaded with 16 GB of RAM. The motherboard has 3 SATA ports, but they are fully occupied, connected to a 240 GB SSD hosting Win10 Pro, a 1GB spinning HDD, and a DVD drive. The graphics is served with an integrated Intel HD 4600. For further expansion, there are 4 PCIe slots: 2 x X1, 1 x X4 and 1 x X16.

Other Discoveries:
* The BIOS still had the name of the prior "owner" (a company), which is probably where many of these came from. It was simple to change, so now is hosts a name appropriate for my lab.
* This PC is not for gaming, so I didn't rate that since I've never run a game on it. With my single high-resolution monitor connected, spinning a 3D model of a modestly complex circuit board is fast - it more than meets my needs.
* And I had no need for Tech Support, so I didn't rate that either.

My Expansion:
* In the pictures you'll see one of the PCI slots is occupied - with the 4-channel SATA adapter that I added. The 3 on the motherboard were occupied but I needed one more for an external HD dock.
* I expect to add a Webcam soon.
* I also expect to add one more PCI card to it, to add USB-C connectors. My newest gear (Laptop, Phone, etc.) all have USB-C, so this will be necessary.

My Summary:
This was the right PC for my needs. It was also relatively inexpensive. It has been running close to non-stop since my unboxing. It "seems" quiet enough for most any location, but my lab isn't the best place to judge that.

It didn't have support for every interface I needed but was more than expandable enough to add to it. I do wish the overall unit was a bit smaller (for my lab space), and in years prior I had a large tower PC, but tired of crawling under the desk to swap cables around.

It was delivered on time and was in like-new condition as advertised. It has a smaller footprint than a full-size desktop which I had concerns about before I got it. However, once I opened the access panel, I was impressed. It has a recessed latched pull handle that removes the whole access panel exposing everything and no screws to unscrew or lose. The drives and optical reader (DVD) are contained within a rack that you just pivot upward to release and you have full easy access to them. Additional expansion slots to add what you like. If you should want to increase RAM from 16 to 32 GB there is nothing around them so removing and replacing them in the slots would be effortless. I was surprised how cool this computer runs even when using multiple high resource software at the same time with no lag.

As for the USB Keyboard and Mouse, USB WiFi Adapter. These are low cost and just so you have something. As low cost as keyboard and mouse are I really like them. If you use something else don't throw them out as others have said. Save them as an emergency back up or give them to someone. I have a Logitech wireless keyboard and mouse but still using the ones that came with this computer. USB WiFi Adapter isn't the best it's not real fast and not great for long-distance so I did buy a better one at the same time. There are a lot of cheap USB WiFi Adapters that stop working after 2-3 months but here is a low-cost $17 good one I use so can avoid the hassle.
Just search amazon for -
TP-Link AC600 USB WiFi Adapter for PC (Archer T2U Plus)- Wireless Network Adapter for Desktop with 2.4GHz, 5GHz High Gain Dual Band 5dBi Antenna, Supports Windows 10/8.1/8/7/XP, Mac OS 10.9-10.14
It increased my transfer speed from 300 Mbps or less and 3 bars signal strength to a transfer speed of 433 to 490 Mbps and 5 bars signal strength.

All you have to do is connect a monitor, the keyboard, mouse, and USB wifi adapter and power up. You do need to set up you user account like any new computer. This is Microsoft so it wants you to use a Microsoft account to have a better "online experience". But all you need to do is enter your login for a Microsoft email account or create one during set up. That step requires connecting to the internet and entering the password. Excellent Dock for Shared Workspaces - HP USB-C G5 is a Winner!
We recently got this HP USB-C G5 Docking Station bundle for a shared office space at work, and it's been a fantastic addition. For an area where three of us rotate depending on who's in, this dock has made things incredibly convenient.
The best part is the single USB-C cable connection. You just plug in your laptop (it works with both regular USB-C and Thunderbolt laptops, which is a huge plus for compatibility), and instantly you're connected to multiple monitors, the wired LAN network, and any other USB peripherals we have set up. No more fiddling with a bunch of different cables every time someone new sits down at the desk.
This particular bundle came with everything needed: the dock itself, the 120W AC adapter (which also charges the connected laptop – I believe it provides up to 65W to the host, which is plenty for most), an HDMI cable, a DisplayPort cable, and a USB cable. title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I did a bunch of research on this and chose this because I figured it should be at least guaranteed to work well with my work laptop, an HP EliteBook 840 G5 (yes, it's old), and it was probably workable with my personal laptop (Windows, Lenovo Legion Pro 7i 16IRX8H). And it turned out pretty much as expected!
Refurbished version came in "like new" packaging. First thing I did was check that both computers could drive my two monitors (one 24" LG 1080p, 100Hz panel and one 32" MSI 4K, 240 Hz panel) through it. They could. Peripherals (my mic/headphones, webcam, and keyboard/mouse) were fine and operational. The dock is capped at 60 Hz for my resolution, which was fine with me, since I directly connect my gaming laptop to my primary monitor when I need a higher refresh rate. The second thing I did was check the overall functionality compared to my old HP dock -- the kind with the proprietary HP-specific port. With my old dock, I could use my work laptop with it closed and wake from sleep using the power button on the dock. (It blinks when my work laptop is asleep and connected). No issues there; I can wake from deep sleep on my work laptop and work with the laptop closed. It also charges fine. So all that functionality was retained in a piece of equipment half the size.
The third thing I did was check the functionality with my gaming laptop. The 4K OLED picture is gorgeous. However, I cannot work with my gaming laptop closed with this dock. I suspect this is an issue with my laptop or its settings, but it could also be the dock. This is fine for me because I half-expected it, and got a horizontal laptop storage situation for that reason. So I just keep my work laptop closed on the bottom shelf and my personal open on the top. This means that all I have to do is move the USB-C cord between the two to switch from work mode to personal.

With all that said, I would probably give this a 4.5 stars if I could. There are just enough USB ports for my set-up (though I have a back-up USB hub for overflow just in case), and I would say I use an average to slightly more than average amount of peripherals. There have been some minor issues with audio routing, but because I tend to use my headphones/mic set-up for everything, this isn't a big deal to me. The biggest problem I faced was attempting to use the HDMI port with my dual monitor display. It did not work properly, and I gave up almost immediately. Instead, I use a DP - DP connection for my main monitor and a HDMI (output) - DP (source) connection for my side monitor. I already had the HDMI - DP cable from previous adventures trying to get a KVM switch set-up to work, so again, this was not a big deal for me. I would, however, definitely recommend, at least for anyone trying a have set-up like mine, using the two DP ports for a dual monitor set-up (even if it means using an adapter cable!) rather than trying to mix-and-match. If you haven't bought your monitors yet, then I would recommend monitors with DP ports over HDMI for this dock. Just make sure to use appropriate cables for whatever resolution you are aiming for.

Other minor considerations would be: cable management. The cable situation can get a little unwieldy depending on where you have your devices situated because while the power cord is cleverly tucked underneath and goes out the back, the USB-C connector to the source comes out the front. The peripheral and display ports are well-located though.

Overall, great value compared to other docks, decent connectivity, and the dock is built solidly. (Can you tell that I added this line just so Amazon would tell me I wrote a helpful review).

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought this to go with a new HP laptop based on the low power Intel Core Ultra 7 processor. Laptop physical connection options are limited to two 40 Gbps Thunderbolt 4 ports and a 10Gbps USB-C port. Newer monitors are equipped with USB-C in addition to HDMI or DisplayPort, but I need HDMI for the somewhat older monitor I use with the laptop.

I've been using the Dock G5 for almost two weeks now. USB-A ports for older USB devices, the wired Ethernet port, and the HDMI port are all plug and play with no problems. The G5 USB-C port supports high-speed charging to my Android phone. It also replaces the charger that came with the laptop, charging it at the same rate.

About the only downside I find is that the laptop is always kept fully charged if I leave it connected to the G5, so I have to disconnect it periodically to cycle the laptop battery.

If you are considering purchasing this and expect it to work as a charger, you should make sure your laptop's USB-C port supports Power Delivery and charging, and make sure the power levels are compatible between laptop and Dock G5. Newer, lower-power laptops that support only USB-C and Thunderbolt 4 physical connections are likely to support USB-C charging, while older laptops often will not.

To be honest, the Dock G5 is probably overkill for my needs and I could have gotten by with a USB-C hub and some adapters. That said, the Dock G5 is well made and works perfectly with my HP laptop. I'm very happy with it and won't be looking back.

title: 1.0 out of 5 stars
text:
For starters simply finding the correct dock for my new HP laptop turned out to be a bad science project. NO description of any kind on HP websites to specifically define to customers WHICH port replicator goes with WHICH laptop. In fact the HP website is nothing short of a labyrinth of opaque worthless instructions and endless do-loops sending you to more and more useless pages with NO opportunity to ever figure out how to speak to a human being. This after paying over $300 for a docking station.

Device often does not boot properly. IF you plug in the dock to the computer (with computer lid down) the device allows boot through bitlocker then the screen goes blank because the computer is only projecting to the built-in monitor. Once you open the laptop you can boot into windows however now the laptop will NOT recognize ANY of the attached screens. You need to shut completely down and reboot with the laptop open and NO docking station attached.

Disconnecting the computer also causes major hassles. I have 3 large monitors and when I either disconnect or re-connect, it’s often a matter of minutes before this desperately slow device decides to wake up. And that’s if it wakes up at all.

Getting all of the proper drivers on this installed was also a major hassle. No matter how much IT support I got from my organization the IT group readily admits this device is notoriously bad.

Computer lag once the dock is attached is EXTREME on all screens including the laptop built-in screen. The dock is either totally underpowered or the computer cannot handle it. In any case the dock sometimes renders the entire setup nearly useless. This is perhaps the single most infuriatingly bad part of this entire disastrous design. It’s possible that some rocket scientist at HP decided to put a graphics card in the replicator itself and it is over-riding the laptop (I have a Zbook G4). After perhaps 5-6 months of trying to get this thing to run I’ve totally given up hope that this workstation will fulfill even the most marginal expectations. Even typing up something in MS Word or Outlook is often near impossible simply because the screen is so phenomenally slow to update. And when it does update, often 30% of the keystrokes are missing. Really HP? Thanks for a trip back to the computing stone ages.

Cables that work fine with the laptop refuse to work at all with the dock. These included display port to DP, HDMI to HDMI, HDMI to Display Port, VGA, and impossibly – the NEW USB C to HDMI cable ordered specifically to work with this dock.

The top of the device is also the power button. As others may have mentioned every time you try to connect something or check a connection it’s often the case you inadvertently turn the device off. Aesthetics are meaningless when they cause such confusion and / or frustration.

There is very little about this product and its quality that is redeeming. Especially in light of the absurdly high price and the fact that for some laptops this is your only HP solution. This HP product is a disgrace to the brand. I guess what makes me the most upset is that docking stations have always been one of the most mundane innocuous computer peripherals out there. You simply set them up one time and they work. Historically they were also relatively cheap. HP has really taken this design in every conceivably bad direction possible. Poor design, poor performance, and a contemptibly bad price.

Pros: Maybe the combo cable? But then again most docking stations connect with relative ease so this is not a big gain.

Suggestions for improvement. Based on all of the issues I’ve encountered with this device the only thing I could think of for improvement would be to somehow add about 700 lbs to the weight of it. Perhaps then it could be effectively used as a boat anchor.

Never again will I own an HP computer UNLESS my corporation requires it. Note: I’m a HUGE fan of all the HP printers I’ve ever owned. Went with a Brother brand about 10 years ago and after about 5 years I tossed it and went back to HP. Maybe HP just needs to stick with printers…

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I was looking for a Thunderbolt dock to get back to a single-cable dock solution like I had when I was smart enough to have a Surface and not a laptop. This is not the latest Thunderbolt 4 dock, but Thunderbolt 3 is more than enough for my current needs.

The biggest downside is that there is no audio out. (Apparently, there's an optional HP expansion module that plugs into the top of the dock to provide audio out, but good luck finding it. I don't really need audio out from the dock for this computer, so it's not a showstopper for me, but you should know about this limit.)

Note: This unit comes with the "combo cable" which is really just a Thunderbolt 3 cable and a coaxial power cable molded together. With a couple of minutes of simple screwdriver work, you can remove the case bottom and cable clamps and replace the combo cable with a standard Thunderbolt cable. (I used a 1 ft cable with a handy 90-degree connector). Since the Thunderbolt connection can also supply power to the computer, this works fine if you want to avoid or don't need the coaxial power plug.)

It's working well, and saved me over two hundred bucks (I bought the renewed model, which is a steal), so I was happy to buy and replace the Thunderbolt cable and give up audio output. Recommended.

text:
I recently purchased the HP USB-C 120W Dock G5, and overall, it is a good and decent product. It lives up to its promise of expanding ports and connecting up to three displays, and its space-saving design is a plus. However, there are some important points to consider.

Firstly, the item does not support two digital displays simultaneously. When two monitors are connected to the digital display ports, one will work at maximum resolution while the other will have reduced resolution. However, if one monitor is connected via the digital display port and the other via HDMI, both will work at maximum resolution. This limitation should have been mentioned in the description, as it can be a deal-breaker for those who need both monitors to work with digital ports. In my case, my Dell E2216H monitors do not have HDMI ports, making this issue particularly problematic.

After some experimentation, I found a workaround. When I swapped the display cables between the ports, both monitors started working at maximum resolution on the digital display ports. This fix worked for me without needing an additional adapter.

Overall, the dock works as advertised, but potential buyers should be aware of the display limitations and the need for some trial and error to achieve the desired setup.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I finally got tired of playing "musical chairs" with the two USB ports on my laptop every time I sat down to work. I picked up this 14-in-1 USB-C Docking Station, and it has completely transformed my workspace from a tangled mess of wires into something that actually looks like a functional office.

The "Everything Everywhere All at Once" Port Selection The sheer number of ports on this thing is impressive. I have two monitors hooked up via HDMI, my keyboard, mouse, a backup hard drive, and an Ethernet cable for a stable connection—all running through a single USB-C cable into my laptop. It even has SD card slots, which is a lifesaver for quickly moving photos and videos without hunting for a separate dongle.

Performance & Setup Setup was about as "plug-and-play" as it gets. My laptop recognized both external monitors immediately, and the picture quality is crisp with no noticeable lag. The 100W Power Delivery (PD) is a huge win, too—it charges my laptop while I work, so I can leave my actual power brick tucked away in my travel bag.

A Few "Pro-Tips" from My Setup:

Check Your Port: Before you buy, make sure your laptop's USB-C port actually supports "DisplayPort Alt Mode" or video output. If it’s just a basic data port, the HDMI won’t work, and you’ll be left wondering why your monitors are dark.

Heat: Like most high-powered hubs, it can get a little warm when you have ten things plugged in at once. It’s nothing alarming, but I’d recommend keeping it in a spot with a little airflow rather than burying it under a stack of papers.

The "Screw" Factor (Again): While there aren't literal screws here, the connection is snug. Just be gentle with the main cable; since everything relies on that one plug, you want to treat it with a bit of respect.

The Verdict If you’re looking to turn a single laptop into a full-blown desktop workstation with dual monitors, this is a fantastic value. It’s sturdy, reliable, and has enough ports to satisfy even the most gadget-heavy setup. My desk is finally organized, and I only have to plug in one cable to get to work.

Installation of this adapter is very easy, as long as you have purchased the correct adapter and have a screwdriver.

It took just a couple of minutes: you just press a latch to release the factory stand, remove it and the press this adapter in its place. There is a screw on top to more securely hold the monitor. This is necessary if you want to prevent any sort of wobble. Then you screw the VESA plate and finally the VESA mount.
All screws are provided.

Overall, a great buy, only necessary because HP didn’t put VESA holes in the monitor in the first place.

This MOKiN hub is a great solution for laptops or tablets that are short on USB ports. The four USB-A 3.0 ports deliver fast data transfer—perfect for external drives, mice, keyboards, or flash storage. I tested it with a Windows laptop and a MacBook, and it worked flawlessly with both.

Only downside: it’s not a powered hub, so if you’re running multiple high-draw devices (like external hard drives), you might hit a power limit. But for everyday peripherals, it’s a solid performer.

Highly recommend for anyone needing a compact, plug-and-play USB expansion—especially for ultrabooks or tablets with limited ports.

title: 3.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I like the product and it keeps my monitor more stable than another adapter I tried, BUT there is a flaw in this design that may affect some users, like me. Normally, a VESA mount would be in the center of the monitor but with this adapter it is down pretty low and that means the monitor is now up higher than it would be if mounted properly. Why is this an issue? I use it with a standing desk converter (Kangaroo) and, when standing, it is fine but when sitting the monitor is now much too high. I sit maybe 50% of the time, so this issue has made it unusable for me. If they just extended the VESA mounts so they fall in the center of the monitor this would be a perfect product. I imagine if you are wall mounting or only using when standing you should be fine. I am using it on an HP 25f monitor, BTW.

There are some other minor issues with the VESA mounting. To keep it secure, you must use nuts at on the inside of the VESA mount holes, and it is pretty difficult to get your hand in-between the bracket and the monitor to hold them steady (needle-nose plyers help). Also the supplied VESA screws have a pretty small head and there is no washer, so they actually fall inside the lower VESA mount holes.

Improvements to make this a 5-star product:
1. Extend the bracket so the VESA mounts fall in the center of the monitor.
2. Thread the bracket VESA holes so nuts aren't required.
3. Include some washers or screws with larger heads so they completely cover the VESA hole openings.

title: 3.0 out of 5 stars
text:
You really get what you pay for with this, but at the same time it’s really good for the price it is.

I’ll start off with the bad: this thing was cheap ($100 on Prime Day), and if you know computers you know 200hz monitors at this price range can be sketchy, but MSI is a known and trusted brand. However, it’s so cheaply made. It’s all plastic and it honestly feels like it could break at any moment just by looking at it in a funny way. The OSD button in the back is a joke, it’s extremely wobbly, like it can fall off at any moment. It’s also a pain to maneuver around with it since it’s not sturdy, so you can end up moving or pressing when you didn’t mean to.

And oh my goodness that stand is godawful. It doesn’t go up or down or move left or right. Thankfully I bought a VESA stand to mitigate this, and now it’s a lot more comfortable to game with.

There’s not much to say about the OSD itself. There are your normal preset gaming modes and crosshairs, but I don’t really mess with that stuff, I’d much prefer to mess with the settings myself. It has an AI mode which I honestly have no clue what it really does, nor do I honestly care; I don’t like to put filters or post processing stuff like that on my monitors.

But oh man this thing actually looks good. The colors are bright and saturated, the contrast is very good, and 200 hz actually makes a huge difference. I’ve played with 144 and 165 hz monitors and I don’t think I could go back. I can actually feel the difference in refresh rate and my games run silky smooth. I normally play fighting games and shooters, and if you know about those games, you know that fast refresh rates actually matter. If you’re in the 120-144 hz range and you play these types of games, I highly recommend making the switch to this.

I also calibrated the colors and brightness and it looks much better than out the box.

Overall, don’t expect a tough or modern looking monitor; it’s $100 for a reason. But I truthfully think that this might be a budget banger.

This is my first time with an OLED monitor, I was very hesitant weather to go for the upgrade or not but this monitor had everything I was looking for and the price was great.
The high refresh rate along with the adaptive-sync function provide a super smooth gaming experience at high fps and I don't notice any visual tearing, the quality is algo great; 1440p is in my opinion is the perfect resolution to experience competitive fps in multiplayer titles and high fps and crisp quality in single player titles.
The monitor controls to adjust picture quality, colors and all of that good stuff is quite simple and user-friendly, and since this is an OLED monitor the colors and contrast are simply next level compared to my old IPS monitor.

Overall I am content with my purchase but it may not be perfect for everyone so I will list some of my pros and cons about this monitor.

PROS
-Great visual fidelity, 1440p is the sweet spot for both competetive multiplayer and single player games.
-Buttery smooth motion with 240hz refresh rate and adaptive-sync.
-Superb color management and contrast overall.
-User-friendly menu and easily updatable firmware.

CONS
-This model in particular (unlike the 271QP and 272QP) does not have an HDR certification and I could not get it to look any good with HDR turned on.
-Really sensible to scratches glossy coating; I've had this monitor for a little over a week and I can already see some small scratches in the monitor when it's turned off and pointing a flashlight against it, however this is completely unnoticeable while the monitor is turned on and without any light directly hitting it (also from what I have read the sensible coating is a thing in almost every OLED monitor out there.)
-The top brightness is still not as bright as my old IPS monitor (like the previous point, this is also the case with most OLED monitors in the market right now except for the really expensive brand new ones.)

The 2560 x 1440 resolution on a 27-inch screen feels like a perfect balance between sharpness and performance. Speaking of smoothness, the 240Hz refresh rate combined with the ultra-fast 0.03ms response time makes a noticeable difference, especially in fast-paced shooters and competitive games. Motion looks clean and fluid, and I haven’t experienced ghosting or smearing. Adaptive-Sync support also helps eliminate screen tearing, which makes gameplay feel even more responsive and polished.

Overall, I’m extremely satisfied with this monitor. If you’re looking for a 27-inch QHD gaming display with incredible contrast, smooth 240Hz performance, and premium OLED image quality, this is an excellent choice. title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought the MSI PRO MP273W E14A for pretty much one specific reason: Xbox Series X + Black Ops 7 at 120Hz. I wanted the smoother tracking and reduced motion blur you get from such a high refresh without turning my desk into a “RGB spaceship.” This monitor nailed that balance alongside superior portability. Clean.

On console, the win isn’t 144Hz (since Xbox won’t use that), it’s that the panel has enough refresh headroom to run a clean, stable 120Hz pipeline when the game supports it. In BO7, the feel difference is immediate:

Smoother camera pans (less judder)
Cleaner target tracking (less perceived blur)
More responsive aim (lower perceived input delay bc frames update twice as often vs 60Hz)

So if you’ve been playing at 60Hz, 120Hz doesn’t just look better — it plays better, especially in fast FPS fights where micro-adjustments matter.

Office + daily use: underrated strengths:

Text looks clean and stable for long coding / spreadsheet sessions
Viewing angles don’t shift if you lean back or sit off-center
Anti-glare + IPS is a great combo for daytime work setups

A quick technical note: 27" at 1080p is about ~82 PPI, so for office work it’s best at a normal desk distance. If you sit very close, you’ll notice pixels more than you would on a 1440p panel — but for mixed gaming + productivity, it’s still very usable (and the high refresh makes even scrolling feel “premium”).

What i Like most:

True high-refresh feel (especially noticeable in FPS)
IPS clarity for work
Clean look that fits an office desk
144Hz headroom helps keep 120Hz operation comfortable and stable

tldr: I came for BO7 at 120Hz on Series X, and I ended up with a monitor that’s legitimately enjoyable for work too. Smooth where it counts, clean where it matters.

Setup tip: On Xbox, go to Settings → General → TV & display options and set:

Refresh rate: 120Hz
Resolution: 1080p
Enable VRR (if your unit exposes it / your HDMI path supports it)
Turn hdmi settings off for peak performance and less tearing

text:
I'm very pleased with this monitor so far, having had it for a week. Playing through the intro to Horizon: Forbidden West, in glorious HDR, is simply incredible. Even the HDR demos on youtube leave me with my jaw to the floor.

What surprised me the most was all the things that reviews of QD-OLED monitors warn you about, and how those turned out to be nothing, at least for me.

- HDR on at all times
I'm using Windows 11, and a GPU that supports HDMI 2.1 (with a 2.1 certified cable). The internet says that HDR needs to be off for SDR (ie standard) content, but I am finding that is not the case at all. I have it on all the time, and everything looks perfect to me. The HDR effect is noticeable in most things, and as far as I can tell, the colour accuracy is also there (caveat: I'm no expert). I went through the Windows HDR Calibration app later, and it claims to have improved the highlights. I had no complaints before, so, yay.

- Brightness
I don't understand what people are talking about when they say that QD-OLED technology is not bright enough. I have mine set to True Black 400, and it's plenty bright. I find I'm reaching for the dark modes in apps even more aggressively than before, since a sudden white screen (eg a website, or Excel) is almost too much for me :). Tip: look for a Chrome extension that automatically turns most websites to dark mode.

- Text clarity
I had forgotten that this was even something I was supposed to worry about. It was days later that I remembered about it, and I went looking for it. I still cannot see the problem, at all. White text everywhere has a healthy white glow to it (compared to my old IPS monitor - I don't mean actual backlight bleed or anything), which ought to improve clarity if anything.

- 1800R curve
Having been used to 3400R for 9 years, I thought 1800R might be too much for me. That has not been the case at all, thankfully. I don't even notice the difference, most of the time. 1800R is very pleasing, and might even be the new sweet spot for me.

- Reflections in a bright room / pink tint
This just hasn't been an issue for me at all. If anything, the situation is better than my old monitor. However, I am usually in a dark room, and the monitor is facing away from the window. Plus, I have dark curtains.

Other easily solvable issues:

- 110 vs 240 volts (power input)
I ordered the monitor from Amazon US, but I live in the UK. Luckily, I had no problems with the mains voltage difference. As stated in the manual, the monitor supports both kinds. I used a UK power cable from another monitor, and that was it.

- The sockets at the back are placed too low, for some reason. I have the monitor on a flexible arm, and I need it to be almost at desk level (long story). That problem was easily solved with angled adaptors, like https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B00T2TP7VM and https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B0BGJ96WHY.

- I used to use VLC as a video player for most things. It seems the current public version has a bug with the rendering of the subtitles in HDR. I now recommend switching to MPC-BE. It seems better in a lot of ways, so far.

Speaking of VLC or MPC-BE, they both play back my own HDR videos beautifully. Both those from my phone (with HDR on) and my camera (HLG mode). Even my photos from my phone look much more pleasing on this monitor.

It's not all positives though. The risk of burn-in is still something to be taken seriously, by all accounts. My experience so far with MSI OLED Care 2.0, and Panel Protect specifically, has been mixed. On the one hand, I got the first popup after 4 hours, and I easily dismissed it with a click of the mouse (via the Gaming Intelligence app). For a few days, I didn't hear from it again, and I even wondered if it's working at all. Of course, even though I switch all my devices off at night, I make sure not to switch this monitor off at all. I can confirm via the monitor's built-in menu (not sure why the Intelligence app doesn't show this) that Panel Protect has been running, seemingly once a day. Great, I thought.

However, I work from home, and sometimes that means the monitor is on for 8 hours for work, and 8 more for my own entertainment in the evening. That's 16 hours, which is the maximum you can go without running Panel Protect. Two nights in a row, it interrupted me during a film :(. That was NOT a great experience. It takes about 6-8 mins, and you can do nothing while it's running. If it ever happens in the middle of some multiplayer game, I'll be extremely annoyed! So, I have started building a habit of manually running it at the start of my lunch breaks, while I prepare food or whatever. That seems like a good compromise. I wish they had a setting to force the protection at 24 hours, or even 18. 16 is just at the limit for me, sadly. (EDIT: see below)

Having said all that, I was thoroughly warned about the issues with burn-in, from all the online reviews, and I expected to face these problems. It is just a limitation of the technology, and we just need to accept it really. If this is the only problem I will ever face, I'll be very happy, considering the amazing picture quality I get.

One related thing that worried me before I bought the monitor was all the Chrome tabs I tend to keep open, usually for months. I even have pinned tabs that are permanently there. Everything else was solvable, with things like hiding the Windows taskbar, switching to dark mode for everything, ensuring the screensaver is active, setting Windows to go to sleep after a bit, etc. There was no solution for the Chrome tabs though. In the end, I did some research, and found that Vivaldi (a Chrome-based browser, therefore easy to switch to it) supports customisation of its window. Some kind person on their forums wrote a script that will auto-hide the tab bar in Vivaldi, much like Windows can auto-hide its taskbar. Search for "AutoHide Tab Bar + Address Bar | Show on Hover". It's not perfect, and you have to keep reinstalling it every week, when Vivaldi updates itself, but it solves the problem.

I don't know how the problem of burn-in will play out in the long term. I will try to remember to update this review, if I ever notice this problem (or any others). Meanwhile, I take comfort from people's burn-in experiments, eg on youtube.

Another issue I noticed, which I was also warned about, is VRR flicker. At least I think that's what it is. I've not noticed it in games so far, only in Windows. I have the monitor set to 120 Hz for every day use, and I use the Windows 11 setting called Dynamic Refresh Rate (Settings > Display > Advanced display). With that, whenever Windows is idling, the refresh rate drops to 60 Hz, which is great in theory. However, with the slightest mouse movement or screen scrolling, the refresh rate instantly switches to 120 for a bit. I think that results in noticeably increased smoothness, but it also seems to cause this almost imperceptible flicker, sometimes. It's only really noticeable in dark or gray backgrounds. Once you notice it, it's hard to unsee, unfortunately. Well, there are easy solutions: stick with either 120 Hz at all times, or 60 Hz (and only switch up for games), or ignore it. I haven't decided yet. Hopefully it will be as easily solvable in games, if I ever experience it.

Overall, I'm assigning 4 stars to this monitor, easily. I'm subtracting one mostly for the amount of effort I had to go through to solve the issue with the Chrome tabs. I'm glad there is a solution to that though, and I can now easily recommend this monitor to most people.

UPDATE (4 months later):
- There is now a firmware update that raises the forced OLED Care period to 24h, which is ideal I would say. Phew. I still have to worry about turning my PC off for just a bit, in case I'll come back to it 5 mins later and the monitor will have started the panel refresh thing in the middle of the day. Overall though, it is now something I just don't worry about anymore. It will never interrupt me again the middle of a film or game. Thanks for listening, MSI!
- No signs of burn in so far. Not that I've gone looking, but it's hopefully way too early to worry about this.
- I've had a stuck pixel, 3 weeks in... :( I decided to return the monitor and get a replacement, and so far, it hasn't happened again. Here's hoping it will stay that way.
- I've switched to 60Hz permanently, while in Windows. No flickering this way. I have a script that I use to launch my games, which turns the refresh rate to 120Hz, and then automatically back to 60Hz after I exited the game. Problem solved.
- I've switched to Peak 1000 mode, for now. I go back and forth on whether this is better and more accurate... On the one hand, HDR-aware apps that query the monitor's capabilities (eg MPC-BE), always seem to think that the monitor can do 1000 nits, and so they adjust their output accordingly, not knowing that the monitor is set to 400 nits (True Black 400). This results in over-bright highlights, ie lost detail. It was obvious with my camera's HLG videos. Peak 1000 solves this issue, and maybe it also improves things in games and films, not that I had noticed problems there. Unfortunately, Peak 1000 does not result in a consistent output... The monitor CONSTANTLY adjusts its output, presumably because it can't maintain true 1000 nits for very long (even if it's only advertised for 10% of the screen). This results in a very obvious "pulsing" of the overall brightness, which is fast enough to ruin the experience. This pulsing happened once as I was writing this update to my review, even though there was no obvious reason for it. Normally, you can tell it happens because of switching from a dark to a bright web page, for example, which I still find distracting. I miss the stability and consistency/uniformity of True Black 400... I may go back to it, and just try to remember to switch to Peak 1000 when I watch content or play games. If only there was a command line tool that could automate the switch... Man, first world problems are the worst ;)

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This thing is such a steal at $98. Although it is now $104 as of the making of this review. But still, for that price this monitor is a steal.

First, the size is 27 inches. An IPS panel this size at this price is great.

Second, the picture quality is great. Of course it's no OLED or QLED but for an IPS panel, this thing rocks. The color accuracy is on par with most IPS panel at higher price out of the box. But you can easily tweak these settings to get the best color accuracy out of this monitor. But then again, you can just turn on HDR and Auto HDR on Windows 11 to get the best possible color profile for this monitor, being it is HDR capable.

Third, it has adaptive sync with 144hz refresh rate and 1ms MPRT. So if you like gaming like I do, this monitor will definitely do the job. It actually punches above it's weight. I have the response time to normal setting in this monitor and I experience no noticeable lag when playing online FPS games even with MPRT is off. There's no noticeable ghosting either. Just absolute smooth gameplay. I also use this for video editing and music production and it has been great on both as well.

But one of the biggest reason why I purchased this monitor was the features it has for eye care. I needed a monitor that will help my eyes be less strained on pro long use of the PC. This monitor has Anti Flicker and is TuvRheinland Certified, which many monitors at this price point does not have.

Overall, the functionality and performance of this monitor definitely makes this monitor a steal at this price. Seems durable enough, not that you're going to punch this after rage quitting an online match but it definitely doesn't feel cheap and on par with most gaming monitors at around and above this price point. You can also VESA mount it if you don't like the plastic, but durable, stand.

For reference, I use this as an external monitor on my 2022 Razer Blade 15. I don't know why I waited this long to buy an external monitor for gaming, video editing and music production. But I'm glad I found this gem. Grab one before the manufacturer realize that this monitor should be more expensive and raise the price.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought this monitor because I wanted to add an OLED display to my computer setup, but I always had an issue with the burn in issues and not really wanting a 4K monitor because that used to be the only way to get one. Now the technology has come a long way, and I am glad to see a lot more 1440p options.

With this model you get the AI features that detect when you are at your desk and will wake-on-approach and lock-on-leave (these have to be enabled). It also has auto-dimming features to protect the panel further from static things like taskbars and logos to even further minimize the risk of image burn in. There are many more AI features to enable that I don't really have a use for at this time, but I could see how they could be useful to some people.

This model also has DisplayHDR True Black 500 certification to give it better blacks and vibrant lifelike colors; I really like the Premium color setting as it looks good and makes colors pop a little more (this is subjective and definitely something you can change to your preference).

I personally don't need the 500hz refresh rate as I don't care to go above 144hz in most games, but I like that I have the option and can set it to 360hz so that I have the extra head room if I do end up needing it with the RTX5080. It also has .03ms of grey-to-grey response time which helps with motion blur and ghosting, I personally don't have a use for it, but I am always down for faster response times even if I don't play competitive games.

All in all, a good well-rounded monitor with a lot of features including some AI features that are useful to protect the monitor. Looking forward to using this monitor for a long period of time and testing if this will prevent issues with burn-in and I won't need to use the 3-year burn-in warranty.

(One thing to point out it doesn't say it supports G-sync in the monitor title or the main description but if you scroll down to the manufacturer information it has it in one of the slides)

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Finally. 500Hz, DP 2.1 (UHBR20), OLED, 27-inch, which GSYNC support. Coming from a 1440p 144Hz IPS panel this OLED is quite an updrade. I have been waiting for a DP 2.1 (UHBR20) monitor that can run 480+Hz at 1440p with no Display Stream Compression (DSC). This means you can use DSR/DLDSR to downscale while still running a full 500Hz. I have been testing some of my favorite games with this monitor, and being able to run Half-Life 2 at 5K (DSR 4x) and 500Hz at 500fps with OLED colors is pretty amazing (running on a PNY RTX5080).

When I first got the monitor, I could not get 500Hz to 'stick', it kept reverting to 480Hz. Updating the firmware to .020 fixed that issue (monitor came with firmware .015).

Ensure you have a DP2.1 UHBR20 cable or else you will run into issues like not having resolutions/refresh rates show up as selections, or black screens. I am running this one (Stouchi 80Gbps DisplayPort 2.1 Cable [10FT/3M], UHBR20) and I was initially concerned that a 3M cable would be too long and have signal issues but it has been working great so far.

This is likely my endgame monitor for some time. Worth the wait and the money. I had been waiting to get either this or Gigabytes 500Hz OLED offering, but this MSI one was availalbe first.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I was on the fence about purchasing this monitor for a little over 2 months. If you're looking to upgrade to OLED from an IPS, this monitor is a fantastic choice.

To sort a little confusion between the models, there is a URX123 and a UPX123, I purchased the UPX (cheaper) model.

The only main differences that I can see are the LED backlights (which add ambient lighting behind the monitor) and additional USB-C and USB-A ports. Otherwise these models are identical spec wise and I believe that the UPX model may actually have lower power consumption.

Contrary to what I read in the comments, MSI DOES allow this monitor to be firmware updated now. Most of the stock has been updated to the most current version of the firmware and mine did not need to be flashed to the new version and was fully updated upon receipt.

The panel itself is easy enough to setup. If you're new to this, make sure you enable adaptive sync to get the full refresh rate active at 4k.

My one and only complaint with this monitor is when using the VRR on some games with locked refresh rates, I have experienced some flickering with VRR on and had to turn it off to make it stop happening.

I would also recommend a locking DP cable if you have articulating monitor arms, the port appears to be a little sensitive to the cable moving at all. The locking DP cable solved this issue for me.

The monitor is plenty bright, HDR is fantastic and the colors pop. This monitor is awesome.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This monitor offers great value: It's a good bang for the buck. If money isn't an issue and you require the very best picture quality for gaming, then you probably should look at a much pricier OLEDs.

This monitor has somewhat good colors, and the picture quality can be nice and crisp. The monitor isn't well configured out of the box. You have to play with the toggle switch to get the advertised feature set. In order to get 160hz you have to turn on DisplayPort overclocking on the monitor in the toggle switch menu. I couldn't get 160hz to work with HDMI 2.1. it only works with DP 2.1. To get the full 160hz, windows display settings and nvidia control panel have to have the same refresh rate settings, along with DP overclocking on the monitor. If these aren't set properly, the screen may flicker off and on and show black screens.

The display has flat colors out of the box so you must also play with the toggle switch to change the color settings. I like the "warm" preset. Adaptive sync/FreeSync also has to be turned on via toggle switch menu in order to remove screen tearing in gameplay.

I have this monitor hookedup to a 5070 ti gpu and it runs games very well at 4k max settings. However, with some fast-paced games, the monitor produces grainy, muddy images with max-out graphic settings. To fix this issue, you have to play with the toggle switch settings and set "response time" to "fastest." The "fastest" setting makes the image quality clean and clear during fast paced action. This setting is only useful with very high graphic settings. It may overshoot or cause arti-facting with lower graphics settings.

Bottom line is that this can be a really good monitor for the price, but you have to play with the toggle switch settings to get the full feature set. there are other more pricier models that a lot easier to use.

text:
I just purchased the MSI MAG 321 UP after a few weeks of research, and I have to say, it has been an outstanding addition to my setup. If I had to pick one favorite aspect, it would definitely be the OLED display itself. The color accuracy, contrast ratios, and deep blacks are simply stunning. As a result, my experience with both productivity tasks and entertainment has become much more immersive. I spend my evenings using the monitor in darkness, and the visual experience is like nothing I’ve had before.

I chose this monitor over a Samsung G5, an LG 27 Ultragear OLED primarily because I wanted OLED + 4K resolution. I wanted something that had high resolution, high ppi, excellent black levels and also high end color reproduction. HDR support is an extra bonus, which makes the balance between dark and light video areas really special. So far it's the ideal choice for me, and it definitely lives up to my expectations. Additionally, the fact that MSI offers a large 32-inch screen at such a high resolution was a key factor in my decision.

This monitor fulfils all the visual needs plus the price of MSI 321UP is extremely competitive. I wanted the buit in KVM switch but for the difference in price from 321UPX I can live without. I have connected my Steam Deck via USB C Alt, PS5 and laptop via HDMI and will eventually connect my next PC build via Display Port. So far it handles all these inputs with ease. 165 HZ is more than enough for me for the gaming I do on these devices, especially in 4K.

The price to enter is still high, but versus the comparable IPS, VA and MiniLED options out there I think it's OLED or bust. I have a miniLED and FALD TV and they do not come close to matching the experience on this monitor. So I'm definitely a happy owner. I find myself enjoying content more than I ever did on my other screens.

There are a bunch of OLED burn in mitigation technologies here and honestly I don't worry about burn-in all that much. I've owned Plasmas in the past and concerns were overblown then as they are now. Plus MSI has a strong warranty which also covers burn in.

I am extremely satisfied with my purchase and I would highly recommend people go a bit over the regular monitor budget to obtain this a top-tier display for work/entertainment/gaming mix.

NOTE: This is a 24-hour review. I will update it within the next 6 months to reflect whether my experience remains positive, neutral, or becomes negative. I am not sponsored, nor was this item given to me for free; I paid for it with my own money.

The monitor is gorgeous straight out of the box. It's spacious and a big upgrade for anyone coming from a 21- or 22-inch screen. I can confidently say that this particular monitor will be an improvement in terms of size and visual impact. However, I’m giving it a 3 out of 5 instead of a perfect score, and here’s why:

While the monitor offers a lot of features, the placement of the ports is awkward. Instead of being directly accessible on the back like a traditional monitor, the ports are hidden, which makes connecting cables unnecessarily frustrating. I assume this design is meant for users who want to push the monitor close to the wall without damaging the cables, but it comes at the cost of convenience.

After turning the monitor on and fiddling with settings, switching between the GPU control panel and the monitor’s menu, I have to say I’m a bit disappointed. Here's why:

Even though the picture quality is sharp, the monitor has a noticeable yellow tint. If you're someone who prefers using your computer in a dark room, this yellowish cast is especially obvious. I spent a long time adjusting the settings, trying to eliminate it, but doing so made the display overly bright and uncomfortable to look at. Reducing the brightness helped, but then the colors became distorted. I read through forums, watched videos and shorts, and dug through reviews looking for a solution, but so far, no luck. Maybe I misunderstood what this monitor was offering, but it honestly feels more like a VA panel than an IPS one.

Ironically, my old HP Pavilion 22xi 21.5-inch IPS monitor was much easier on the eyes. The colors were beautiful, even if slightly washed out, and I never had to deal with this kind of eye strain.

If I had the option to return this monitor, I probably would, but I’ll keep it to avoid the hassle. Most buyers feel the same way when it comes to expensive electronics: once you buy them online, you’re stuck. If there were an option for a partial refund, I’d gladly take it. That way, both sides would come out ahead. But as it stands, I’m stuck with it.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a beautiful monitor with vibrant colors. But the yellow tint and excessive brightness have significantly hurt my overall satisfaction. When I bought it, there were no reviews available, so I took a gamble. Lesson learned: Never buy a product without hundreds of reviews.

That said, my negative experience comes from someone who primarily uses a computer in the dark. If you tend to play or work with the lights on, your experience may be entirely different.

text:
Great monitor for general productivity use. Colors are sharp. Text is clear. The vast amount of display area is amazing. The curve seems just right: the whole screen stays clear at normal working distance.

Many 3440x1440 (UWQHD) monitors are available. I chose this one in part because it is a good value, but also for the adjustable stand. The stand is a triangle with widely spread legs: it is very sturdy. I've used large monitors with tiny stands and they tend to bounce around. The stand is fully adjustable: I was able to get the height and tilt exactly right -- without using packs of printer paper as for other monitors.

The 3440x1440 resolution and 34" size is the sweet spot for everyday, boring text-based apps such as text editors, IDEs, the command line and so on. I use Linux Mint which is a great Linux distro. However, support for high resolution monitors is limited. I tried using a 27" 4K monitor. While that monitor worked great with a Mac, Linux Mint just can't use it correctly. Scaling is either normal (text far too small) or 2x, which makes text blocky and provides no more space than the 1080p monitor.

So, a better solution is this monitor. The larger size, coupled with greater resolution, gives about the same dot pitch as the 1080p monitor, so no need to mess with scaling. Text is clear at normal scaling, if just a bit smaller than with the old monitor. To see how this will work for you, measure your old monitor's height and divide by 1080. Compare that to the specs of your new choice. Confusingly, some specs list dpi (dots-per-inch), some list "ipd" (inches per dot). One is just the inverse of the other.

I've not used newer OLED monitors, so I can't compare colors with one of those. On the other hand, unless you are watching movies or playing games, it hardly matters. On this monitor, web pages are amazingly crisp. There is more space for my development tools. PDFs now display full page large enough to read without having to zoom in and scroll each page. There is plenty of space to display two apps side-by-side to minimize Alt-Tab window switching. Display technology has come a long way: this monitor is amazing when compared with the five-yer-old one it replaces.

The monitor is rated at 144Hz refresh. My poor old hardware delivers only 50Hz at this resolution. Perhaps it would be higher if I used display port rather than HDMI. This seems to not be a problem for development work: I can't type that fast anyway. Videos seem fine. Perhaps the higher refresh rates are most important for gamers.

In short, this is a cost-effective upgrade for work use when coming from an old-school 1080p monitor. I'm very pleased so far. Just make sure your graphics can handle the resolution.

I have only had the monitor for one day so this review will reflect that. I plan on updating this review in a month or so after some decent time has been put on it.

Firstly, this is my first monitor upgrade in nearly ten years since I purchased dual Dell 22" P2211ht monitors-- and it's astounding to see first hand, not just on YouTube reviews, just how far diplays have come in that time even on the low end of spectrum. The wow factor here is 10/10.

34" of screen space is much more impressive when it is on your desk. I have a sizeable desk, and I'm now looking at side tables to put my full tower PC on. At the same time though, not having to swing my 22" forward on the vesa arm it was mounted on is saving valuable real estate and now it's not as cramped feeling when I have my hotas or wheel out for sim racing/flight sims.

I was concerned about the curvature coming from a flat panel but it's actually very nice, feels natural and took less than an hour for it to feel like the new normal. Zero dead pixels on the display from what I can tell, no manufacturing defects-- a big relief after seeing some other reviews complain of those things.

Ghosting/smearing is not really noticeable in my use case (sim racing) but is present. I got used to it pretty quickly and it doesn't bother me. Once I'm in game I don't notice it. I don't notice any blacklight bleed but I don't play in pitch darkness, either. Other games can produce more noticeable effects.

The color needed some adjusting. The OSD is functional and I had no issues adjusting contrast and brightness to tone down the oversaturation that was present out of the box. It does seem a bit washed out but still looks nice. I don't have a real need for HDR so I can't comment on that yet. The display is plenty bright, brighter than my old monitors.

USB ports would be nice but this isn't a dealbreaker, my PC has plenty for my needs. Wish the RGB worked with mystic light or was at least adjustable since I don't really care for rainbow RGB.

As far as build quality, it doesn't seem terrible but isn't premium. The stand is sturdy and while the plastic gives off flimsy vibes I was adjusting tilt and height just fine without anything other than plastic-y creaks and pops that seem slightly more pronounced than my previous Dells.

I have a GTX 1070 (thanks, cryptominers!) so not too many games I play can make full use of the refresh rate but the ones that I could push there felt great. Very fluid and smooth.

All in all, first impressions are very positive. A pretty big leap in technology for myself and I feel the price is fair. I can easily recommend it at the sub $500 price point and have zero regrets so far.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Upgraded my computer this year and got an OLED for AAA gaming. Wanted to buy a secondary LCD for productivity work and some light gaming. Was looking for something with a decent HDR performance as well as an accurate and wide color gamut. First got a KTC mini LED but the quality of that monitor was so bad I had to return the day I got it. The white balance of the KTC was way off on HDR, the local dimming algorithm was terrible, the view angle was so bad that if you look at the center of the screen 3ft away the edges would be a silvery mess, and worst of all, you can see each individual backlights which made the monitor look like something from the 2000s. It was so bad it scared me quite a bit, until I heard sources saying KTC pay their reviewers to get positive reviews. So I decided to give mini LED another chance and bought this monitor which got quite high praise from a more reputable reviewer.

And I was indeed not disappointed. The HDR performance is great. Local dimming level 3 gives you a close to OLED HDR look while keeping it at level 2 is surprisingly great even on regular productivity tasks, both KTC failed to deliver. The viewing angle is great, the response boost is great and did not cause any artifacts on texts like some cheaper monitors did. The factory calibration was very accurate and I did not had to change a thing in my own calibration. And most of all, you don’t perceive the backlights as singular pixelated mess. Over all I’m very happy about the monitor and think it worths the (discounted) price. (If it’s full price please just buy the mpg version instead of mag. Same panel just more features).

The only a couple downsides I observed - although neither severe enough to make me less like the monitor. First there is a vignette effect on the edges of the screen. Level brightness setting improved it but didn’t completely eliminate it. Second, there is still visible blooming on darker scenes with smaller bright objects. Both are very tolerable however and are well within the limitation of the technology.

Also to set the expectations straight - it is just not gonna be as good as OLED. Contrast is never going to be as sharp as OLED even though it’s like 3 times brighter. Color is not really going to be as realistic either. But I’d say it’s 80% there with only about 60% of the price of a comparable OLED. So it’s great as a secondary monitor if you have an OLED, or if your budget is limited.

Attached pic 1 is a comparison between my OLED (left) and the e16m (right). Color difference is an artifact of phone camera and the gamut difference in the panels. But the relative brightness level between the 2 monitors are surprisingly similar, demonstrating the good local dimming algorithm e16m has.

Pic 2 demonstrates a scene with high contrast and e16m is very capable rendering it.

Pic 3 shows the blooming effect on the e16m (right) compared to OLED (left). It is visible but not as bothersome. You can use this to make an educated decision.

text:
Positives are mostly as advertised.

There aren't many reviews for this particular model, but MSI sells another monitor with the same display panel - the MPG 274URDFW E16M - so the performance results should be similar; this monitor (MAG 274UPDF E16M) just has slightly fewer features than that more expensive model, i.e., no USB hub, no RGB on the back, etc.

Pixel response is fast and clean enough that you likely won't have issues unless you're extremely sensitive to issues like this.

Out of the box, the SDR color is oversaturated (which is not unexpected for a wide gamut HDR monitor displaying SDR content), however, switching to the sRGB preset returns the image to a more natural presentation.

HDR brightness was slightly overtuned, making each backlight LED bright enough to bleed through, however, running a basic Windows HDR calibration tool eliminated this.

Edit: The big thing to note is, this *IS* still a Mini-LED. Dark scenes noticeably more detailed than a similar IPS display without FALD, however, in scenes that are dark, but not completely black, there is some still noticeable glow from light leaking out from behind the LCD layer, which wouldn't happen with an OLED. The strength of Mini-LED is in scenes that can take advantage of the full screen brightness miniLED can offer./Edit.

MSI's default local dimming logic prioritizes minimizing blooming instead of brightness at the cost of making small bright spots less bright, however, there is a setting in the OSD that allowed you to manually tune the logic to your preference. For pure media consumption, a VA Mini-LED will provide better contrast, at the cost of worse motion clarity. An OLED will provide better contrast and motion clarity at the cost of lower full screen brightness and burn in risk.

While I don't have a proper calibration tool, color calibration out of the box looked good; I didn't feel like I needed to make any adjustments.

My only real issue is that after years of using a curved monitor, this monitor looks like it's bent backwards, and that'll take a few days to get used to.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I really wanted to love this monitor without reservations - and in many ways, I do. The setup was painless, the build quality feels good, and the dual-device support is genuinely useful. Once it's powered on, the panel is a joy to look at: sharp, vibrant, and impressively accurate in DCI-P3/Display P3 mode. Motion is buttery smooth at 144Hz, and everyday use is fantastic.

But here's the part that left me disappointed: despite being advertised as a 4K 160Hz display, this monitor simply cannot reach 160Hz under any real-world scenario. The ports it ships with - DisplayPort 1.4a, HDMI 2.1, and USB-C DP Alt - none of which can provide enough bandwidth to drive 4K at 160Hz. The panel itself may be capable of that refresh rate, but the actual inputs make it impossible to achieve. The best you can get is 4K/144Hz, which is stilll great, but not what's advertised. If you're happy with 4K/144Hz - and honestly, it looks fantastic - this is a wonderful monitor with excellent color performance and smooth motion. Just don't expect to ever see 160Hz, because it's not going to happen with the ports MSI chose to include.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Coming from a QHD 27in OLED monitor as my main display for a 90/10 split of programming and gaming, this monitor has been an amazing upgrade in terms of text clarity, higher SDR brightness, and peace of mind due to no burn-in risk. As of this review, I am on the latest firmware version .026.

As for QC, I wanted to give my experience, and thankfully I got a good unit. I did multiple thorough scans using the eizo.be monitor test. My unit falls in line with ISO 9241-307 class 1 standard, as it has one malfunctioned sub-pixel at the top-left corner edge (can't display blue), and a single dead pixel near the bottom edge of the display. Neither of these are noticeable from reasonable usage (especially as they're at the edges and I use my monitors around 1.5 feet away), and achieves the strict ISO class 1 standard of reasonable defective pixels. That is much better than class 2 or class 3. It isn't class 0, but that is not something usually expected from a consumer-class display, particularly at this price point.

The text clarity for programming and other productivity tasks is amazing, and a massive upgrade from my 1440p 27in monitor. And, it's not just due to OLED's non-standard sub pixel layout in my previous monitor. It's a huge improvement from my secondary 1440p 27in IPS monitor too.

SDR brightness is a large improvement over my OLED monitor. Due to fear of burn-in from all the static desktop apps I use, I always kept my OLED at around 50% brightness. The E16M is already brighter than that at 50%, and I can freely set it much higher when there's more ambient light.

HDR performance is decent for my gaming needs, with level 3 Local Dimming enabled. I will admit, it is nowhere near as impressive as my previous OLED monitor. Sure, large parts of the display can get very bright. But the smaller highlights feel a bit dead, being significantly darker than my OLED. And, it can't beat OLED's perfect black level. But, it's still good enough for most cases and looks great for the most part. There isn't much blooming either, unless you view from the sides.

The KVM works well too, with the USB-C connection being really convenient to charge my laptop, use the monitor's USB-A ports, and display all through a single cable.

I also tested the 1080p dual-mode, and it is incredibly ugly. I only use it for one game where looks don't matter, to get access to 320Hz. Besides that, I never use it.

Overall, I would say I am satisfied with the product I got. It is unfortunate that many other people are getting unlucky with QC, but I would say mine is one of the better ones. For the price, it is decent for what you're getting.

Well for starter I have purchased 3 of those for duel monitor setup with intention of 80% productivity and 20% gaming in mind. why 3 ? because the first one came broken and it never tuned on.

I did go for them as they have mini led screen with good HDR picture decent motion handling and KVM option as I am switching constantly between my desktop and my laptop.
but once I started using them I found a few issues that made me return both of them and now I am waiting for my refund.

The good:
Build quality is great and it's looks awesome.
The 4k HDR is really impressive to my eyes, it gets bright like very bright, playing games where you have snow made me want to put my sunglasses like in the real world.. that bright.
the blacks are quite deep and I have not seen major blooming issues but it did lower the brightness of small items in dark rooms where it distorted the colors quite a bit, but for me it was fine.
The menu of the monitors is simple to use and the joystick is a joy compared to others I had.

The bad:
This monitors supposedly have KVM hub...
on paper it does but it does not work at all, the usb b and dp connection to my desktop worked fine, but the other connection the usb-c simply cannot hold the data it should pass, every 3-5 minutes it would disconnect from my laptop and require to reconnect it, for me to be able to work IU had to return to my usb-c hub and use them at 60hz refresh rate without HDR capabilities.. another thing the audio drivers are horrible, if you connect the speakers you will loose about 70% of the volume.
SDR image, this is a big one... the colors no matter how much I've tried (did not use colorimeter) could not remove the reddish tint, the colors are absolute crap, it has made up certificate claiming de < 2 SRGB but, no way it had horrible colors maybe because of poor gamma I don't know but it was a pain as everything looked reddish, even when I had video call people were telling me my face looks like a tomato because of the screen radiating so much red light.
Panel uniformity, I think it's an mini led issue but if you do intend to purchase this monitor for work related purpose, don't.
When you sit and watch static screen as I do doing my job you will start notice that the supposedly white screen looks like cloud and it hurts, my eyes got sore after just 3 hours of work, I thinks it the mini led itself as the zones failing to produce exact lumen count on each zone but that's just a theory, anyway it's annoying once you notice it.

If you intend to use the screen for it's KVM don't it's just not working, if you intend to work on them or do anything color related, unless you do professional calibration they are bad for it.
IK would say they are not worth it unless you want extremely bright
HDR experience with the games you play, otherwise for that price I would go for Oled monitor.

text:
9 month update: Shopping for a second monitor, so KTC is first on my list. I’ve had this UHD 160HZ monitor for 9 months and it’s still perfect after daily contact use. The clarity on this thing is so crispy. I’m a data engineer and spend hours on end viewing tabular data. My eyes are happy.

———- original review ———
I wanted a 4K high refresh monitor. I chose the KTC H27P22S, or the UHD 160hz, non-mini-led version. I have a MacBook Pro with a mini led display, and it’s amazing. It has over 2,554 local dimming zones. I love the tech, but am not sold that 526 zones offered on current 4K 27” monitors is enough when there’s 5x that on a screen with less than half the size.

I wasn’t sure what to expect, since the price was much lower than well-known brands. Did my research and KTC started in 1994 and has been making OEM monitors for the name brands. They only recently started selling direct. So I took a chance.

The reason the price is so low isn’t a reflection of quality, because the monitor is absolutely gorgeous playing Control at 4K with ray tracing and DLSS Quality mode enabled.

It even brought new life to surfing the web.

I’m coming from a Samsung CRG9, a 49” QHD monitor. Got it months before COVID hit and have been using it to work remotely since. The move to 4K for productivity work alone makes me very satisfied with my purchase. Both have high refresh rates.

60hz is perfect for a second/third monitor, but for your main? Once you experience 120hz+, it’s hard to go back.

High quality monitor. Excellent picture quality out of the box, which I wasn’t anticipating, and well thought out packaging.

Hands-down, I have no regrets. My guess is the price is so low because they’re sacrificing profit for glowing reviews like this. Get one before they inevitably earn a strong reputation and raise their prices to the inflated rates name brands can charge.

It’s day one, so if anything bad happens I’ll update. There’s few reviews for this “lower-end” monitor. I’ll do my part to keep it transparent.
