title: 3.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Before, I had used a portable monitor from Acer that was hardmodded to have an HDMI port instead of USB-C. Since I’ll be traveling for college soon, I needed a monitor that wasn’t modified as it’ll have a far better chance of clearing airport security. This one was cheap and appeared to offer a lot of features. It appears that this monitor is an upgraded version of the previous Optix MAG161V model also from MSI.

The case that the monitor comes in appears very high quality and is made of leather. The case and the monitor itself both feel very tough and feels like they could take a beating without breaking.

This monitor’s screen is brighter than MSI’s older portable monitor and can get up to 250 nits of brightness according to the specs (180 nits before). That’s enough brightness for any indoor setting, but it’s barely visible in an outdoor setting. The brightness can be adjusted in the settings menu and turning off echo mode (on by default) will also increase the brightness a bit.

The colors on the screen are average. MSI had advertised the display with consisting of 6-bit colors, but Windows on my laptop had identified the display being able to support 8-bit colors. I don’t have the proper benchmark hardware to confirm for sure but just by looking at the monitor, and comparing it to the colors of other monitors, it appears that it is in 8-bit colors with about 80-90% of sRGB color space. The contrast ratio is alright, but not really anything special. MSI advertises the contrast ratio of this monitor at 1000:1 (700:1 on the older version).

The speakers on the monitor are alright. They aren’t really bad but they also aren’t really good.

The monitor also comes with all necessary cables for configuration (1x Mini HDMI to Regular HDMI, 1x USB-C to USB-C, and 1x USB-C to USB-A). All cables look about 3.5-4ft in length which is just enough for connecting to peripherals on either side of a (at most, a 15.6”) laptop.

The biggest problem I have with this monitor is that there is a noticeable screen bleed in the upper left corner (see pics). It’s not so bad to where I have to return it, because it’s only visible when displaying dark colored content, but it shouldn’t be something that I have to experience.

As for the so-called “gaming mode” and “night vision,” both are overrated features. Changing the modes just change the contrast and/or gamma and nothing more, which just makes the colors more washed out. Just stick to the default modes for both.

La qualité d’image est très bonne. La dalle VA offre un beau contraste et les couleurs ressortent vraiment bien grâce à la couverture sRGB élevée. Pour regarder des vidéos, travailler sur des documents ou même faire un peu de retouche, c’est largement suffisant. Le 100Hz apporte une fluidité appréciable, même pour quelqu’un qui n’est pas gamer.

Le mode “confort oculaire” est très utile quand on passe de longues heures devant l’écran. Il réduit la fatigue visuelle et je sens vraiment la différence en fin de journée. J’apprécie aussi le fait qu’il y ait des haut-parleurs intégrés — ce ne sont pas les meilleurs du monde, mais pour de la bureautique ou des appels, ça fait largement l’affaire.

S’il fallait relever un point un peu moins bon : le pied ne permet que l’inclinaison, pas la hauteur. Ça ne m’a pas dérangé parce que je l’ai mis sur un support, mais ça peut compter pour certains. J’aurais aussi aimé un peu plus de luminosité en HDR, même si c’est déjà correct pour cette gamme.

Globalement, c’est un excellent écran pour le travail et le confort quotidien. Grand, immersif, très agréable à utiliser. Je ne regrette pas une seconde mon achat.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Was shopping online with my son for his first gaming PC (which we decided upon an AMD Ryzen 5 3600 CPU with Nvidia RTX 2060 Super GPU model) and I quickly realized handing him down my old Samsung 27" 1080p 60hz LCD monitor as was the original plan would have been a total waste of his new computer!

So having saved a couple hundred bucks buying a pre-built instead of building our own with the same specs (as PC components are experiencing shortages cause of COVID-19 and have gone up drastically in price), I told my son he could pick out any monitor on Amazon he wanted on a budget of $300, and he picked out this one.

I could instantly see why he chose this model which at 30" was bigger than most other gaming monitors with decent specs at this price range and it was an ultrawide, which made me proud (like him being a chip off the old block) as I game on a 49" super ultrawide monitor myself. But the real "wow factor" of this model, of course, is the 200hz refresh rate which is a rarity in itself especially for ultrawides but almost unheard of at this price range.

The only thing I wasn't sure about was I wasn't familiar with the Sceptre brand. Generally as a rule I've stayed away from buying displays from lesser-known manufacturers as with panels you often get what you pay for and "cheap" usually turns out more "expensive" in the long run, if not just "frustrating" and "disappointing".

But this was my son's computer and his pick for the monitor and I was proud that he did all his own research so I wanted to support him. So Sceptre it was!

Well I'm glad I didn't say anything cause this monitor rocks! The colors looked great straight out of the box and I haven't felt the need to do any calibration of any sort. Contrast and blacks are above average on this display and well beyond my expectations for a sub-$300 model. Even though there's no HDR and I believe it's rated at just 250 nits, it looks much brighter than that, possibly because of its high native contrast.

But what both my son and I were most looking forward to see, of course, was how it performed at 200hz. So I fired up 3DMark and ran a few benchmark tests and...WOW!

The motion on all frame rates was buttery smooth. On some tests we were reaching fps of over 600 so we knew we hit the monitor's 200 frames per second limit and it looked incredible! No tearing or ghosting or any sign of distortion whatsoever. My own 49" super ultrawide only goes up to 144hz and I could see a discernible difference in frame rate running identical tests on our PCs both of which were pushing frames well beyond the limits of our monitors. This monitor's 200hz refresh rate is legit!

Another great feature of this monitor is its support of AMD Freesync. It worked flawlessly with my son's RTX 2060 Super both in fullscreen and windowed mode, even though the Nvidia Control Panel said the monitor wasn't "validated as G-SYNC Compatible". I've actually had problems in the past getting this compatibility feature to work on other Freesync monitors so was really relieved to find it working perfectly on the Sceptre.

Overall this is a fantastic gaming monitor that performs well in all its highlighted and advertised features, and phenomenally when you also factor in its price. Highly recommended and most importantly for me is my son couldn't be happier!

Mine was defaulted at 1920 x 1080p (this setting did not utilize the full 30" screen) So I went to the Search box, down by the start button, and I typed NVIDIA control panel. Then, under display, I clicked on: Change Resolution and chose 2560 x 1080 (native). It stretched the screen out to the actual full screen.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text: This review is for the ViewSonic VA2246MH LED 22 inch monitor and I use this as a second monitor with an I-Mac. I wanted a monitor that is roughly the same size as the I-Mac’s screen to maintain visual uniformity. The monitor sits lower than most others, the distance from the monitor bottom to the desk is 2 inches and the lighted screen bottom is 3 1/8 inches from the desk surface. I have mine sitting on a FITUEYES clear monitor riser and this brings the I-Mac and ViewSonic screens to almost perfect matching heights. Overall, I’m pleased with the monitor, especially for this price range, so with price and functionally in mind I give this 5 stars. So now the negative stuff. To get a proper looking picture you have to be looking straight into the monitor, the picture quality (color accuracy) falls off quickly at the slightest left-right angle, the up-down angle is more forgiving. By using the color profiles built into the Mac I was able to find one that matches the I-Mac’s screen so when you look at both monitors they match up reasonably well. If you need a monitor that tilts often this may not be the best choice. The tilt action is so stiff that I was convinced that the information provided by ViewSonic about having a tilting function was wrong. I had to take the stand off the monitor in order to get the pivot action to free up enough to move. Even then I had to use a screwdriver as a lever to get it to move the first time. The sound quality is pretty lame, but hey most monitors don’t even have any kind of sound capability. The speakers are fine for the normal PC sounds but not for music or videos. I share this monitor with a seldom used Windows PC and the sound is fine for that, the I-Mac has nice sound so that's covered in my case. The monitor has overall good looks and for anything near the 100-dollar price point you should not be picky. I would buy it again and would also recommend it to others on a tight budget. Overall, I give this monitor 4 stars because of the viewing angle and tilt action weakness.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Favorite Features: VERY Lightweight, 200hz is amazing for gaming (via DisplayPort), Settings/Setting up is beginner friendly, 3 input slots, Blue Light Filter <3, Freesync, HDR, 1ms response time, Settings are complex enough that you can make it your own experience, Warranty and Warranty Extension (if you register the product in the Z-EDGE website)

Some features I didn't like: Not height/tilt adjustable using the monitor stand it came with, controls via back joystick takes a bit of getting used to, Built-in speakers could be a lot better (not a big problem for me), the default tilt and height could be too low for some (me)

At first I was very hesitant to purchase this monitor. I was really looking to upgrade from FHD to QHD. But it had all the features I wanted: Freesync, 144+hz, HDR, 1ms response time, multiple input slots, and curved 27. And at the price point of $180 (as of January 2023), I just had to try it. I saw this specific product in a "Best Curved Gaming Monitors" list so I was enthused. I have to say that I am very very impressed with the picture quality, refresh rates, and response times. I can barely notice that it was FHD because my gaming experience was so smooth.

Games tested: Valorant (4/5), League of Legends (5/5), Guild Wars 2 (5/5), Sims 4 (5/5), Overwatch 2 (4/5)

Overall, I love this monitor. I can barely notice that it's FHD unless I am really close to the monitor. The refresh rate and response times makes up for the lack in upgraded resolution. I would say that this monitor would be a great upgrade from your FHD ~60/75hz monitors. You can definitely tell there is a big difference in smoothness. I think what matters the most is the system you're running on and its specs. I have a mid to high-end custom built pc and it works excellently with it. I also use a Nintendo Switch with this monitor and it runs as expected.

Considering what I have said about all the features and what I liked/didn't like my true rating for this monitor is a 4.5 / 5. I would highly recommend these for any gamers on a budget but want some higher-end experiences.

I did see some concerning video/photo reviews so I would have to update this score as time goes on.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This laptop is a solid machine for gaming, image editing, and for having hundreds of tabs open like the monster I am. What got me to write this review, though, is that this laptop is built to last.

I'll admit, I'm rough on my machines. I take my laptop into the woods on camping trips, throw that sucker into my backpack without thought for what else is in there, and chuck it into the backseat of my car without regard for where it lands. The MSI Stealth's metal body appealed to me, and it was doing great with my rough handling.

Then I managed to set my (black) laptop down on the hood of my (black) car, and drive away. The laptop impacted the ground going almost 45 miles an hour, which as you may imagine, isn't great for laptops. I expected a total loss. The right screen hinge was snapped off. The screen and keyboard were warped. The back right corner of the computer was bent at a 45-degree angle.

When I got home, I crossed my fingers, held my breath, and booted it up.

The laptop booted just fine. There were no damaged pixels on the screen, the keyboard worked flawlessly, and because the fans aren't all linked together, only the one bent fan failed to run. I lost no data, was able to prep for my conference, and the only annoyance was that the screen didn't stand up well with only one hinge. Honestly, I was amazed.

If you need a reliable laptop that can stand up to your active lifestyle, this is the machine for you. I already loved MSI - now they have a customer for life.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
REASON FOR PURCHASE - I purchased this laptop because my Dell XPS 8100 desktop kept freezing/restarting several times a day. A fresh clean re-install of Windows 10 was not remedying the situation, and I had no desire to troubleshoot every component to see what was the underlying problem. Overall, this issue was seriously affecting my productivity, as well as sanity.

POTENTIAL ALTERNATIVES - I was mainly looking for a desktop replacement - not a laptop. I checked Dell, Amazon, BestBuy, as well as other 'PC build' websites such as 'ibuypower', but found prices too high overall. Basically, the price was the driving factor for me in purchasing this laptop. The final price was slightly under $1,300 w/ taxes, and I found that to be a fair price for performance ratio.

MUST HAVES - Since this was my first PC replacement in nearly 10-years, I wanted to make sure I got a 11th Gen i7 Intel processor, as well as an RTX 3000 series graphics card. I was looking for a RTX 3060ti minimum, but I could not find a match within my budget.

PREVIOUS HARDWARE - My Dell XPS 8100 was still using the 1st Gen i5 650 processor, with a PNY GTX 970 updated graphics card. I honestly would have gone another year or two before changing my PC, if these freezing problems were not there.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS - Seems well built - I also liked the keyboard lighting. Chassis seems solid, and I liked all the available ports on the sides. The design was appealing, being perfectly rectangle with the lid closed - no protruding sections to put the shape out of balance.

HOW IT IS USED - I use this laptop as a desktop replacement - I only open the screen lid to power it on. Otherwise, I use an external monitor and keyboard.

HOW OFTEN USED - I keep this laptop on for at least 8-hours a day. It was purchased roughly a month ago, so it's been used rather frequently.

GAMING (@ 1080p only) - It is a notable upgrade from my Dell. Previously in games like WoW or FFXIV, I was getting under 60 FPS frequently in crowded areas. Now, I get dizzy by how quickly the screen rotates in-game, forcing me to lower the mouse-sensitivity. In WoW, I am constantly at 100 FPS with the occasional dips to 90 FPS. I'm also currently playing Ubisoft's 'The Division', but the max I can get is 60 FPS with regular dips to 47 FPS @ medium settings. Not killer performance, but a huge upgrade nevertheless.

FAN NOISE - For everyday non-gaming use (i.e., web browsing), it is a low hum you can only hear if you're within 20-inches to the laptop. When gaming, it can ramp up to a constant loud whirl.

HEAT - Similarly to fan noise, heat is negligible for non-gaming use. For gaming, it can get warm over time, but I use this product: 'Zimilar Monitor Stand Riser', to keep it propped up for heat dissipation. It seems to work well in keeping this laptop cool.

STORAGE - It only comes with one 512GB M.2 device, so storage for my gaming needs is very limited. I looked at YouTube videos to see if it can be upgraded, but it honestly looked like a PITA to do so. So, I have invested in external SSD solutions for space.

WIFI – My router is roughly 25-feet away (through walls), but I get consistent download/upload speeds with the occasional dip. No major connection loss or issues otherwise.

BLOATWARE - It comes with a lot of MSi propriety software, as well as Norton Security Suite. Also, a trial version of Microsoft Office 365. I spent a good amount of time sorting through, and uninstalling a lot of them.

BATTERY - I've only tested it off the plug once. Even without gaming, it was eating through the battery pretty quickly. I surmise it'd only go about 3-hours before draining out. This laptop is definitely not recommended if longevity off the plug is a priority of yours.

PROBLEMS – The only ‘issue’ I’ve come across is if I’ve gamed for a long period of time, or I’ve been moving large files around. The performance of the laptop may drop significantly. I remedy this by a simple reboot, which clears up the issue. Also to note, this laptop has not frozen on me once.

CONCLUSION - When I purchased this laptop, I considered it an intermediary, until I gathered the necessary funds to invest in a desktop with a minimum of RTX 3070. However, it has proven to be a mini-powerhouse. I don't play above 1080p, and I can live with medium-settings if performance seems to dip. It performs excellently on non-gaming tasks, and I now have a mobile gaming platform if I want to take it to a friend's house. All-in-all, I am quite satisfied with my purchase, and may now wait until the RTX 4000 series come out before I consider a desktop.

Overall, highly recommended for purchase.
--------------------------------------------------

UPDATE 08/28/2022

CURRENT STATUS - Yes, it's still working fine. Performance has not dipped, and I only re-installed Windows 11 once because I replaced the 512GB M.2 with a 'Samsung 970 EVO 2TB' several months ago. Also, despite being on 8-hours a day or more, the keyboard LEDs are still functioning bright. That's more than 2,900-hours that this laptop has been on since its purchase.

HARDWARE ISSUES - None. Screen, ports, fans, WiFi, Bluetooth, and trackpad are all still working fine - of course given the caveat that I still strictly use an external keyboard/mouse/monitor setup.

NEW REVELATIONS - Only one. Gaming off the AC Adaptor is a fool's errand. Performance throttled severely after 10-minutes because the laptop was getting so hot, and the battery lasted no more than 35-minutes tops. This was while playing 'Aliens: Fireteam' on Steam.

PRODUCT OVERVIEW - I am still happy with my purchase and see no need to change for several more years. Of course, if I find myself with a lot of disposable income, I can see myself getting a new gaming desktop. But beyond that scenario, I am perfectly content with its performance and durability.

text:
I've been using this for a few weeks, primarily for gaming, and have been very pleased. The colors and contrast seem really nice - I've used several different monitors over the past few years at work and home and this is certainly one of the nicer ones in that regard. I really like strong colors and depth without needing to tweak a bunch of setting and right out of the box I was really happy with this one.

The little knob on the back for menus and settings took a bit to get used to, but I've come to appreciate it. It's kind of an odd way to navigate, but now I can get through menus much quicker than bouncing between different buttons.

I'm not a huge fan of the v-shaped stand, but that's largely personal preference. Most monitors I've used have a square-ish base, which I tend to prefer. The v-shape stick out into your desk just enough that it can get in the way, but you can't really easily put anything on top of it or around it - it's just a bit awkward.

I've also noticed that when I'm in a game but the screen it completely black, there is a bit of light bleed from a few spots around the edges - nothing serious, just some lighter areas. It's not noticeable at all while playing and this is probably not super abnormal.

Only does 1080p, but I knew that going in and would expect a higher res monitor to be much more expensive. The 180 refresh is nice - was looking for something that did 144 and not sure that this is a noticeable difference for most people, but nice to have as an option.

Overall, if this was a super expensive monitor I might be more picky but at this price you're getting a great basic monitor with fast refresh and better than average color depth. No major complaints at all and will happily continue using this as my main monitor for now.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I'm writing a review comparing this to the equivalent Razer Blade with the 2080MQ. I purchased both with the intention of keeping one of them.

Both were $3000 and included the latest I7 9750H, NVidia 2080MQ graphics, and a 240Hz screen. For the same price though, the MSI includes 32GB of ram while the Razer includes 16GB, and the MSI includes 1TB of storage while the Razer has 500GB.

While I agree with others in that the Razer has a better build quality with a Macbook Pro like aluminum chassis, the MSI still has a very nice build quality. Externally, the MSI has a plastic or composite case, but still feels very solid. It's not creaky, and the material that MSI uses shows finger prints much less than the aluminum case of the Razer. Also, the plastic case of the MSI is MUCH less hot to the touch than the Razer and more comfortable to actually use in your lap since it transmits less heat to your lap. In addition, the MSI has more cooling vents in the case so it seems to cool better than the Razer. Lastly, the MSI is about 1/2 pound lighter than the Razer.

The screen on both are comparable, and are probably made at the same factory, although I think the Razer's screen is factory color calibrated, and not sure the MSI is. Both are bright and with 240hz refresh, have very little blur during fast movement. I DO WISH that they implemented G-Sync like Asus laptops do, but unfortunately, neither MSI or Razer do. The ONLY ding I have about the MSI screen is that it has one single stuck white pixel when viewing a black screen. It's very small and hard to spot, but is slightly annoying. I thought about returning it and trying for another, but who knows if I would get something worse (it's tiny and almost looks like a piece of dust, but isn't).

I don't like the keyboards of either laptop. It's not the typing pressure or the feel, but the layout. On both keyboards I end up hitting the wrong keys when trying to use the arrows or other keys on the right hand side of the keyboard. Why can't they just use the Lenovo layout?????

The touch-pad on both work great and are glass smooth and accurate. Both are Windows precision, and use Windows settings to configure. The MSI touch-pad is larger horizontally, but both work fine.

I did performance testing on the processor, memory, graphics, and storage. I used Crystal Diskmark for SSD testing and both came out very close to each other. I hesitate to publish the performance numbers because both companies use different models of SSDs depending on the pricing they get when they are building them - meaning if you buy today, you might not get the same SSD that I got in either the Razer or the MSI. I do though like that the MSI includes TWO spaces for NVME drives while the Razer has only one, so you can get twice the storage on the MSI (or performance if you do RAID 0) - a big plus for the MSI.

Performance of the CPU and graphics was testing using the Unigine benchmarks (heaven, valley, and superposition). I also used 3DMark PortRoyal to test ray-tracing performance. I ran two runs of each benchmark, and both came out very similar, although the MSI came out about 1-2% ahead of the Razer, probably because it cools slightly better and throttles less (the MSI has more cooling vents in the case). I did not under-volt either.

I'm a software developer and upgraded the Windows version to PRO on the MSI - and boy was that a mistake. It's a dual purpose laptop, to be used for coding and gaming. The reason I upgrade to Win10 Pro was so that I could run hyper-V. Unfortunately, that kills gaming performance by approximately 50% frame-rate wise, so when I game, I have to disable hyper-v using BCDEDIT from the command prompt (then reboot).

I ended up keeping the MSI and returning the Razer for the following reasons:

- The MSI is lighter and carrying it around in a backpack you can feel the difference
- The MSI includes more memory and storage for the same price
- MSI has an option for a second NVME SSD (RAID 0 performance)

My only hesitation on choosing the MSI was that MSI support is pretty poorly rated, but I have called them twice to ask questions (one about chargers), and they did fine. I just worry if I have a real problem.

If you have any questions on something I didn't cover, please don't hesitate to ask.

text:
DELL XPS 8700 Windows 8.1 this card works just fine for dual monitors. But you will need to go into BIOS and disable secure boot mode. I used the onboard graphics while setting this up. I used the HDMI plug (it has a cap hiding it, just pull the cap out and plug in your HDMI TV or monitor). Take your graphics card OUT when doing this. Restart you your computer and Hit F2 when you see the Dell splash screen. Now arrow over to BIOS and change the setting to disable secure boot mode. Exit and restart your computer. Now shut down the computer and put in the new graphics card hook up the HDMI TV and monitor and restart. You should now be good to go.

BLACK screens and 5 Beeps!
I started out assuming I could just plug and play. But I ended up with black screens and was getting 5 beeps. People kept saying the 5 beeps meant the battery on the mother board was bad or needed to be reseated. That is if you get 5 beeps over and over not 5 beeps and then stops. Luckily I could put my old card back in to do the research. I did not realize there was an onboard HDMI hook up on my DELL until I kept exchanging the cards in and out. I had a hard time getting rid of the drivers I loaded from the start, I used the CD that came with the card. But with the drivers loaded the method above would not work. I had to delete them first which I could not do without the card in place and could not see the screens with the card hooked up to the motherboard. I ended up refreshing my computer to a date before I bought the graphics card and could start from scratch.

I have been using this MSI Geforce 210 for a couple of weeks now and I am very happy with it. I did not want to spend a lot since I am not a gamer.
I just wanted to be able to watch movies on my big screen.

text:
Originally brought an AMD video card that did not work out and had it exchanged for this MSI GeForce 210. First impression is a professional product; all ports and connector have protective cap/cover; circuit board is of high quality; on top it comes with a pair of low profile brackets that could save me another $15. The installation is as smooth as it could be.
Without doing any pre-installation steps, simply turn off the computer, plug in the card, connect the monitor to the VGA port, turn everything on, and the standard 600x800 screen comes up. That is it, the video card automatically becomes the primary display. Unlike the previous video card, I got blank screen all the way. The downloading of drivers and utility is smooth but with a minor glitch. The latest version download button on msi web page is grey outed and need to choose the next one down on the list. There is one problem though once the drivers are installed.
The on-board audio speaker is disabled. After some googling, it seems to be a rather common issue; the solution is to get into the computer's BIOS setup to re-enable the on-board audio! However, this audio issue does not affect the HDMI output; there is good sound if the video card is hooked up to a TV via HDMI.
For dual display, simply connect a second device, no need to do anything in Windows, as in my case a hd tv is added seamlessly and effortlessly. Finally, another plus for this card is the cooling fan; without a fan like the AMD one, the heat sink could be to too hot to touch. Over all, I am very pleased with this msi geforce card. The installing and setup is as smooth as it should be. Performance wise, it serves my basic needs well. Highly recommended. By the way, my computer is a HP low profile desktop with on-board video and audio running Windows 7 Home Ed.

I bought this to be my central monitor for my home office setup. I do coding and automation workflow development and need a lot of pixels and my 50-year-old eyes need those pixels to be not super dense so I can actually read what's on the screen. 32" 4k for me is the sweet spot. I also find that at this size curvature becomes important so you don't have to turn your head as much to see what's at the edges. Unfortunately 32" 4k *curved* monitors tend to be mostly aimed at the gaming market, with high refresh rates, RGB lighting, and other doodads that add no value for a productivity setup but add a lot of cost. I finally found this one and despite being a no-name brand I took the plunge and have been pleased so far.

The picture is good and the color matches my other monitors well without any tweaking, though your mileage may vary.

The curvature is just right. Subtle but definitely helpful, and it helps prevent screen glare.

The stand the the monitor comes with seems a bit... not flimsy exactly but not well-constructed either. Also it does not afford any adjustability whatsoever. Furthermore it leaves the screen fairly low to the desk and tilted slightly forward, which really is not ideal for ergonomics unless you use it leaning back in a reclined chair, which for me at least isn't how I work.

But I was planning to mount the monitor on an arm to keep my desktop uncluttered, so the stand was not a concern for me. However, what I discovered is the VESA mounting holes are too shallow for the screws I had on hand (including the screws that came with the monitor for mounting the stand). I was able to shim them with washers but I feel this could have been handled better with design.

In the couple of weeks that I’ve had the MSI Cubi N ADL, it has been a good, aesthetic mini PC and fast enough for my basic computer needs. I gave it 4 stars but it could’ve gotten 5 stars if:

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I want to start this review by stating that this monitor arm does not support stacking your monitors vertically although the store page would make it seem otherwise. Attached is a photo of my 34" monitor at its lowest height and a 27" monitor at its tallest and there is zero clearance for vertical stacking, unfortunately.

What I love; these monitor arms are absolutely stunning, the RGB is a nice touch but don't imagine I'll be using it too often. They also feel very hefty and have no issues supporting my monitors. I have a 34" and a 27" on the dual arm and a 27" on the single arm. The flexibility of these monitors is also great, as long as the arm is mounted to the side you can have your monitors fully extended to the side, flush with the back of your desk, and still be capable of pushing your desk up against the wall.

Having both a clamp option and a grommet option is also very nice but I opted for the clamp as it seems extremely sturdy, especially on my butcher block and I'm prone to changing and moving things around with my setup very frequently. Would hate to put permanent holes in the desk. The cable management is also very nice although I'd rather the cables be routed on top of the arm rather than the bottom to better conceal them.

I didn't feel the need to fully tighten down any of the bolts used for adjusting the arms. My arms stay in the position I like without any sag and if I feel like it I can easily move them without having to loosen any bolts.

Other than the arms not being capable of vertical stacking my only other complaint is that I did reach out to MSI directly to ask if the arms supported vertical stacking. It's been almost a week and haven't heard back to what is a simple yes or no answer. At the end of the day, I'd much rather have this monitor arm simply because of how great the clamp is compared to a lot of other brands. There is an adhesive pad you attach to the top of the clamp to help prevent scratches on your desk but nothing to prevent scratches on the bottom of the desk if that's something you care about.

Die Installation war relativ unkompliziert. Die mitgelieferten Platten, die an den Monitoren verschraubt werden, um diese dann einzuhängen, haben allerdings nicht gepasst. Beim älteren MSI-Monitor kann ich das noch nachvollziehen, aber dass sie auch beim neuen Modell nicht gepasst haben, hat mich überrascht. Mit längeren Schrauben hat es dann aber doch funktioniert.

Die Gasfederung lässt sich je nach Monitorgewicht gut einstellen. Einmal alles installiert, macht die Halterung auch, was sie soll.

Ich bin insgesamt zufrieden aber ich denke, wer nicht so viel Wert auf das Design legt wie ich, findet wahrscheinlich günstigere Alternativen mit besserem Preis-Leistungs-Verhältnis.

text:
I recently picked up a used Lenovo Z580 laptop off of ebay that joined my collection of 3 other Z580's that I use on a daily basis. This "new" one arrived without a battery and without a charger/power supply. Fortunately I ran across this FLGAN 20V AC adapter. It is rated at 90 watts of output, which is significantly more than the standard issue Lenovo power supply that comes with the Z580. Because I have a Bachelors Degree in Electrical Engineering, I know that (in most cases) it's OK to use a power supply that has the CORRECT voltage output (20V in this case) but that has more current output capability than is required (because the device being powered will only draw as much power as is needed moment by moment!) The key is to find the CORRECT Voltage, Connector Size ( 5.5*2.5mm in this case) and Connector Polarity (center positive!) to match the device being powered. As long as the device being powered doesn't ask for more current than the power supply can supply (2.25A capable supply being asked to supply 3.5A for example won't work!) it will just work as expected.

5 stars for supplying more current than I need for the laptop and just the right voltage!

text:
Being a Mac user, after the demise of my dated 2017 Intel 27" 5K iMac, and after some research, I came across the BenQ MA27OU. With all the hyperbole I've read about this display, but with some pessimism, I ordered one for my new Mac Mini M4 Pro... and I've been very pleasantly surprised.

This is not an Apple Studio Display... but BenQ doesn't claim it is. It's a high quality monitor, roughly two thirds less expensive than the benchmark display that the Apple Studio Display is.

My particular model BenQ MA270U 27” 4K monitor, across all corners, has the least light bleed I've ever seen in a monitor before. That says something about BenQ manufacturing Quality Control at a monitor in this price point. Downloading and installing Display Pilot 2 provides additional fine tuning of the display. Using DP2 even allows keyboard changes to volume. With Hi DPI enabled in Display Pilot 2, unless you pixel peep, displayed text is essentially as sharp as the Apple Studio monitor.

The only downside of this display, if you could call it that, which won't matter to many, is the built-in speakers are nothing less than terrible. My dead iMac had absolutely outstanding speakers, but the built-in BenQ monitor speakers immediately required cluttering up my relatively small desktop space with a pair of quality speakers.

All in all... the BenQ MA270U 27” 4K is an extraordinary monitor at a great price-per-performance value... and a purchase I'd make again without hesitation.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This monitor offers incredible value for the price. It's truly impressive how well it adjusts to the surrounding lighting. This feature is particularly beneficial for home use, where we often have less control compared to an office setting, where desk lights are usually available. At home, you might find yourself sitting near a window, and as the clouds move, the brightness in the room can fluctuate. Even with ceiling lights, sunlight is generally much brighter, and this monitor excels in those conditions.

I don't think the monitor simply adjusts brightness; I believe it also adjusts contrast and other settings in tandem as the screen dims or brightens. For instance, I usually have it set in standard mode, coding mode, or eye care mode. This way, I rarely need to manually adjust the settings. I have not felt the need to change the contrast or colors during usage.

However, the speakers are very poor quality. They are virtually useless, and I wish the manufacturer had opted to exclude them altogether, as they are an environmental waste. Additionally, a more adjustable monitor stand would have been a welcome improvement.

There is a Dell monitor that is quite similar with the same contrast ratio and superior speakers and stand. While the image clarity is comparable, it lacks the brightness sensor found in this monitor. If you prioritize eye care and the brightness sensor, I recommend this monitor. On the other hand, if sound clarity and a more robust stand are more important—or if you lack a monitor mount—then the Dell might be a better choice. I believe both monitors fall within a similar price range. I originally purchased this one for $200, but have since noticed it is now priced around $150. At the time, the Dell was priced at $150.

It's also worth noting that they offer a programming series monitor with significantly better hardware. However, the color space on this monitor is quite basic, which I see as an advantage since much of the internet is designed around this color space. In contrast, the programming monitors support a wider color range, like DCI-P3. I initially tried a programming monitor and appreciated its features, but I don't believe it's worth five to six times the price of this monitor, which offers about 80 to 90 percent of the performance.

I'm amazed by the advancements in monitor technology. I only wish they would produce a 32-inch model or at least explore other aspect ratios. A 16:10 ratio would have been ideal, but they currently only offer a 16:9 option. There is a programming monitor available in a 3:2 ratio, so I hope they eventually release a 3:2 monitor utilizing these technologies.

Until the issues associated with OLED monitors, such as burn-in, are resolved, I see this monitor as a solid mid-range option. Mini LED technology provides excellent brightness, but lacks built-in eye care features. Overall, while this monitor is strong in most aspects, it could be greatly improved by removing the subpar speakers. If the cost of the speakers were allocated to a more adjustable stand, the monitor would be outstanding.

Given the low price of $150, I don't think it's reasonable to expect features like a docking station or integrated power delivery. While I doubt they could incorporate a 65-watt or 90-watt USB-C power delivery system, a direct USB-C port would have been a nice addition.

In conclusion, I highly recommend this monitor. It is fantastic and earns five stars from me, despite the minor quirks I mentioned.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Overview

The BenQ 27” QHD Ultra Wide 1440p Monitor is a high-quality display designed for productivity, content creation, and media consumption. With a matte screen surface and QHD resolution, it delivers crisp visuals, accurate colors, and reduced glare. However, while it excels in video quality, it may not be the best choice for competitive gaming.
Key Features

27-Inch QHD (2560x1440) Resolution – Provides sharp details and vibrant colors for work and entertainment.
Matte Screen Surface – Reduces glare, making it ideal for bright environments.
16:9 Aspect Ratio – Perfect for multitasking, watching videos, and general computing.
Multiple Connectivity Options – Features HDMI and DisplayPort for flexible connectivity, though it only includes an HDMI cable. If you prefer DisplayPort, you’ll need to purchase a separate cable.

Performance
Video Quality

The QHD resolution and high-quality panel make this monitor an excellent choice for users who need sharp visuals and accurate colors. Whether you're watching 4K content, editing photos, or working with detailed spreadsheets, the display provides excellent clarity.
Gaming Experience

While the monitor delivers beautiful visuals, it is not the best choice for gaming, especially for fast-paced shooters or esports titles. If it has a standard 60Hz refresh rate and a slower response time, motion blur and ghosting may be noticeable in high-action games. If gaming is a priority, consider a model with at least a 120Hz refresh rate and a lower response time.
Pros & Cons

✅ Pros:
✔ Sharp and vibrant QHD resolution for detailed visuals
✔ Matte screen reduces glare and enhances viewing comfort
✔ Good connectivity with HDMI & DisplayPort

❌ Cons:
✖ Not the best for fast-paced gaming due to refresh rate and response time
✖ Only includes an HDMI cable, requiring a separate DisplayPort purchase
✖ Lack of advanced gaming features like G-Sync or FreeSync
Final Verdict

The BenQ 27” QHD Monitor is an excellent choice for professionals, casual users, and content creators who need a high-resolution display with great color accuracy. However, gamers looking for high refresh rates and ultra-smooth gameplay may need to look elsewhere.

✔ Best for: Office work, content creation, and media consumption
❌ Not ideal for: Competitive gaming or users needing a high refresh rate

Would I recommend it? Yes, for users prioritizing video quality, but gamers may want to explore higher refresh rate alternatives.

text:
As an old-school Mac user in the creative space, the Apple/Mac look… and feel (display and interface) is very important to me. From my very first computer, a Mac IIci paired with a Radius display card and a huge Radius Precision Color Pro moniter to my last computer, an iMac 27” Retina 5k, I have become accustomed to that “je ne sais quoi” that only Mac displays provide.

Well, the time finally came for me to upgrade from my trusty Intel based iMac to the M series based machines that I envied from afar. I would have pulled the trigger on the M4 mini last year, but I couldn’t find a monitor that wouldn’t have put a hurting on my pockets. I could have purchased an iMac, but in my mind it fell short in terms of I/O, its small screen dimentions and its price. So, I waited for Apple to release a 27” version…

…As the year passed, I decided to “do my research” to find the best monitor I could find not necessarily based on price, but in the “bang for your buck” range. My memories from when I went through the “maxed out MacBook Pro (Intel series) as my main computer stage” where I relied on a 3rd party monitor at my desk left a bad taste in my mouth about non-Apple displays. My thinking was — get the best monitor for the cheaplest price for now and start saving up for an Apple monitor later down the line.

My year of “research” convinced me to buy the BenQ MA27OU 27” 4K — wait until next year and get an Apple! In my mind I was thinking it would be a step down that I would just have to deal with. That’s why I didn’t go the BenQ’s 5K version for which I hear is outstanding but costs too much for my buy Apple later strategy. Anyhow, I loaded up Amazon fully prepared to pull the trigger on the BenQ MA27OU 27” 4K, knowing that I would be taking a hit on my druthers, like having to settle on a matte screen, lack of Apple sound, etc! That’s when I saw the new BenQ MA27OUP 27” 4K — the GLOSSY sister of the BenQ MA27OU 27” 4K for a few bucks more!

I pulled the trigger, it’s in my possesion — and I am impressed! Text is crisp at most of the higher monitor settings even at 1080. Next to my iMac 5K the colors match quite well. BenQ’s software integration is well implemented — dare I say — almost Mac-like! I’ve only had it set up for about 3 days now. For the most part, I feel right at home. The only thing that’s missing is Apple sound - the built in speakers are no match vs the iMac and the Apple Studio Display. Oh yeah and Apple design — although the design is fine on this monitor - mostly silver and black - no guarish colors or offensive branding - thin bezels on three sides - solid stand with easy height adjustment from very low to pretty high - nice.

If you’ve read this far and noticed that I talked more about my Mac history and my upgrade strategy than I’ve given this product a review — understand that that in itself gives creedence to my good review! To wrap it up, I am totally impressed with this monitor! I may even wait until Apple comes out with a new display before I buy this current gen Studio display. It’s only been 3 days, so I may come back and edit this review to add any strengths or weakness as I find them, but for now — CONSUME!

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
TL/DR: Amazing monitor. Great picture, Great Features. HotKey Puck - the accessory I didn't know I needed, but can't live without! Wish it had 1 or 2 more USB ports & Ethernet port.

I shopped for a monitor for months. I have used dual 27" monitors for at least a decade. I've recently started to have trouble with vision - more than just my eyes getting old, but they are too. I thought getting a slightly larger monitor would be nice. Then my docking station for 2 laptops (built-in KVM) started to fail - and it had been discontinued and there were no replacements available. I had 2 choices, buy 2 docks, plus a KVM and all of the extra cables, or reevaluate my entire setup and consider a monitor with a built-in KVM. Frankly, it was a really tough decision. Lots of monitors with built-in KVM - not many that also have daisy-chain capability. And without daisy-chain capability, I'm back to needing 2 laptop docks and all the cables that would require.

This monitor from BenQ was the only one that also let me take advantage of the Thunderbolt connection on my laptop. Another key requirement was 4K resolution capability.

The Good:
The picture quality is really good and the features are fantastic. The display is plenty bright, without being too bright. It is flicker-free and has settings to minimize blue light. The color calibration is far more than I need. All the various color settings and features are interesting and cool. I don't really use them but did find them interesting enough to check out. There is also a boatload of software that you can download, including eye care software that reminds you periodically to look away from the monitor etc. All good things to help preserve eye health.

The Freakin' AWESOME
The most exciting feature of the monitor is the hot-key puck. With other monitors that have a built-in KVM switch, the switch to changing computers is usually on the monitor itself - not always convenient or easy to reach. The hot-key puck has a 3–4-foot cord and allows you to navigate the on-screen menu without needing to reach the monitor. You can even customize the buttons (hotkeys). This handy-dandy device allows me to change the computer with a click of a button on the hot-key puck. While the cord is plenty long to be within reach without stretching, I do wish it was a tad bit longer or could use an extension cable, so that I could run the cord under my desk to minimize cord clutter. But that's a really petty complaint for a spectacular feature.

The monitor stand is an outstanding feature with a well-thought design. The stand has quite a bit of heft to it - it's downright heavy. It has a flat plate that sits on the desk. It's suitable to place any number of small items you want to place below your monitor. It's almost large enough for my 13" Ultrabook to set on top of, but not quite. The monitor connects to the stand with a quick-release type of connection giving the back of the monitor a very finished look. Putting it together is a one-person job.

The meh
There is a single headphone jack on the side of the monitor. I made sure to get a right-angle plug to minimize the impact on the monitor alignment on my dual-monitor setup.

Most of the connections are on the back of the monitor but facing upward - meaning it's impossible to see the connections with the monitor standing upright. It is much easier to plug everything in, then attach the monitor to the stand. I keep my user guide handy so that I can find the connection diagram if I need to unplug or reconnect anything.

The Could-Be-Betters
There is no ethernet port. You can certainly use one of those ethernet-to-USB adapters and plug that into a USB port. I found that to be slower than when I plugged the ethernet adapter directly into my laptop. It also uses a USB port. Which leads to....

There are only 4 USB 3.1 ports (3 USB-A, 1 USB-C) for peripherals. 2 of these ports (1 USB-A & 1 USB-C) are on the side of the monitor. Those are easy to reach, but when in use, they prevent smooth alignment with another monitor for multi-monitor set-ups. 4 USB ports are typical of many, if not most, KVM switches, but fewer than I need. I have a USB hub connected to one of the ports on my monitor.

I do wish that there were an option for a monitor arm that was compatible with the quick-release feature. It is so easy for one person to attach, and it looks very finished. (One of the new BenQ monitors has an arm like another brand's arm that does fit. I haven't tried the other brand's arm long-term because there isn't enough room for all the cables with the monitor's KVM switch). I do wish that the new BenQ monitor arm was compatible and available to purchase without the new monitor. I would buy it in a second.

Prior to researching for a new monitor, I had never heard of BenQ. Given my experience with this product though, they have moved to the top of my list for future monitor purchases.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I've been using a BenQ PD3220U for over a year now (for graphic design and video editing), and liked it so much I bought another to pair with it as a second display. The BenQ compares very favorably to previous monitors I've used from NEC and Apple, but for less than half the cost. The color accuracy is excellent, build-quality is superb, and the display's brightness is more than adequate in my workspace. There's a good selection of ports, although accessibility to the ones on the back is a bit frustrating if you can't vertically rotate the monitor (mine sits under a bookshelf).

Some of the setup instructions could use better clarification, particularly in regards to daisy-chaining displays and setting up the KVM switch, but BenQ's customer service has been very responsive to any questions I've had.

The included Hotkey Puck is a convenient way to access the monitor's controls, however the icons on the buttons are nearly impossible to see, so I stuck my own P-Touch labels on them for better visibility (see photo).

The monitor's stand is rock-solid and well-built. It's easily adjustable and has a good range of motion. The base is very flat and low-profile, so you can set things on top of it and it doesn't intrude on your usable desk space.

For an excellent, color-accurate, yet still affordable monitor, I'd highly recommend it.

There are three minor complaints I have with it:
1) At only 24", the included Thunderbolt 3 cable is effectively useless. If you plan on connecting with Thunderbolt 3, measure where you'll be installing your system before purchasing, so you can order a cable of the proper length.
2) If using more than one of these monitors together, each monitor must have its own dedicated Hotkey Puck. You can't control two monitors with one Puck (even if the monitors are daisy-chained together). Not a big deal, but it does increase desk clutter. (The Puck isn't required to use the monitor - there are buttons on the back to access the menus.)
3) I use the built-in KVMs to switch both monitors between two Macs. Mostly, it works fine. But there's an issue where if one of the connected Macs falls asleep, and I attempt to switch over to it, the Mac will not wake up and the monitor's entire USB bus and everything plugged into it will stop responding - keyboard, mouse, Puck, and all USB ports - and the KVM will get "stuck" on the sleeping Mac. If this happens, there are two fixes: 1) unplug/reconnect the USB (or Thunderbolt 3) cable going to the sleeping Mac, or 2) plug a keyboard directly into the sleeping Mac to wake it up. In either case, once the Mac is awake, the monitor's USB ports and all connected devices will start working normally again. BenQ customer support says this is a MacOS issue (which I fully believe).

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Everything works. No errors. No dead pixels.

The RD280U/RD280UA 28.2" is the only high resolution monitor that has a 3:2 aspect ratio, aside from the (discontinued) Huawei MateView that had the same specs. It's becoming a winner for serious work, programming, media, multitrack production. It took a day or so to visually adapt. I'm using it as a middle monitor in a three monitor setup.

FYI:

1. You should have enough depth on your desk to place it further back for a comfortable field of focus.

2. You need a DisplayPort cable if you're not using USB-C for display. It's an odd oversight by BenQ. To use the monitor in full native 3840x2560 resolution 60 Hz, you have to use the DisplayPort or USB-C connection. You can't use the HDMI port because it's HDMI 2.0 which lacks the bandwidth for full resolution at 60Hz. The odd part is that BenQ provides cables for all of these USB connections and HDMI, but not the DisplayPort cable. No problem. Get a DisplayPort 1.4 cable.

The cable I got from UGREEN is perfect, 6.6 ft, braided, on sale for $7: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B088GQM9CV --- OR --- Alternatively, if you don't have a DisplayPort on your GPU, but your GPU has an HDMI 2.1 port, get a "DisplayPort 1.4 to HDMI 2.1" cable.

3. LED lights under it, in front, and in back can all be turned off, as you'd expect. Turn them off by hitting the toggle button (the middle button underneath) > Coding Booster > Function Bar > Power Key LED and the LED Indicator. MoonHalo settings are nearby.

4. Yes, the speaker sound is expectedly bad. That's fine. No one buys monitors for the speakers. If it meant making the monitor rim smaller, I'd assume they not include it. On the other hand, it's a nice rudimentary backup selling point for sound, alerts, talk radio streaming.

5. The adjustable MoonHalo is a genius add. Very handy to help eyes when you're in a darker area. I keep mine on all the time now with the 270 option. Nice adjustable glow as the sun sets.

6. I was hesitant, thinking the extra grey bulk and notch at the bottom of the monitor would be distracting. I prefer pure black and uniformity, no weird notches, no flashy branding. Luckily, when you start using it, it mostly fades out of sight in contrast to the illuminated screen, both in daylight and night.

7. To do firmware upgrades using the Display Quickit software, make sure your USB upstream cable (included) is plugged in and into the computer, with no other USB cables in the monitor, along with your DisplayPort cable, as the software will tell you: it only tells you all that just before an OK click initiates the attempt. The firmware upgrade takes a few minutes. Or, if you're using USB-C, I think that's all you need as the connection.

8. 60 Hz isn't a problem whatsoever. Games will be fine for most casual folks. Video is good. Negativity surrounding 60Hz could be justified if your life is more focused on gaming, but then you're probably reducing your resolution anyway to achieve more frames and choosing a smaller monitor. If or when monitors in 3:2 go to 120Hz+, yes, that'll be great too, and I'm sure it will boost sales. That's probably no time soon. Even so, serious productivity, dragging windows, scrolling browser pages, reading, writing, production, and the like doesn't require higher refresh rates. The vast portion of your time spent interacting and reading is in the continual pauses between dragging and scrolling. You won't notice a deficit. It's good.

9. BenQ, if you're reading this:

- Keep making 3:2 monitors.

- Also make 16:10 monitors with the same or better DPI at the 27/28" range. There are no serious 16:10 monitors on the market larger than the 24-inchers. I think most people would find 16:10 to be the sweet spot for general computing for work and entertainment. BenQ appears to have the only 24" 16:10 monitor with a higher resolution, also part of this "programming" product line: RD240Q. Great. Yet I've been using 24-inch 16:10 monitors for 17+ years. There's a crazy huge gap in the market that would buy every larger high resolution 16:10 monitor in sight. I'm not alone.

- Remove extra stuff at the bottom of the monitor, the notch. Make rims uniform and black, not grey. I took a chance and found it's not a serious problem in practical use, but I prefer the cleanest look. If it means removing speakers, do so. Or do both. People are capable of choosing their own speakers or soundbars.

- Linux. Hire Linux developers. Make all Linux software you produce open source. Take a serious presence in the Linux game. Calling yourself a "programming monitor" and not supporting Linux in your added software is a miss. You can run the monitor normally in Linux. It's just that the optional BenQ software (Display Pilot 2 and Display Quickit) that provides a GUI to tweak settings and firmware upgrades (settings you can still access through physical controls) doesn't run on Linux. Not a deal breaker.

I hope to see more 3:2 monitors and larger 16:10 monitors in even higher resolution. Meanwhile, RD280U is a winner.

text:
Good:
- Large screen with a rare but immensely sensible 3:2 aspect ratio – significantly more vertical space to open browser dev tools, panels in the IDE, etc.

- The combination of all of the above is incredible for productive work with reduced eye strain. Everything fits on one screen, without excessive horizontal space, and without squinting at tiny text.
- Many input signal options, USB host, speakers, etc.
- Good colors (after some configuration)
- Able to control brightness and speaker volume from MacOS using open source MonitorControl app. Make sure to give it the permissions it wants.

Bad:
- No easy way to adjust brightness via monitor's controls. You need to go several layers down into the OSD menus every time to change the brightness. There a shortcut to easily change the brightness of the "moonlight" on the back of the screen, but NOT the brightness of the screen itself. Frankly unbelievable. I read the whole manual for this, to no avail.*
- There's a feature to automatically adjust brightness based on ambient lighting, but I can't use it because it doesn't work with sRGB "color mode".
- And it so happens that sRGB color mode + sRGB color profile setting in MacOS produces the best color result for me, closely matching Macbook's color. The default color mode was worse, I had to change it. It does have one fully customizable color mode (that does support automatic brightness) that I could fiddle with (contrast / gamma / sharpness / RGB), but so far I haven't bothered.
- I don't plan to use their other color modes because they distort colors. They may be useful for niche use cases but I need both text and visuals to look good, so I can't use color modes
- The monitor has three USB-A outputs, but only one USB-C output (the other I use as input) – that's not nearly enough USB-C ports in 2024. Using a dongle for this is lame.
- BenQ offers their own computer app to control the screen... but I don't want to install proprietary apps for such mundane things. Maybe it solves some of these annoyances, I don't know. And keep in mind that it's Windows + MacOS only, no Linux.

Even though I'm rather annoyed that real ergonomics was bypassed in favor of unneeded marketing gimmicks, I still rate this monitor a full 5 stars because there is nothing else like it on the market with its banger combination of aspect ratio, screen size and DPI, and I would happily buy it again.

UPDATE 1 year later:

So far so good, everything is still working the same, still happy with the monitor.
- One more annoyance I've discovered in the meantime is that the monitor's USB-C port stops providing power when the computer goes to sleep. So you can't connect any e.g. hard drives / storage drives to the monitor because they will lose power and will be force-ejected when the computer goes to sleep.
- The monitor does have some kind of "Power awake" option which lets you wake the computer from sleep by e.g. tapping on the external keyboard connected via one of the monitor's USB-A ports, so at least that works.
- I have a logitec webcam connected via the monitor's USB-A port. When I disconnect my computer from the monitor, the webcam starts glitching – seems like it's trying to boot, its light ring lights up, but then after about one second it loses power, and then it starts booting again. Not sure why this is happening, but this can be worked around by buying a USB power switch – with it, you can manually depower the camera when not in use.

---

*While reading the manual, I learned that you shouldn't clean monitors with alcohol as it can damage the finish, which was frankly new information to me, so – at least something good came out of that.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
My office isn't well-lit. For years, I've been using a desk lamp, which is essential for reading and writing, but my desk isn't huge and the lamp reduces the amount of useable workspace.

Amazon somehow sensed my frustration and suggested this BenQ monitor light bar. The price ($120) seemed a bit high for what you get, but I figured I'm not just getting a light, I'm freeing up space which will really be useful almost every time I need to work at my desk. So I bit the bullet and ordered one.

I've been using it for a month now, and I really love it. Setup was easy and fast. All the controls are on the top of the light bar and they're touch controls. It's easy to adjust the brightness and the color temperature (warm vs. cool light) to your exact liking. There is no learning curve, everything just works, you don't have to think about it or read a manual.

It has a feature that turns the light on whenever it senses movement within a couple feet. Practically, it turns the light on when I sit down at my desk and turns it off about 10 or 15 minutes after I leave.

I love that it's powered by USB-C, rather than batteries you have to replace when they wear out. Like many monitors, mine has extra USB-C ports for peripherals, but the ports also provide power to accessories like this light.

Okay, so why should you consider NOT buying this?

Simple: Amazon sells other monitor light bars that do almost everything this one does for half the price (or less).

I decided to get a second monitor light bar for my office at work, and I was about to buy another one of these. But the Amazon algorithm showed me other monitor light bars that cost less, by a brand called Quntis. They make a variety, ranging from $40 to $70. I bought a 20" wide Quntis model for $55.

For me, the Quntis has one disadvantage. Almost all of their models, including the one I bought, has a separate remote controller that's about the size and shape of a hockey puck. And it uses 3 AA batteries (included in the package, thankfully). I strongly prefer the all-in-one operation of the more expensive BenQ. My desk gets pretty cluttered, and things on my desk sometimes get misplaced. Without the Quntis remote, you simply cannot use the light bar. Also, the adjustments to brightness and color temperature have only four levels; with the BenQ, it's easy to dial in the exact brightness and temperature you want.

Looking at the user reviews of the Quntis light bars, many people say they like the separate remote. You might, too. Hardly anyone complains about the lack of fine adjustments to brightness and color temperature that you get with the BenQ but not the Quntis.

I really can't recommend spending $120 for the BenQ when for $55-ish you can get a Quntis that does practically everything the BenQ does, with very minor compromises that most people can life with.

That said, I'm not sending my BenQ back to get a refund and buy another Quntis.

Beleuchtung & Funktionalität
- Die Lichtleistung ist beeindruckend: Mit bis zu 1.000 Lux in der Mitte und einer großflächigen Ausleuchtung (bis zu 115 x 60 cm) ist der gesamte Arbeitsbereich optimal beleuchtet – kein Vergleich zu einer klassischen Schreibtischlampe.

- Besonders angenehm: Das Licht blendet nicht, erzeugt keine störenden Reflexionen auf dem Monitor und ist augenschonend – gerade bei langen Bildschirmzeiten ein echter Pluspunkt.

- 16 Helligkeitsstufen und 8 verschiedene Farbtemperaturen lassen sich individuell einstellen. Von warmem Licht für entspannte Abendstunden bis zu kühlem Licht für konzentriertes Arbeiten.

- Der Bewegungssensor ist im Alltag super praktisch: Die Lampe schaltet sich automatisch ein, sobald ich am Schreibtisch sitze, und nach ein paar Minuten Abwesenheit wieder aus – das spart Energie und ist einfach komfortabel.

Persönliche Erfahrungen im Homeoffice
- Ich habe die ScreenBar Pro sowohl an einem flachen als auch an einem Curved-Monitor getestet – sie passt bei beiden problemlos und sitzt stabil.

- Besonders in dunklen Wintermonaten oder bei langen Abenden am Rechner ist das gleichmäßige, blendfreie Licht eine echte Wohltat für die Augen.

- Die Lieblingsfunktion: Ich habe mir einen Modus mit etwas wärmerem Licht gespeichert, der perfekt für Videokonferenzen ist – so sehe ich immer frisch aus, ohne künstlich ausgeleuchtet zu wirken.

- Die Bedienung direkt an der Lampe ist intuitiv, auch wenn ich mir manchmal eine kleine Fernbedienung wünschen würde, um nicht immer zum Monitor greifen zu müssen.
Kritikpunkte

- Die Lampe ist nicht ganz günstig, aber die Investition lohnt sich für alle, die viel Zeit am Schreibtisch verbringen.

- Der USB-C-Anschluss braucht etwas Platz hinter dem Monitor – bei sehr engen Setups sollte man das bedenken.

- Wer eine Hintergrundbeleuchtung für den Raum sucht, sollte wissen: Die ScreenBar Pro leuchtet nur den Bereich vor dem Monitor aus, nicht dahinter.

Fazit
Für mich ist die BenQ ScreenBar Pro zu einem unverzichtbaren Begleiter im Homeoffice geworden. Sie sorgt für eine angenehme, augenschonende Beleuchtung, spart Platz und lässt sich flexibel anpassen. Wer viel am Schreibtisch arbeitet und Wert auf Komfort und Ergonomie legt, wird mit dieser Lampe sehr glücklich – klare Empfehlung für alle, die ihr Homeoffice auf das nächste Level heben möchten!

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
The TL;DR is simple: I have found the SW321C to be a phenomenal, no-compromises, nearly flawless monitor. Great stand, great user interface (I love the puck), outstanding image quality, even backlight, no backlight bleed. It's superb for work and leisure. There's IPS glow, but that's unavoidable.

I'm a programmer who spends most of his time on his computer -- reading/writing text, watching video, and playing games. Previously I was using 2 Dell U2518D monitors, which, even after calibration with an iDisplay Pro Plus, had the following issues:
* Crushed blacks
* Poor contrast
* Uneven colors
* Uneven backlight
* Backlight bleed
* Glare, despite the matte surface

After deciding I didn't want to put up with those issues any longer, I did a week or two of research on what the best no-compromises monitors were in late 2020. That led me to the SW321C, a professional monitor rather than a gaming/consumer monitor, because consumer models -- no matter how fancy they claimed to be or how slick the marketing -- all seemed to fall short and require me to resign myself to compromises in at least one area (and I didn't want FALD).

The BenQ SW321C is expensive (though not as expensive as the EIZO and Dell screens that it's often compared to), but I consider the money well spent. The image quality is outstanding. Colors are stunning. Images and text are markedly sharper and crisper than they were on my 25" 1440p monitors (though this would be true of any 4k 32" screen). The backlight is the evenest I've ever seen. There's no backlight bleed that I can detect. I love the shade hood and never take it off. The matte coating is far and away the best I've seen/used.

For the movies and tv shows I've watched on it (Blade Runner, Ex Machina, The Witch, The Expanse, The Man in the High Castle, The Midnight Gospel), I couldn't be happier with the quality of the picture. The HDR may be "fake," but it still massively improves the viewing experience, especially in regard to handling of darkness/shadows.

Last year I bought and returned the BenQ SW271. I loved it, but the backlight was uneven, there was backlight bleed, and 27" was too small for 4K". (32" is, for my eyes (late 30s), the perfect size for a 4k screen.) If I was going to spend $1,500, I wasn't willing to put up with those issues.

The SW321 isn't as bright as the SW271, which is a shame, but it also fixes every issue I had with the SW271.
==
Update: the blacks aren't as dark as I'd like them to be. (EDIT: correction, for $2k you can NOT get a very decent oled tv with perfect blacks. You will experience burn in.) The monitor also seems to produce a lot of heat. I'm not sure I regret the purchase. It still ticks all the boxes for me, and I consider the money well spent, but if I could do it again, and my living quarters allowed it, (EDIT and recantation: I would not opt for an OLED)

Update #2: Scratch that. I still wish the blacks were darker, but this is as good as it gets on an IPS panel. OLED TVs aren't meant to be used as PC monitors, and if you use one that way, there will inevitably be burn in. I'm still quite happy with the purchase, despite the one, single, occasional stuck sub-pixel.

I've seen a few reviews here that fault the hardware calibration, but for me it has been superb -- certainly better, to my untrained eye, than the i1 Display Pro Plus's software calibration. That being said, I encountered a couple of bugs/problems when using the Palette Master software: it didn't detect my calibrator until I set colors to 10 bit, full output, and I had to plug it into a USB port on my desktop, not one of the SW321C's USB ports.

Update #3: The stuck pixel started to occur more frequently, so I contacted BenQ customer service and asked them to service the screen. The customer-support staff, who were phenomenal -- prompt, professional, understanding, knowledgeable, and incredibly to work with -- helped me, despite a couple of mix ups (which weren't their fault), resolve the matter to my satisfaction.

Update #4: The top review is... awful. What on earth sort of person brags(?) about bossing around delivery people? The top item in this person's list of pros is "high Quality Display Monitor," but the review also states that the screen was defective, that s/he has seen better image quality on $200 monitors, and that the colors look "horrible." Garbage. Neither of us is an expert. Ignore amazon reviews. Read reviews written by professional photographers, for whom this monitor is intended.

Dec 2022 update: my sw321c is one of my favorite possessions. Even my partner who isn't finicky about screen quality loves it. Watching movies or shows on it is always a treat. I can't praise it highly enough. And I can't believe I omitted from my review that its cardboard box is the nicest, most thoughtful I've encountered for anything I've purchased. It's huge but well worth keeping, as it protects the monitor perfectly and stores and organizes everything incredibly cleanly and effectively. No loose cables. No textured carton compartments. Everything has its isolated section, or its own box (which perfectly fits into only one place). My only complaint with the monitor concerns the shade ood, which has started to fall apart easily. I doubt it's meant to be handled, put on, or taken off as much as I have though. I cover the screen with several layers of cloth when I'm not using it, e.g. at night, because I want to keep it pristine, and they don't fit over the hood.

27 Sept 2024 update: I love this thing just as much as I did when I first posted this review. There are now OLED monitors, and I guess people think matte screens aren't maximally sharp. Maybe that's true, but I've never had a problem with that, and neither, as far as I'm aware, have the photographers who apparently love the SW321C.

I really like this monitor, but it has one flaw that it shouldn't have.

Things I like:

It is a big, beautiful, clear, and clean image.

I really wanted a glossy screen and searched high and low to get one.
While the monitor specs for this unit say that it has a matte finish, it is not like other matte screens that I have seen, and I am very happy with the glossy look, unlike most other matte finish screens that I have seen.

It has advanced specs, including a good HDR, high refresh rate, remote control, and more

On the downside:

There is a feature that was the most difficult to find, and it was near the top of my requirements list:
A built-in KVM switch. That said, my one disappointment with this monitor is the built-in KVM switch. It just plain doesn't work. According to the company, the KVM switch can only be used if the main video source is outputted from USB-C! While the monitor has input ports for DP and HDMI as well, according to Ben-Q, the KVM will not function correctly unless the main GPU output happens to be USB-C. Thus, I had to find an external KM switch, because without trying to control the V portion of KVM, the monitor does let me manually switch between DP and HDMI sources as well as the corresponding audio sources.

I also am not too happy that some of the items that need to be plugged into the monitor, plug in at the bottom, leaving visible cables hanging down from it (and necessitating the use of a mirror to plug them each in).

I wanted this monitor in black, but this monitor was only available in white. Adding insult to injury, the included documentation states that the white monitor color will turn yellow in a year or two. Oh, great :(

The monitor arrived with a remote control that had a stripped-out screw on it. I called the company and they quickly sent me out a no-charge replacement, which I really appreciated.

If not for my disappointment in having to work around the faultily designed built-in KVM switch, I would have given this monitor 5 stars, because I really like it overall.

text: I'm very satisfied after viewing the 1920 x 1080 display setting for 1 day. I've looked at internet, photos, and videos. All are excellent. I can't comment on games since I do not use these. I've adjusted brightness, blue light, and speaker volume. This was a little tricky. The button on the bottom of the screen which brings up a menu for these adjustments is a "joystick" type of button which can be manipulated forward, backward, left, and right. The Quick Start Guide which is the only supplied documentation that provides information about operating the monitor did not tell me how to select menu options. Only after downloading the User's Guide did I learn how to make adjustments. I tried different settings for Low Blue Light Plus, speaker volume, and brightness. I found the joystick button inconvenient. It's small and rather sensitive. It's easy to accidentally select an unintended direction. However, I think that most users will seldom manipulate this button after they initially set things up. The Low Blue Light Plus setting seems a matter of preference. I liked it either entirely off or at a level 1 setting. Speaker volume was by default set very low. When my sound was playing through the monitor speakers, I had to adjust my computer's volume setting to 100 in order for the sound to be barely audible. I adjusted the monitor's volume setting to 95 which made the volume better. However, the monitor speakers are, as many reviewers have commented, very tinny. If you have any interest in audio, you will likely do as I did and connect the speaker output of the monitor to an external speaker which will boost it and let you control bass and treble settings. I downloaded and installed the Eye Care app, but didn't find it useful. It allows you to adjust volume, brightness, and other settings by using a mouse to make your settings. This is better than using the joystick button, but I don't expect to change those settings often. It also had a timer that can be set to remind you to take a break from looking at the screen. I can easily do that by means of a clock... I really like the dual HDMI inputs which allow me to share the screen between 2 computers. I connected my laptop to one HDMI input. text:
First the cons: I am running the latest version of Mac Sequoia OS with everything updated and the BENQ monitor software would not work. It appeared to load fine but abruptly shuts down seconds after opening it. I'm not using virus software so I'm not sure what's going on there. Luckily, most manual controls are located on the back edge of the monitor so you can adjust settings without the software (such as blue light reduction, brightness, and refresh rate). I don't like additional software for a monitor anyways so no big deal for me. The speakers show up in my settings but will not work either. I'm not sure if the software package (which doesn't work) also includes drivers for the speakers. Again, I don't want to use the included speakers and I have another pair which work fine. So, right out of the box I encountered problems which could prompt the average user to return this monitor. The attachment of the stand to the monitor could be improved from an aesthetic standpoint. To allow tilt, there is a half inch gap of visible hinge metal between the stand and monitor back. It's just looks, but still. The power cord is too short for me. I feel it should come with an eight foot cord.

For the pros: This monitor has great clarity, color, and sharpness of text, etc.. The bezel edge is thin and unobtrusive. The adjustment buttons on the monitor are easy to use and no mouse or keyboard is required. I like the location of the on/sleep light which is located on the underside corner of the monitor and is not too bright. I love the multiple settings for blue light reduction as the jury is still out on whether blue light can cause permanent eye damage and/or bleaching of the retina over the long run, rather than just making your eyes tired or preventing you from sleeping. I like to turn blue light protection to 3 or 4, and set the brightness to about 10 for most tasks.

It has a nice medium weight and a fairly wide base for stability. The viewing angle is good. The startup time is instant from the moment you hit power. I think it says a lot that I am willing to keep this monitor even with some flaws. If the additional software could be removed altogether and all controls were manual, I would be even more happy with this monitor. The price point is good.
