text:
I am very impressed with the build quality of this display. It has a stiff plastic housing with a “leatherette” finish that looks nice and is easy to grip. A solid aluminum stand-up frame is hinged to the back. When the frame is folded flat against the monitor it covers and protects the connection ports and switches. The monitor stands on rubber feet attached to the stand and the bottom edge of the housing. Between the grip of the rubber feet and the solid build of the stand, it is surprisingly stable on a flat surface. Two mounting holes on the back are 100mm apart to fit standard VESA brackets. On the right side there are two USB-C ports for supplying power and/or signal as well as a Mini-HDMI port for signal. On the left side there is a standard phone jack for audio out to headphones or speakers plus three buttons for power on/off, brightness, volume and menus for other functions. Power can be provided through either of the two USB-C ports. Video signal can be provided through USB-C or the Mini-HDMI port. I successfully provided power and signal from my notebook computer using a single USB-C to USB-C cable. I also successfully powered the monitor from my notebook using a USB-A to USB-C cable while sending the signal using an HDMI to Mini-HDMI cable. All three of these cables are included. A nice padded pouch case with a Velcro closure is also included. At only ½” thick, you will probably be able to carry this monitor inside your carry bag with your computer. I was equally impressed with the image sharpness and color of this display. It actually outperforms the display on my notebook on both counts. If you need extra display space for your notebook and still want to keep your kit small, you will be very happy with Kado’s monitor.

This is an excellent 15” monitor for second-display portable applications.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This is THE monitor to get if you care about the picture, want 1080p, and don't want touch. I am a digital artist and while I don't use this monitor for that purpose, I know what to look for and how to test. If this is what you want, feel free to ignore the rest of my review and proceed to purchase the sRGB 100% version I bought.

Before I go on, a note about the blinking on and off issue some others report: IT REQUIRES POWER. Oy vey. To be fair, unlike some of this monitor's cousins, this monitor does not come with a power adapter. That said, it should require a 15w, 5v connector or Power Delivery brick. Either should work. I'm using a cheap PD one. They're easy to find here if you need one, or use an old laptop charger that has Power Delivery. The power delivered over HDMI is NOT sufficent and if you read the troubleshooting portion of the digital only manual, this is quite clear.

Now, the negatives:

- The stand arm covers the ports when closed, but it can be closed in the OPPOSITE direction. Not a big deal
- VESA mount holes are only two, not the full four. Again, not a big deal and very common on portable monitors.
- The menu buttons are a little small and awkward. Nice, clean design though! And you won't be messing with them THAT much and they're really not that bad. I prefer this to accidentally pressing a button like on some other designs.
- The gamut is actually 86% of sRGB and 102% gamut volume coverage; this is standard, but just know that while it can show the full range of the sRGB gamut (and then some), it is slightly off in a small number of places. Your eye will NOT be able to tell the difference, and even on my expensive art monitors, this is common.
- It does not come with a power brick, so you must provide your own. A 5v 2a phone charger may work. Again, not a big deal for the price; you're going to collect power bricks over time anyway if you haven't already.

None of these are deal breakers. I love this monitor. I wish it had touch, but I value picture quality over a touch interface and I knew what I was getting: a quality monitor from a semi-name brand.

You get exactly what you think you're getting. Have the bare basic technological knowledge to, you know, plug it in, and it will serve you well. Insanely good monitor for the price. Sceptre knocked it out of the park with the 100% sRGB upgrade to their Kado line.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Supper accurate little monitor.

Overview: It's basically a laptop screen in a lightweight body. I've really impressed at how they managed to get the rigidity high enough for the kick stand to function well.

Inputs: There are 3 inputs: 2 USB-C and 1 Mini HDMI.

Color and performance: Windows reports that it is a 10 bit, 1080p, 60hz screen. During color calibration I was able to get a stellar Delta-E and you can see that the Gama Volume was sRGB 105%. It is an IPS display so coverage will be less than 100% because it can't product those inky blacks that OLEDs can. Viewing angles were acceptable during gaming and productivity tasks. The built in menus were easy to navigate and had more built in functionality than I was expecting (including the option to fine adjust individual RGBCYM saturation levels.

Power: You can power it with just your USB-C display cable, or from a second USB-C cable. To get max brightness you may need to use one USB-C cable as dedicated power. With only one cable (Video through USB-C from my laptop) brightness was acceptable for indoor use.

Audio: The included speakers actually sound pretty good. Just don't expect them to get very loud. I think they did a good job powering the speakers for sound quality without driving them past their capabilities. They had plenty of volume when I was using it with my SNES Mini sitting on my bed last night.

Bottom Line: I really dig this thing. I plan on using it as a travel 2nd monitor with my laptop, a portable gaming display for my retro devices, and a multi cam preview screen for my mobile video switcher.

One last note: A+ for including every cable that you might need and for a durable quick start guide that fits neatly into the protective sleeve with the monitor. It comes with a mini to full HDMI cable, USB-C to USB-C cable and a USB-C to USB-A cable.

text:
I needed an adapter that could reliably provide 12 volts at 5 amps (50 watts) with a 5.5mm tip, and this one met every requirement without compromise. From the moment I connected it, the power adapter performed exactly as expected. The connection was firm, and it delivered a consistent, stable output that powered my Sceptre monitor smoothly, with no flickering or voltage fluctuations. That consistency is especially important for monitors, which rely on clean power to protect internal components and maintain picture quality.

The overall build quality is excellent. The housing feels durable and solid, made from sturdy plastic that doesn’t flex or feel fragile. The cord is thick and flexible, designed to resist bending or fraying even with frequent use. The 5.5mm connector tip fits securely into the monitor’s port, with no looseness or intermittent contact issues, which gives me confidence in its reliability.

This adapter is rated for 12V 5A 60W output. It’s compatible with multiple Sceptre monitor models—ranging from 15-inch to 32-inch displays, including both flat and curved screens like the E248W, E225W, E275W, and C325W series. I also appreciate its versatility with other brands such as AOC and Gem LCD monitors, which makes it useful to have on hand as a universal backup for anyone managing multiple displays. I personally needed this particular voltage for a test harness I created to test RV lights and other lights that are 12 volts. It works perfectly for that. 

The functionality of this adapter is solid and dependable. It runs cool during use and doesn’t emit the faint buzzing sound that lower-quality adapters sometimes do. The performance protection features are another plus: it includes over-voltage (OVP), over-current (OCP), and short-circuit (SCP) protection. Those built-in safeguards mean it’s not only efficient but also safe for the monitor and connected components.

In terms of value, this adapter delivers excellent performance at a fair cost. For anyone with a Sceptre monitor in need of a replacement or backup adapter, this power supply is an excellent choice. For anyone who just needs a 12 volt 5 amp power adapter, this power supply is also an excellent choice for you too. It’s well-built, reliable and delivers clean, steady power through a perfectly fitted 5.5mm tip. I highly recommend this power adapter.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I purchased three of these to mount three LCD monitors side-by-side. They're very solidly constructed and the hold is very secure. All in all, the product does the job. However, the included documentation was not helpful. For example, the installation instructions called for using bolts that weren't actually included with the product (it came with screws in place of the bolts). Second, it only gave instructions for installation in a couple of different scenarios, neither of which applied to me. Therefore, the instructions were nearly worthless and I had to figure out how to install it on my own.

In my case, I mounted the three LCD monitors to a 1"x8" board. To attach the rear mounting plate to the board, I decided to use the four 8mm holes in the "square" pattern on the rear mounting plate. I drilled four clearance holes in the 1"x8" board, one hole for each of the ones in the mounting plate. An 8mm drill bit is preferable for that task, but you could use a similar size fractional bit (e.g., 17/64th bit). Once the holes are drilled, you will want to use four M8 size bolts, four regular M8 size nuts, and four flat M8 washers. These will give you a very secure hold between the rear mounting plate and the board. Because they are properly sized to fit the hole pattern in the rear mounting plate, you will have little to no "play" in the position of the mounts -- this makes the fit nice and snug. Note that the drill bit, the bolts, washers, and nuts will need to be purchased separately from the mounts as this hardware isn't included with the mounts.

It does exactly what it purports to do: Mont a VESA monitor something like a half inch off your wall. Any thinner would be a drawback.
If you have a really thin monitor, there won't be enough room for fingers behind it when you have it on the wall, so think about connecting the cables before hanging the panel.
It doesn't pivot and you might find that you want it to pivot because the angles aren't perfect - tough luck! The price we pay for flush to the wall is that there is nor room for pivoting. In my application, I put up with suboptimal angles because I need it to sink into the wall as much as possible. For me, if it stuck out any more, the panel would obscure another monitor that I can't move.
So think carefully about if you need it to pivot! If you need to pivot, this is not the mount you are looking for. Actually, it's the other way around - this is the mount you want ONLY if getting it as close as possible to the wall is the most important thing.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text: So I bought this to put on a 32" TV that I use as a monitor. Of course the little legs that came with the TV provided zero adjustments for height, tilt or swivel. I used it that way by propping up the front of the feet to provide some backwards tilt. I finally got tired of that and decided it was time to buy a proper stand. Now the stands that come with most monitors are generally a little nicer then this one. Normally you can adjust the height by simply pushing it up or down with minimal force and they'll stay were you leave them. On this guy, you have to remove a bolt and move the monitor bracket up or down a set of slots and replace the bolt. This isn't an issue for me because I don't move this monitor around and don't really need to adjust the monitor height - if you do, this could could be a deal breaker for you. I do occasionally adjust the tilt or swivel and those two things are easily accomplished. BTW, a lot of factory table top monitor stands don't proved a swivel capability, which this one has. The stand is plenty sturdy and easily supports my 32" monitor. It came with a pretty good supply of hardware that I suspect will be more then adequate for most installations and it was very simple to assemble. I needed m4x20 screws for my monitor and of course it came with a set that was too short and a set that was too long. It was no big deal to use the supplied spacers with the longer screws to make it work. The next time I'm in a hardware store I'll either buy a couple nuts so I can thread them on the screws before I cut them shorter and then take them off to straighten out the threads or I'll simply buy four new screws of the proper length. For the money, I think this is a great little stand, I'd buy another if I needed one.

I noticed that the strap was loose and didn't appear to be under stress. I loosened the strap a little more and let it slide off while I held the arm with both hands and slowly let it open. In my case, it wasn't anything too sudden or violent and I had no problem with any sudden expansion.

There wasn't' much to assemble except the bottom clamp which just hooked onto a bracket on the arm. I tried sliding the mount from the edge of my desk a could of times, but the clamp part kept coming off, So I got some duct tape to join the two pieces while I slid the bracket in place. It was easier than expected and there are 2 positions to attach the clamp to the bracket for thiner or thick desks. Mine was less than an inch and I was able to tighten it from the side of my desk instead of having to get underneath it.

Since my desk is against the wall, I placed my mount to the side of where the monitor would be used. If I were to place it directly behind the monitor it would limit how far back I would be able to place my monitor. Being on the side works pretty well and allows me to move it up and down and back and forth. I use a dj mixer and found I could place it low so it looks like one unit while hiding a lot of cables, hubs and hard drives. This looks way better than the old set-up i had without the mount. Having the bracket to the side does limit some of the way to move the monitor, but I do not plan to do any major swiveling from left to right.

The mount appears to be really study and has no problems supporting the monitor. There are adjustment for the tension to move the monitor up and down. There were long and short screws for a mounting plate to attach to the monitor, although there was no clear instruction on which ones to use for best results.

I definitely would recommend it you're up against a wall and want something that is pretty adjustable. This has to be one of my favorite computer accessories purchased in a long time.

text:
I needed to quickly replace a defective power adapter that came with the LED light ribbon I bought to fab a giant candy cane decoration as seen on YouTube. In my search, I found numerous nearly identical products being marketed (product labels look like they are from the same manufacturer) under different brand names so it seems logical to pay attention to specs, not necessarily what it is supposed to fit. I also discovered a wide range of conflicting information in nearly all of the listed power converters.

For example, this specific product listing includes a photo showing a three wire plug between the transformer and 120v side - which is not the same as the two wire version I received. This doesn't matter to me, however maybe it does for your project. Other differences include data conflicts such as but not limited to the product voltage data (240 volt or 100 - 240v), wattage data (65 watts or 60 watts).

The conflict appears to be generated in part by the seller including too much wide-scope information intending to convince the buyer that this is “the one” for them; however it ends up conflicting with other provided information so it chases away careful shoppers. I suggest proof-reading, cleaning up and simplifying the listing; and verifying that the photo is a product match. This will be a GREAT help for potential customers.

What I needed was a 60w 120vAC to 12vDC with a US type 120vAC 15 amp plug into the wall and a barrel connector with a positive center on the 12v side. Specs looked good for me and my attached photo shows my test which proved output voltage was correct for my needs. I’ll be updating this review later if any quality issues arise.

text: I got this AC adapter as a replacement for the one on my cable modem that failed. I tested it first with a voltmeter and it measured a steady 12.15v, which is very good and well within acceptable tolerance. The AC adapter has been running under load with my cable modem for 4 days now without any problem. The adapter case is cool to the touch, not warm at all. The adapter is rated for 5A and it replaces a 2A adapter, so it should be running cool. The 12v output plug is 5.5mm O.D, 2.5mm I.D., which is a popular plug size for monitors, external hard drives, cable modems, routers and other peripherals. And 12v is a popular voltage for these peripherals as well. So this AC adapter is likely compatible with many such devices, including my NetGear CM1000v2 cable modem, and my Motorola MB7621. There is no Underwriters Laboratory (UL) certification printed on the adapter. But it does have a European Market (CE) safety certification. UL certification requires third-party testing, which costs at least $5,000 per product if done by UL, while the CE certification can be self-certified for many types of devices including this one. I should note that nearly every adapter I’ve used here in the U.S. has had a UL certification. The seller of this adapter does advertise many safety features that are standard in the industry for AC adapters like this one. The adapter itself does not identify the name of the manufacturer, or even the city of manufacture. It just says it is manufactured in China. The Amazon product listing indicates a seller or manufacturer, brand name “Rolada.” If Rolada is the manufacturer, this name should be printed on the adapter to give buyers more confidence in buying it. To be clear, I am giving this AC Adapter five stars based on its performance alone to date.

text:
I work remote, so I work from different locations often, and need a full workstation setup similar to what I'd have at home. As such, I need everything I carry with me to be compact, light, and as functional as possible. I carry my laptop, full TKL mechanical keyboard, mouse, 18" 4K monitor, and all the cables/adapters I could need. Space and weight are at a premium as a result.

I previously had a super heavy (yet robust) portable monitor stand that did the trick, but didn't offer much height to get to near eye-level at a desk - so I had to prop it up with a book, or a ream of paper. Not an ideal solution.

Then, I found this portable monitor stand. Honestly, I'm blown away at the quality of the build- it feels solid and well-made, and it stands firm (remember, the trick is to adjust and tighten the screws, and balance the screen to the position of the feet). The VESA stand fits and works perfectly well with my portable monitor's 75 x 75 VESA mount, and is stable. For the price, this is sincerely one of my most favorite pieces of kit in terms of value, because it's not just a portable monitor stand... you can use it as a selfie stick, a tripod for a camera/phone/GoPro/Insta360, etc. ALSO - HIDDEN BONUS - everything takes a standard 1/4" tripod screw, so you can mount the system to monopods, or anything you can think of. And, finally - portability... this can be packed "horizontally" with everything taken apart, or you can keep the tripod + pole + ballhead together for "vertical" storage in a backpack... so it's super portable. EXACTLY what I needed for my remote workstation bag.

Seriously, no idea why Amazon says this is "frequently returned", because I freakin' love this thing. Buy this *NOW*.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
My 15 year old LG M237WD 23" Flatron Monitor/HDTV finally died on me leaving me in a strange new world where you can no longer find a new, low-cost Monitor/HDTV with a built-in antenna input and tuner. Today you need a monitor with 2 HDMI inputs and a separate HDTV tuner with antenna input to do the job. The question today is which ones do the best job at the lowest price? After extensive online research, I decided on the AOC 24B2H2 24" LCD Monitor and the Mediasonic HOMEWORX HW250STB Convertor Box/Tuner. In short, I am extremely happy with the choices I've made. Before you make your decisions, I highly recommend you download and read the online user manuals available by searching for them online. In particular, you need the online AOC user manual to properly describe and utilize the the 5 tiny buttons on the bottom edge of the screen used to power on and access monitor settings. The paper guide included with the AOC monitor does NOT describe how how to use these buttons. The HOMEWORX manual omits fully describing how to prepare for, record, and playback TV programs on a USB flash drive. If you are computer savvy, formatting, recording, playback and deletion of TV programs is easy to figure out. If not savvy, you may need to ask HOMEWORX for help.

The AOC monitor is very easy to set up. You just need to insert the neck at the bottom of the screen into the base. The screen can be tilted from 20° up to -5° down. You plug in your 1 or 2 HDMI cables from the HOMEWORX tuner and your computer, the power cord, and your speaker or earphone 3.5mm connector cable, and you're done! The HDMI button under the bottom screen edge allows you to easily switch between the tuner and your computer. Audio is automatically switched between devices with the HDMI button. On Windows 10, a 24B2H2 Intel(R) Display Audio interface is automatically installed by the AOC monitor and becomes the Default Playback Device. I have an audio cable running from my computer to my speakers in addition to the HDMI cable. If needed, I can switch the Default Playback Device back to Realtek High Definition Audio to enable me to record audio using Audacity software, which I use to record stock market Earnings Webcasts. (Note: Audacity requires a wire connection between the Realtek audio output and input to enable recording audio off the Internet.) The AOC display itself is excellent, strong clean colors and high definition. The screen is matted, NOT glossy as incorrectly listed by Amazon.

The HOMEWORX tuner has a handy easy to use large remote control along with manual control bottons on the tuner itself. In addition to the HDMI port, it also has RCA jacks and can act as a HDTV converter box for an old analog TV or as audio output for a stereo amplifier. It has a USB-A port for a USB flash drive or other form of storage drive. When not turned on, the HOMEWORX digital display acts as a clock showing the time of day. Signal reception by the HOMEWORX is excellent. This has the best reception of any HDTV tuner I've used so far, and I receive stations I could not receive before so long as the weather and temperature inversions permit.

So, I needed a new monitor for my Xbox. and I wasn't looking to break the bank. I stumbled across this monitor and figured for the price, it was worth a shot. Here's the lowdown after using it for a few weeks:
What I Liked:
* Easy on the Wallet: Seriously, this thing was a steal! I was able to snag it on sale, and it was way cheaper than a lot of the other monitors I was looking at.
* Looks Pretty Slick: I'm not gonna lie, the "frameless" design gives it a modern vibe that I dig. It definitely elevates the look of my desk setup.
* Movies and YouTube Look Great: The picture quality is pretty darn good for everyday use. Colors seem vibrant, and I haven't noticed any weird blurring or anything when watching videos.
* No More Eye Strain: I tend to spend hours staring at a screen, and I've noticed my eyes don't feel as tired with this monitor. I think those "Flicker-Free" and "Low Blue Mode" things actually make a difference.
What Could Be Better:
* Not So Great for Photo Editing: I tried touching up some photos on this monitor, and the colors seemed a bit off compared to how they look on my laptop. It's fine for casual use, but if you're a pro, you might need something more color-accurate.
* Not Enough Ports: This is kind of annoying. It only has one HDMI port, and I need to switch cables depending on whether I'm using my work laptop or my gaming console.
* The Stand is Meh: The stand is kind of bulky and only lets me tilt the screen. I wish I could adjust the height too.
Overall Thoughts:
For the price, its a solid monitor. It's perfect for everyday tasks like browsing the web, working on documents, and watching videos. If you're a casual user who needs a decent monitor without spending a fortune, this one's definitely worth checking out. Just don't expect it to be perfect for professional-level color work or hardcore gaming.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I picked up the AOC Q27G4XN for my second setup, and I’ve been really impressed so far. For the price, this monitor delivers a lot more than I expected.

SETUP AND FIRST IMPRESSIONS

Right out of the box, setup was quick and easy. The stand is sturdy and lets you adjust the height, tilt, and swivel, which makes a big difference if you use it for long sessions. The overall build feels solid and not flimsy like some other budget monitors.

DISPLAY AND PERFORMANCE

The 27-inch screen with 2560x1440 (2K QHD) resolution looks sharp and clear for both games and everyday use. Colors are bright, and I didn’t notice any dead or bright pixels. The 180Hz refresh rate and 1ms response time make games look super smooth, and Adaptive-Sync keeps things free of tearing or stutter. I tested it with both a PC and an Xbox, and had no issues—HDMI 2.0 and DisplayPort both worked as expected.

FEATURES

The monitor comes with two HDMI ports and one DisplayPort, so you can easily switch between devices like consoles or a laptop. The 3-year zero-bright-dot warranty is a nice bonus for peace of mind.

PROS:

Crisp, sharp QHD picture with good color

Super smooth 180Hz refresh rate and 1ms response

Adjustable stand for better comfort

Plenty of ports for different devices

Great value for the specs

Reliable warranty

CONS:

Built-in speakers are average (like most monitors)

The menu buttons could be easier to use

SUMMARY

AOC might not get as much hype as other brands, but this monitor is solid. For gaming and everyday tasks, it’s been excellent - especially at the price I paid. Highly recommend for anyone wanting a quality QHD monitor without breaking the bank.

Lesson #2: "Driver works for Ubuntu" does not mean it's gonna work for other Ubuntu-type distros (Linux Mint in my case). Perhaps it's my laptop (Lenovo) but unlikely. Anyway, I couldn't for the life of me get that driver to work in Mint 19, or 20. The display came on, but displayed a very linear-distorted image, like with a loose VGA cable, or V-Sync issue. But neither of those obviously. Just a personal experience, could be any number of things. This laptop is the same resolution, that's why I went for this model. Anyway, YMMV.

UPDATE EDIT: Partial luck. I did some testing. Had the same issue on Ubuntu 20.04. So figured it's my laptop. But then I changed the resolution to 1024x768 - voila, works great. Ditto in Mint 20. Unfortunately this res is below-spec and the wrong ratio (being 4:3, unlike the native 16:9). I'm going to blame this on my laptop for now. Seems like it doesn't have enough throughput for the video signal, IDK. This is good enough for me, albeit a little janky it's better than one screen, and it's not my primary work platform so I'll survive.

I hope this helps someone. I' saw a screenshot from someone on Mint forums with this exact monitor working fine in Mint 19.

I like the kickstand, I like the USB position - might not work for everyone, as another reviewer noted (see his pics).

Viewing angles are not very good - we're rewinding to 2010. Just keep that in mind for portrait and angling.

I can't say this is a bad price for what it is. I don't mind the thickness. It's a big jump to thinner, I'm not trying to invest that much.

text:
Because of my work as a writer/researcher and working with editors I use three screens - my laptop and a screen on each side of my laptop screen. And recently I have been traveling. Four different destinations for a few weeks at each destination over the past four months. Three screens is fantastic for the kind of work I do. It would take me maybe three times longer to do my work if I didn't have such a great little system.

I plug these monitors into a powered USB hub and all is good. I needed to configure my displays so that I can drag something from the AOC on the left, through the screen on my laptop, and onto the AOC screen on the right. Elegant. It works perfectly.

When I needed to travel I found that these monitors and my laptop and cables ... ALL went beautifully into my computer bag. And I can set the system up in only a few minutes and then do my writing efficiently.

I am VERY happy and would buy these again. And, in fact, I DID buy them again ... and here is the caveat:

These are SENSITIVE products. They can be damaged easily through mishandling ... but still ... too easily blemished.

In a hotel in Niagara Falls they didn't have a big enough desk so I propped everything up on an ironing board ... with my additional keyboard on the table below. The ironing board tilted and one of the AOC monitors fell maybe 8 to 10 inches ... and there was a small blemish - about 1.25 inches by .5 inches in the top part of the monitor near the upper rim and about 3 inches from the right side of the monitor. And a similar blemish (half the size) on the bottom near the monitor rim on the left side. BUT ... it still had a great picture except for those two areas. I had no serious problem using the screen. On my FOURTH trip ... something happened to the other blemish-free monitor WHILE it was in my bag. I don't think I hit it with anything but ... the screen was almost useless ... it had a 1 inch wide section from the top rim to the bottom rim ... exactly in the middle of the screen ... and it was blank. Disturbing looking so ...

I ordered two monitors AGAIN.

Remember, these were purchased in Canada for like $116 EACH! I have never seen a better price. Yes, they are sensitive, but the price is excellent and the picture quality is, to me, also excellent ... just not the durability. I have two bigger and more durable monitors at home ... but THAT set up was about $550! And is big, heavy, cumbersome. I can't travel with them.

So ... I LOVE these AOC monitors. They are perfect for what I need. They help me work away from home ... and in my new home coming up I will have no reason to use the large monitors from my old home so I will give them to another writer/researcher friend.

BUT ... while I strongly recommend these monitors I strongly recommend that buyers get the extra warranty ... in case your AOC monitors get too 'sensitive' and are a bother to look at. I did NOT get the extra warranty for the first two. I have never damaged a monitor before ... but I had never traveled extensively before. I have the extra warranty with the second two monitors. It is not expensive for an extra level of protection ...

Enjoy these monitors. I do. Every. Day.

text:
I was offered this monitor as a warranty replacement for a different AOC monitor, and I almost didn't take it. It is ugly, and loud. And, it turns out, I love it.

The bad - the screen is prone to stuck pixels that come and go. It gets scratched very easily, even under circumstances where other computer monitors haven't scratched for me. I really didn't like the bold and black League of Legends text on the bottom of the stand, to the extent that I removed it with acetone. The colors outside of gaming are likely completely inaccurate. When I use Zoom or a web browser, there's a red tinge. Text isn't the most legible either. The headphone stand is absolutely LAUGHABLE and serves no purpose, especially if you keep your secondary monitor to your right. It's hard to get in and out and I don't know why they bothered putting it in.

The good - I love the little navigational thingy that allows you to change all of the settings in the monitor. It's very convenient and it allows you to set profiles to change the colors quickly. There are many settings, and the RGB on the stand of the monitor is interesting and there's fun settings. It's big, it's got a nice refresh rate, and in gaming, I love the rich colors.

Would I recommend this monitor to other people? You know, I'm honestly not sure on that. Because the thing that makes me love this monitor more than any other monitor I've ever used is subjective.

It doesn't hurt my eyes to stare at it for hours. I'm very photosensitive, and every other monitor I've tried, including my secondary monitor, does hurt my eyes. I don't have headaches, I can game for hours, and it's just a lovely quality of life thing for me. I bought another one when it looked like it was getting discontinued because nothing else has done right by my eyes.

Well worth the money, even though it needed some modification to not offend me with its absolute ugliness.

The difference, as has been stated so many times before, is absolutely night and day. If you have never experienced the glory that is 144hz+, and are on a budget, this monitor is the monitor for you. Everything except one thing about this monitor is better than the ones I used before. Color accuracy, brightness, smoothness (obviously), design (both aesthetics and build quality), its bezel size, AND a curved panel. There is only one issue I have with this monitor. From my very amateur testing, it seems this monitor suffers slightly in terms of corona artifacts, or inverse ghosting. But that in no way, at least to me, makes this monitor a bad purchase. Sure, I could have gotten a monitor without that issue. But to me, it's just not worth another 50 dollars I would have to pay over this one. On a scale of 1-10, I give this monitor a 9.5, because to some people corona artifacts are a bigger deal than to me.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Fantastic monitor. Curve is perfect for how far back I sit from it. Very responsive, bright colors, dark darks, has the connectors that I needed, I'm using the DisplayPort and the USB-C connectors. More DisplayPort connections would have been preferable to the HDMI connections that it has instead, but USB-C is doing extremely well so I can't complain too much.

When I first turned it on, it had a weird splotchiness to the color. In the menu it turns out there's an option to refresh pixels, basically making the monitor turn off for 10 minutes then turn back on, and after doing a refresh it looked much better. I didn't see anything in the setup directions suggesting to do this, I found it scrolling desperately through menus looking for anything that would fix what I otherwise was going to return the monitor for.

Solid colors look a little bit grainy, but I only notice this when large expanses of my screen are darkish grays and get up closer than I'm usually sitting at my screen to look at it. Playing games or watching videos it's totally fine. With a dark enough dark mode (I use 0x000000 black for large expanses of my color schemes and custom CSS, which is part of why I wanted to spring for an OLED) it's also not a problem. I may not have noticed it other than when I looked closely because of the earlier splotchiness from when I first turned it on, but successive pixel refreshes haven't made the faint graininess go away.

Controls for the monitor are a bit difficult to reach, on the back if you reach underneath the right side. I don't like that I have needed to use a remote to control my monitor, but the remote has been working acceptably well.

It's pretty large but also very thin, so if you bump it, it'll sway and bounce for a little bit. I think it's an acceptable compromise, since I don't bump it often, but it did surprise me.

It was disappointing that there are so few monitors that can meet the specs of this one, and the only other one I could find had a big ugly ROG logo underneath it that I didn't want to stare at all day. Loud branding is incredibly obnoxious, so the subtle branding on this one was a welcome alternative.

This is the best monitor I've owned now that the splotchiness is fixed. I don't know if I can ever go back down from 240Hz or OLED.

text:
A little background, I had many OLED monitors in the past ranging from QHD to 4K, WOLED and QD-OLED and while I was happy with them, because I work from home 90% and play games/watch movies 10%, I needed to move away from OLED to stop my burn-in anxiety and to get better text rendering.

That is when I switched to Mini LED

I was happy with my previous AOC Q27G3XMN, but one thing that bothered me was the fact that I couldn't run it @ 180Hz since it only has HDMI 2.0 and my Razer Blade 16 2025 laptop only has an HDMI 2.1 port. Yes, I could've just connected it via USB-C and gotten the 180Hz. Still, when I did that, the signal was coming through the integrated GPU, not my nVIDIA GPU, causing a slight performance hit and disabling RTX Video Enhancement in the nVIDIA Control Panel.

So I scoured the net looking for a QHD (I don't want 4K anymore for performance reasons) Mini LED monitor that had HDMI 2.1 and preferably a USB hub. I was surprised that there were no monitors to meet all those requirements. There is a Samsung Odyssey G7 4K Mini LED (which I had before and returned it), but I didn't want to get a 4K monitor.

That is when I came across the AOC Agon PRO AG274QZM. I was surprised there are no reviews of this monitor anywhere, and it was released in 2023, yet it still beats everything out there in terms of features!

- HDMI 2.1

- IPS panel (more on that later)

- 750 nits of brightness in SDR

- 576 local dimming zone (yes, not the best, but better than the Q27G3XMN, which only has 336 dimming zones )

- USB Hub with 4 USB 3.2 ports and a USB-C port

- 10-bit colors

- 240Hz refresh rate

The Amazon reviews leave a lot to be desired, most of them complaining about receiving the monitor with dead pixels. I took a chance anyway, as Amazon has a great return policy.

The monitor arrived, the box was almost as big as a 42-inch TV, and it's enormous. So many parts, including a privacy/bright light hood

After unboxing the monitor and turning it on, I was a bit worried, it had this matte grainy effect, but the moment you crank up the brightness, it becomes crystal clear

It also comes with a controller to navigate through the OSD settings, so no more fiddling around with awkwardly placed buttons on the back / underneath the monitor. It is so easy to change settings using the controller

The colors are very punchy and vibrant, the brightness makes everything pop so much.

Even though it is an IPS monitor, which I was skeptical about as I hate IPS glow, this monitor has 0 IPS glow, it's almost as good as having an OLED monitor but without the OLED downsides such as burn-in or text fringing or low brightness.

Turning on local dimming slightly reduces the brightness in SDR (not in HDR), but not as much as it did on my AOC Q27G3XMN. So I turn off local dimming in SDR but turn it on in HDR.

The monitor is also G-Sync compatible, and I had 0 flickering issues.

I highly recommend this monitor. I still can't believe this monitor was released in 2023, yet it rivals and beats monitors recently released in terms of features and performance

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text: If you've been wanting to make the plunge to 21:9 Ultrawide but don't want to spend 700 to a 1000 (entry, some are double the price), this is the monitor. I got mine for $370 on black friday, but the mid $400's they are current asking is still a steal. First off, the specs are out of this world and they hold true. 3440 x 1440p is the best resolution you can get without going 4k, and with 4k you need a proper rig to run games at decent FPS. Check your CPU tho, if it's older it might struggle a bit with this res, but not much. 1ms response time is pretty much best available, the 1500R curve is simply the best balance between a nice curve and not feeling like you are surrounded. It's not flat, but appears somewhat flat while viewing, but there's just the right amount of curve. The colors are nice, very accurate. Doesn't quite pop like an IPS panel, but it looks fantastic. Even in mid 2022, 1440p gaming is still considered the sweet spot unless you've got the budget for a $300 CPU and $1,200 GPU, not counting RAM, MOBO etc... The onboard controls could be a tad better, and are difficult in low light until you memorize the button patterns, but that is easily forgivable. The brightness is well bright, I never go over 70 even in a well lit room. Overall, I can't say enough about this monitor, AOC really hit it out of the park with this model. It's kind of been glossed over by the thousands upon thousands of dollars for an LG or Samsung, and that's a shame, because AOC should be praised for what they've done here. No dead pixels, everything has been beyond smooth, easily the best monitor I've ever owned, I'll NEVER go back to a flat panel. Oh and did I mention this thing is 34 inches? Most monitors with these specs are 1080p 27 flats, or maybe a 32 if your are lucky. As a gamer for over 20 years, I promise, do yourself a favor and pick this bad boy up.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This review is for the 34" CU34G2X UltraWide QHD 3440x1440 monitor. Used for about a week before writing this.

This is the best monitor I've ever seen with my own eye's! The curve is perfect, not too much, not too little. It's really immersive for gaming in particular. And for reading online and working for long durations the curve still looks great and is not distracting.

Looks amazing on its own, even without content! Solid metal stand and wide metal feet. Very sturdy. The metal feet have lots of solid, grippy rubber pads on them so it stays right where you put it. The screen isn't too glossy or too matte. The red trim is well placed and not over done. It looks very modern and professional, but still calls attention to itself like a gaming monitor should!

Refresh rate does indeed go up to 144hz no problem in games and in Windows 10. Color reproduction is really good to my eyes. They include a printed sheet with the color calibration results for your specific monitor with serial number, so AOC really is going the extra mile to prove that these really are high-end monitors.

This is a super low latency "VA" type panel. So it is the best looking panel type from a technical and color reproduction perspective. IPS panels traditionally had lower refresh rates than VA panels, but this monitor proves you can have the best looking VA panel type, AND super low 1ms refresh rates.

Games look amazing in the ultra-wide format. Halo on PC for example actually gives you a full field of view with this monitor, same with Rocket League. So you do actually get an advantage in some games. You literally can see more of the field of play with the ultra-wide aspect ratio 21:9, than anyone else stuck on the 16:9 ratio that most 1080p or 4k monitors use.

Brightness is great, even too bright at highest settings unless your in a really bright room. So that's nice to have if it's needed. All brightness and contrast settings and even gaming profiles are adjustable through physical buttons under the monitor, but also through the G-menu software. So using the G-menu software you don't need to fiddle with the physical controls of the monitor at all to fully adjust and control the monitors settings. G-menu even has hot-keys so you can change your monitor settings to different profiles almost instantly. You can download the G-menu software from AOC's support website.

Make sure to use the included DisplayPort cable with this monitor. The HDMI ports don't have the same capabilities as the DisplayPort connectors. To get freesync, 144hz, and native 3440x1440 resolution all together; you MUST use either of the two DisplayPort connectors on this monitor. AND make sure your not just converting from HDMI at the source to DisplayPort. The source signal from your PC also needs to be DisplayPort.

There is also a usb3.0 cable included. You can use it to hook it to your computer, then you can use the monitor as a USB 3.0 hub. Power Delivery is off by default on the USB 3.0 ports, but you can enable it via the monitors settings menu, or through the G-menu software.

Amazing monitor, highly recommended.

text:
Be careful when reading the reviews here on Amazon this page has several monitors on it, I'm reviewing the 34 inch 21:9 CU34G2X.

I compared this monitor side by side with the LG 34GP83A-B, Samsung C49RG90 and Acer XB273K, it has by far the best quality per dollar. The only area the other monitors were noticeably better in was brightness, this monitor is bright enough but just not super bright like those 3. I work in a very bright room and it's good enough, the bright frame feature helps a lot here. There is a great description of how to calibrate all the settings on Reddit by collective_dysentery, just search for "cu34g2x calibration" and you'll find it. I recommend using that as a starting point then tweaking to what works for you.

The colors were also better on the other 3 out of the box, especially the LG and Acer which are IPS, but I found that it was pretty easy to use the controls to get them close to the same level. This monitor has much better contrast than the LG of Acer which I found made a much larger difference to image quality. The Game Color feature is nice for giving colors some extra pop for games, for work I found leaving it at the default 10 to be the best however.

This monitor has by far the best anti-glare of the 4, I do not notice any significant blurriness on small text. It seems to be a tiny bit less sharp but nothing worth worrying about. The XB273K was much sharper of course as it's 4K.

I found the 1500R curve to be really helpful for making the edges of the screen useable and the curve only took a few hours to get used to. Even though the XB273K is not as wide and 16:9 it was noticeable how far away the edges are on it. At 34 inch 21:9 a flat panel would have unusable edges.

Shadow Control works really well for adjusting how dark/light the shadows are in a game, if you want that dark game ambiance with deep blacks and tons of contrast just drop the Shadow Control down one or two notches.

I have not noticed any brightness flickering from G-Sync in games, it did happen in Amazon Workspaces that I use for work but that's easily solved by turning off windowed G-Sync or temporarily turning it completely off. There is absolutely no reason to use G-Sync in work applications like Workspaces.

The build quality is very good, the best of the 4, although they were all well made.

All 4 of the monitors I tried are great units I would recommend any of them to anyone, for me the AOC CU34G2X just made the most sense even mostly ignoring the cost. If the Samsung C49RG90 was $800 or less I would have went with it because of the extra screen space of 32:9 and higher brightness but even at that price it would be close. It's not curved enough so the edges aren't usable and it's just massive.

text:
I've been using this monitor for the last few months now (bought in August, reviewed in December) and think I can now properly list its strengths and weaknesses.

Pros:
- Massive amount of screen real estate.
- Great for work when you need to have multiple windows/apps open side by side. I work in software QA and amount of space as certainly made a positive impact.
- Gaming is a good bit more immersive thanks due to not only the wider image but also the slight curve.
- Fast response time and 144Hz refresh rate make everything feel smoother. It's really hard to go back.
- Editing photos, the colour gamut and accuracy out of the box are decent and certainly good enough for an amateur photographer like me.
- Comes with all the cables you need for the full resolution and frame rate experience, just make sure your video card supports DisplayPort
- Supports AMD free sync and also works with G-sync for Nvidia cards (GTX1060 in my case)

Cons:
- It's weird when you're sharing your screen on a call and everyone gets confused by the size and aspect ratio, same goes for full screen screen shots :)
- Not every game supports the ultrawide format and finding the right compromise of resolution and black bars left and right can be tricky.
- The default colour depth is only 8-bit and I am pretty sure I noticed that during my first photo editing session when colour transitions looked a bit rougher than I was used to. A quick online search revealed that the panel does actually support 10-bit depth but you need to force it through the video card (Nvidia in my case) driver.
- The curve and aspect ration take some getting used to. Especially on a browser window, the curve threw me off and I kept missing information on either side since it was too much in my peripheral vision. By now, I am well used to it though.
- Viewing angles are not great for someone coming from an IPS panel but they're decent for a VA panel. And since it's only me looking at it straight on, it's alright.
- It does generate quite a bit of heat at the top and the bottom corners - might be an issue for stuffy (home) offices in the summer

In short: You get a great monitor with plenty of space and features. The support for free and G-sync and the 144Hz refresh rate are tough to beat at this price!

title: 3.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Tried having this monitor replace my 27" LCD display. I figured that gorgeous OLED and an extra 100Hz would be enough to sell me. One might figure "my phone is OLED, my Switch is OLED, my Steam Deck is OLED. They all look amazing, surely this is a no-brainer!"

It was not a no-brainer.

The WOLED subpixel layout is atrocious. For those who aren't typically bothered by visual artifacts, it will be an annoyance at best. For anyone more particular than that, it will be a complete dealbreaker by itself.

Unlike your OLED handhelds, this monitor requires you to babysit it. Every couple of hours, an alert will come up saying it needs to refresh itself for up to TEN minutes. You can disable this warning if you're fine with voiding your warranty and aren't already tired of how *dim* OLED is compared to its LED contemporaries. Don't waste your money on OLED this year. Wait for affordable nano IPS displays with good brightness and a boatload of local dimming zones, or wait for LG or Samsung to come up with a halfway decent subpixel layout for a monitor and a solution for OLED to not require you to manually refresh the screen if you watch a long movie in a single sitting, god forbid.

If you can get past all of that, this is a great monitor for media consumption. Decent price compared to monitors using the same panel, good peripheral features, feels pretty sturdy. Setting it up for a monitor arm is a little funny, as you need to additionally install the (included) mounting plate. OLED looks really nice in games and media. HDR is a mixed bag, as this monitor doesn't overdrive the panel as much as some other models using the same panel.

text: Man, $115 was a steal for this monitor! For that price, you can't even find a 75-90Hz monitor, let alone this one. Now I'm going to answer the number one question about this monitor. Yes, it does have ghosting right out of the box. BUT, you can reduce it drastically by tinkering with the settings. In Luminance section, my Eco Mode is set to "Standard", with Brightness and Contrast at 50, and my Gamma is set to "Gamma3". In Color Setup, my Color Temp is set to "Warm". In Game Settings, my Overdrive is set to "Medium", and my Adaptive Sync is "On". Game Color is set to "10". These are my personal settings, you might like them or hate them. Every monitor is going to have a little bit of ghosting, that's why monitor settings exists. When it comes to Overdrive, Medium or Off is your best choice. The Strong mode has the best affects on lighter objects, but it over ghosts on darker objects. For the best results on this monitor, I highly recommend using a Display Port cord if your graphics card or motherboard supports it. HDMI is fine, but it doesn't carry color accuracy as well as the Display Port. But like I said, there's nothing to complain about at this price point. I'm thankful that I even got a working monitor for $115.

text:
Alright, my first time doing a actual...review on a gaming monitor in a while, however, I honestly have had zero issues with this monitor in the few months I've had it, so let's get into it.

Pros:

- First off, the screen is BRIGHT. If you need a portable sun, this monitor is your best friend, but its not a "dear God this hurts" bright, but a bright that can be tuned down if need be.

- The 144Hz does seem a little Tracey, but its not much of an issue, the picture is still nice, so don't get too down, I still noticed an immediate increase in quality over my old monitor.

- The options for this guy are pretty slim, however they all have their separate use, color depth, color temp, etc.

- If you play a game that has a HORRIBLE cross hair, don't worry, simply flick the "nipple" down and the monitor has its own built in crosshair, its rather simple, but it helps a lot when a crosshair is too small or too simple.

Now, there are some issues:

Like I said before, there is a tiny "trace" when doing simple tasks, mouse movement, etc, however it isn't that bad when you get into more screen-filling apps and games.

The I/O is rather barebones, an HDMI, DP, AUX, and a power input, however if you're using this for gaming, that shouldn't be an issue.

The build quality does feel kind of plastic and cheap, but then again, that is to be expected with the price.

I haven't had any experience with the included stand, due to me using a third party stand for my dual monitor setup.

Mounting could be complicated with certain mounts, as the back does pop out a bit, however a little bit of tough love solves every issue.

Overall, I enjoy this monitor, of course I'm replacing it down the line, but as of right now, it's comfy.

Thanks to whoever read this and I hope this review helped in the smallest amount, and that you guys have a good day!

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Assuming you have an adequate video card, this a great gaming monitor.

My primary use case:
I run a MacBook Pro M1 Max and PC simultaneously. I had some issues with PBP early on, and I actually started the return process, but I found a solution.

Initially the monitor would lose the USB-C connection whenever the screen saver engaged or the monitor went to sleep. I had to either unplug the monitor or disconnect/reconnect the USB-C or both to get it working again. It was a pain. I was using the USB-C cable (connected to the Mac). I replaced the AOC USB-C cable with a TB4 cable, and it's been working great ever since.

I was not happy having to use a $75 dollar cable to make the PBP work properly, but it does work now. I'm keeping the monitor.

Tip:
If you use PBP, you can use the monitor USB hub which works great. I've found using a Mac and PC is a bit of a challenge because of the difference in keyboard configurations, so I have a keyboard that is compatible with Mac and PC, but not wanting to use the monitors USB hub (less wires), I use synergy. It's allows you to share KM between multiple machines. It works great between a Mac and PC if keyboard is compatible with both. I'm very happy with it.

March 26, 2023 Update at the 5 month mark:
Using PBP - If you're using the HDMI ports, PBP really is plug and play, but when you mix HDMI with USB-C, it works, but you may have to mess with some of the video settings on the monitor connected to USB-C. I had a M1 Macbook Pro Max connected to USB-C. I had to manually change the MBP video settings to 2560x1440 using an aftermarket application (on board MBP settings didn't have that option). Using SwitchResX I was able to get 2560x440 @120hz, and it maintained the setting through reboot. Also, waking the MBP up was a chore sometimes. Occasionally I had to either turn off/on the monitor, reboot the MBP, and/or disconnect/reconnect USB-C.

AS for DP, forget it. I have yet to find a way to get PBP to work properly with DP. In PBP mode the monitor connected to DP aspect ratio will not change (on that 1/2 of the screen monitor maintains native ratio of 32:9-really stretched out), no matter the settings on your video card. In PBP mode, I got the same result connecting DP using a M1 MBP Max, M1 IPad Pro, and a PC. On the PC I tested using both an AMD VEGA 64, and NVIDIA Geforce RTX 3070 PCIe cards.

Bottom-line, if you use PBP often, both monitors on HDMI is pretty much seamless.

I use the DP connection whenever I'm NOT in PBP mode. Assuming your video card can handle it, DP can take full advantage of this monitors capabilities.

Comment: Even though HDMI 2.0 (monitor's ports) can handle this monitor's specs, my RTX 3070 (HDMI 2.1) connected to the monitor's HDMI will not get 5k resolution natively. I had to create a custom resolution using the Nvidia control panel, but I could only get it to 120hz so far, but it does seem stable.

Unlike the Acer version of the same panel, this monitor works really well with SDR and HDR modes, you just flip the windows HDR switch on and off. Acer has had this problem for many years with multiple monitors (I personally experienced) and it's a huge hassle they should've fixed many years ago. So I cancelled my ACER order and went with INNOCN. I think there might be some confusion with how it's picture defaults\modes are set up, but this is an unbelievable monitor! This will save you a lot of time: First off, if you are playing games with this monitor, HDR games, set the picture mode to SRGB and let NVidia auto switch between standard 8 bit and HDR 10 bit color. Works great, no glitches, huge difference in SDR desktop color and HDR games. Then calibrate HDR in windows, setting the lowest value to 0. You will get great blacks even with low local dimming. Put dynamic overdrive on 3 and local dimming to low. That's it, it works without effort and you're done!

I've been playing on an LG C3 for 2 years, and it's an amazing experience. I would pick this monitor over it any day. Any day! You get used to the dimness of oled and you think it's bright. Then you get a monitor that has 1100 nits of glorious HDR with mini led and sooooo many whole bright scenes put my C3 to shame. I'd say around half of the time my games look better with miniled than my oled. I think it has to do with the amount of lighting zones and it's resolution. It has as many minileds as the 4k versions so it appears 27inches, 1440p is the sweet spot for great miniled local dimming. The clarity, response time are wonderful. The color is wonderful at all times, not overblown, just vivid and clean. The sense of real light in my games is really noticeable with miniled over oled. It's like oled does a great expression\spin on HDR but miniled just brings the real thing. I don't worry about burn in anymore or my organic tv slowly degrading.

Here's the thing right now: from a gaming standpoint, the VA panel minileds are vastly inferior to the ips panel minileds. Be sure to nail that down before getting one or you might be really bummed. VA ghosting is unacceptable. Also, until the amount of miniled backlights increase, a 1440p 27 inch miniled monitor works better than the 27inch 4k versions because they have the same amount of backlights, so it's more accurate at 1440k. Review:
I purchased two of the Koorui 34‑inch curved ultrawide monitors for a dual‑monitor setup, and so far I’m very pleased with them. The picture quality is sharp, the brightness is solid, and the “Normal” color preset looks natural without any adjustments. For the price, these 34‑inch panels deliver very good performance.

That said, there are a few important details the product listing and reviews don’t mention — and knowing them ahead of time would have saved me some stress during installation.

1. YES, the 34‑inch model DOES include stand‑offs (spacers)
This is not mentioned anywhere in the listing, and even Amazon’s Rufus incorrectly says they are *not* included. They actually come in the small accessory packet with the manual.

If you’re mounting these monitors, you will need those stand‑offs because of the recessed VESA pattern. They are already in the box — just not advertised. I rushed to order a separate spacer kit because the listing didn’t mention it, so I’m putting this here to help the next person avoid that.

2. One of my monitors flashed briefly until I disabled FreeSync
On one of the two monitors, I noticed a quick bright “flash” when moving the mouse. Turning off Adaptive Sync / FreeSync in the monitor’s menu fixed it instantly. The other monitor didn’t have this issue, so it seems to vary by panel.
Not a defect — just something to be aware of if you see flicker or brightness pops.

3. Color and brightness match well once set manually
After setting both monitors to the same brightness, contrast, and color mode, they match very well side‑by‑side. The “Normal” color preset looks the most accurate on these VA panels.

4. Build quality and packaging are solid
Both monitors arrived well‑protected, and the included cables work fine. The stand is basic, but I’m using monitor arms, so that wasn’t a factor for me.

5. Too early to comment on long‑term support or durability
I’ve only had these monitors set up for a few hours, so I can’t speak yet to long‑term reliability or how responsive Koorui’s support is. I’ll update this review if anything changes over time.

Bottom line:
These 34‑inch Koorui ultrawides are excellent for the price, especially for gaming or a dual‑monitor setup. Just be aware that:

- Stand‑offs ARE included (despite the listing not saying so)
- FreeSync may need to be turned off on some units
- Picture quality is great once you match settings manually
- Long‑term support is still unknown

If the listing had mentioned the included spacers, it would have saved me a last‑minute order — so I hope this review helps the next person.

Today I set up my dual KOORUI 27" model N07 monitors. I was somewhat worried by multiple reviewers reporting that this model isn't really a 4K screen. So while I don't usually write reviews, I'm here to assure you the N07 is in fact a 4K screen with resolution of 3840x2160 and refresh rate of 60hz.

And I know why some people got this wrong. When I unplugged my old 1920x1080 monitors and tried to use the same HDMI cables, Windows identified the monitor as having a 1920x1080 native resolution. But my cables were very old. I plugged both my new monitors in using DisplayPort cables and they were instantly reporting 3840x2160. My monitors did not come with DP cables, just new HDMI cables. But my office had extra DP cables laying around.

If you're still having trouble getting 4K on one of these, be wary of adapters, such as DP-to-HDMI, DVI-to-HDMI, etc. Also try shorter or newer cables. You CAN get 4K out of HDMI cables, but remember that HDMI has been around since 2002 and that standard has gone through many versions with new capabilities over the years.

As for reviewing the other aspect of these monitors... they look great to me! Neither of mine had dead or stuck pixels. the colors look good and image is sharp. I'm not a professional monitor reviewer, but these seem like perfectly good office monitors for a fantastic price compared to big brand names. I took a chance on some of their smaller screens several months back and was blown away at the quality and low price. I'm glad this higher end model hasn't let me down!

UPDATE: My original review was written 10/13/2023 and now it's 5/16/2025. I have never had a single issue with these monitors in the 1 year 7 months I've been using them. text:
I am pretty skeptical about something holding a $1000 monitor, but I read the reviews here and decide to purchase one. It arrived in a neatly packaged box. All the components felt very sturdy (and a bit heavy). The instructions were really easy to follow for installation. It also comes with tools required to get everything tensioned correctly and installed.

The VESA bracket fit my 45” LG OLED ultra gear monitor almost perfectly (the monitor has a few minor plastic bits that stick out around the VESA mounting area, but was still able to get it to work.

The arm itself comes with integrated cable and tool management. I thought those extra were really nice and so far have worked really well.

You can adjust the arm sections to either rotate 90 or 180 degrees from their center (basically full rotation). This helped a lot with how I have mine setup.

The tension is adjusted pretty easily. For a monitor that is large and curved, you’ll definitely want someone to help you get the monitor mounted to the arm and screwed in. The pre-tension was pretty loose for me so we had to spend a few minutes tightening it, moving it around, and making sure it wouldn’t slowly fall down. Once it’s set though, it’s very easy to move, doesn’t make any noises, and blends right in with the other matte black items I had.

It’s a very nice monitor arm and I would recommend it.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
The monitor I am using is the SAMSUNG 49" Odyssey G93SC Series OLED (27.80 lbs). There are different versions of this type of monitor, with minor variations in the back mount. I read all of the reviews where people said this monitor arm would fit the G9, and during installation, those statements came into question.

If you take the factory monitor mount off of this monitor, you cannot directly connect this VIVO Premium Monitor Arm straight to the monitor as is. You will need the black metal wall/VESA mount that comes with the Odyssey monitor. I received my monitor about a month ago and, luckily, held on to it. With this part in hand, installation is rather easy.

As others have noted, there is some sagging taking place with this monitor once installed. I've tightened (greatly, as it seemed to have too much torque) the specific bolt that manages this articulation, and the sagging is no longer present. We will see how this holds over time. I will update this review if I have future issues with sagging. I live rather close to a railroad, so the slight vibrations will really put this bolt to the test. We will see.

The movement of the arm could be better, but for the price, this is great.

To any who has purchased or plans to purchase the SecretLab Magnus Pro XL Desk, this monitor arm definitely fits this desk. During the extensive research of building my office, this was a concern I saw all over the internet. I bit the bullet and purchased this monitor arm without knowing for sure if it would fit or not, a sacrifice for my fellow computer nerds that paid off. Currently, SecretLab does not have a monitor arm for sale that can support a monitor of this weight, but that is supposed to change soon, according to their website. Please do note that you will come across some installation issues when installing this monitor arm to the Magnus Pro XL; luckily, I am here to walk you through that process. *kiss face emoji*

The cable management tray is not too shallow to initially place the monitor arm, but it is too shallow to tighten the bolts on the bottom of the clamp to ensure your arm doesn't slide around. There are at least two ways to tighten the bolts; I know this because I mounted the arm in the center of the desk, fastened the bolts through a rigamarole process, and then realized that the monitor arm needs to sit several inches to the left to properly center the monitor on the desk. The second go around, I found a quicker way that involved tools that didn't come included. Below are both of the methods I used.

How to tighten the clamp on a Magnus Pro XL Desk WITHOUT extra tools::

- You will need to remove the two screws on each side of the desk that hold the cable management tray in place (4 screws total). Then you make your way to the remaining four screws on the bottom of the desk that hold the cable management tray in place. You DO NOT need to completely remove these screws; only loosen each screw a couple of turns, and the tray will sag enough to allow you to get the Allen wrench inside to tighten the monitor arm clamp bolts. Don't make my mistake; ensure that your monitor is positioned on the desk where you want it before tightening these bolts. You don't want to have to do this again. I moved mine 5-6 inches to the left of the center. The center can be found by looking at screw placements on the inside of the cable management tray. Once the bolts are tightened, tighten the 4 screws on the bottom, and reconnect the 4 screws that go on each side.

How to tighten the clamp on a Magnus Pro XL Desk WITH extra tools::

- Take a Dremel tool or any other saw/torch/etc., and cut the Allen wrench to a shorter length. I've included a picture of how short I cut my Allen wrench. This method is 100 times easier than the first.

I gave this monitor arm an overall rating of 5 stars, mostly because of the price. As for Sturdiness, I gave this monitor arm 4 stars due to some crucial parts being plastic, Easy to assemble got 4 stars, and Range of motion got 4 stars.

I would recommend buying this monitor arm, though if you have the patience, the SecretLab Ultrawide Monitor Arm should be available soon; that one will likely be a better quality and also look better.

text:
Does exactly what it claims to do. If you’ve purchased almost any of the available inexpensive portable 15.6” monitors off of Amazon, this literally fits it like a glove. I have a few portable monitors now, including the new Espresso. On my Innocn units, or my UPerfect or even my DragonTouch 4K portable monitors, even with their protective cases/screen covers attached, this padded case fits them like a glove. It’s not rigid in any way and as such does concern me a little when I’m carrying it in my Tumi backback on my back as I’m always worried about flexing the thin monitors. But thus far, it’s worked perfectly.

On the Espresso, which I really like overall, it -does not- fit. That’s not the fault of the case, really, it’s because the Espresso Touch 15.6” monitor has a fairly sizeable lower bezel resulting in a monitor height of just over 10” as opposed to most other portable 15.6” monitors being closer to 9.25”. Thus, as you’ll see from the photo, the Espresso stick out past the zipper.

But as long as your monitor fits, this is a good case. I may look to get some stiffening device to slide inside of this and then sandwich my monitor in there with the panels. These portable monitors aren’t much different than a monitor on a laptop, but when you close a laptop the lower part acts as some protection to the monitor.

But for the prices on here….and this is likely just a re-branded 15.6” laptop sleeve if we are honest….this is a good case. Just not for Espresso’s.

Installation was tedious but not hard. I haven't put a screen protector on any of my devices in years but its essentially the same process you go through, just at a larger scale, which made the bubble removing portion take longer. There were several bubbles I couldn't get out after spending maybe 45 minutes with the squeegee included, but they aren't visible unless the screen is off, so its not too big of a deal to me.

The reason I got this in the first place is because I have a 27" Apple thunderbolt display that I still use and the screen is very reflective and not retina, so the glare during certain times of the day makes me strain my eyes. But when I finally pulled the top off the protector after applying it, the glare was essentially gone. However, I had to increase the resolution on my monitor because now the text on the screen does have a slight blur to it, which is a concern because I do design work and clarity is really important.

TL;DR: this product is a bit tedious to put on, does reduce glare if you have a reflective screen, but it does downgrade the clarity of what's on the screen.

I’ve been using this Lenovo Legion 27QD-10 to replace my monitor and it's been a great upgrade! I now use my old monitor as a second one. The 27" display is just the right size that I was looking for as my old monitor was too small at 24".

Setup was easy as I expected and compatibility hasn’t been an issue. I’ve connected it to my PC without any trouble. It includes HDMI ports, along with DisplayPort and USB-C options so you'll have options regarding your setup.

Picture quality is very good on this monitor. The QHD resolution looks sharp and detailed and the 240Hz refresh rate makes motion feel very smooth. Colors look rich and not oversaturated. The visuals look natural whether I’m gaming or watching some videos.

The build quality feels/looks good and it is definitely well constructed. The stand is sturdy and completely adjustable so getting the right height and angle was easy. It’s also VESA mount compatible which is great if you prefer a wall mount or monitor arm setup. I currently have this on my desk without a mount but will be planning to get a monitor arm in the future.

The built in speakers work fine but I personally use a headset.

For the price, especially when on sale, I think this monitor offers a good value. You’re getting high refresh rate performance, good color accuracy, multiple connection options including HDMI, and a sturdy, adjustable design in one package.

Overall, this has been a well-rounded monitor that works great for my setup.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Since I have been quite of bit of hands-on data as well as report production and design work for the last few months, I recently tried several options for a portable monitor to use with my 14 Inch MacBook Pro. My requirements when I started were: light weight, single USB C/Thunderbolt (eg no separate power needed), and for it to be approximately the same size as the MacBook at least height-wise.

With my first purchase (and return) I quickly found out that despite the many options all touting the same specs, I had to add a few requirements. Shape (needed it to be 14 wide), built-in ability to stand on its own vs a floppy cover solution, and most importantly, reasonably accurate color. Also, pass-through power is a very nice-to-have so that there's only one USB C Thunderbolt cable connected to the Mac and power can connect to the monitor and pass back through to the Mac through the one Thunderbolt cable.

This monitor met all the requirements above. The color is -very- accurate. A side-by-side comparison to the other portables was instantly clear. No need to run through lots of tests (although I did try extensively to adjust them. The ThinkVision worked perfectly out of the box.

Another really nice feature is the way they implemented the "kickstand". It's not really a kickstand but more of a fold-out base. The connections are built in to that which offset them from the edge of the screen unlike all the others, which means you can stand it up right against the Mac even with cables plugged into both sides.

I -thought- I was going to have to trade off weight when comparing choices, but I am certain this is the same and possibly lighter than the Arzopa, my second choice. I don't have a precise scale to verify this. However I did a blind "place one in my hand" test and picked the lighter as the ThinkVision. If I can get my hands on a scale while I still have these I will update. Be aware that the specs claim the others are all lighter than the ThinkVision, which again I doubt. In any case, it is negligible either way.

Lastly, as a nice feature, it comes with a felt sleeve. This is perfect for my bike bag and backpack to protect against scratches or worse.

The one trade-off that is real is the price. This is approximately 90ish dollars more than several other appealing-looking options currently. Make no mistake, this monitor is worth that and more if you are planning to use it often at all. Personally I will always pay for true quality if a piece of equipment is clearly better than the rest. If you are a Mac user you probably feel the same. This monitor is a worthy companion for a road warrior, anyone who moves their work spot often, or just wants to keep their work space flexible.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
As far as portable monitors go, this is hard to beat. I initially selected this display after purchasing an ASUS MB16AC. That monitor was OK, but I found the case/ stand a deal breaker. The purpose of a portable monitor is to be _portable_ and the stand with the ASUS is not robust or easy to configure on an uneven surface. The crux of the issue is that the ASUS and other folio-style stands is that they don't allow continuous adjustment.

Enter the lenovo. It weighs about as much as the _case_ for the ASUS. It's stand offers stability and continuous adjustment just like a laptop. It offers 45w passthrough, which should be enough if your laptop only has one USB-C port or you're using a phone. And not only does it have ports on either side, they are not flush with the display surface. This allows the display to sit flush with your laptop display – something I didn't anticipate being one of my favorite things about this monitor.

All in all, the display panel itself is about as good as it could be. It's incredibly lightweight, easy to use on a variety of surfaces, it can be adjusted flush with your laptop panel, and the polyester sleeve / case does it's job. It would be nice to have a more robust case, but having seen older portable lenovo models with slide-on plastic cases that are cracked from use, I appreciate the durability of the sleeve provided with this model. There is also some coil whine when I power my Macbook Pro 13" from the display, but that doesn't bother me much personally.

I've gotten more use out of the Lenovo in the first week than the ASUS in about a year.

text:
It's well-built productivity monitor with excellent image quality for the price.

Text is easy to read and colours are accurate (albeit slightly washed out). Like most IPS panels, the contrast ratio is just okay. Viewing angles are good. Brightness is acceptable, but glare can be an issue in some conditions, e.g. a window behind you during daylight.

My 2021 Macbook Pro defaulted to driving this monitor at 960x540, but the image is perfectly sharp when "scaled" to its true native resolution of 1920x1080 -- though, with the Mac, that means UI text is quite small. However, if you're more than about 50cm away from the screen, the lower resolution may be preferable.

I would prefer a somewhat higher pixel density, but at 14" the FHD resolution is an acceptable 157 PPI -- about 70% of what would be considered "HiDPI".

I would also prefer a 16:10 aspect ratio over 16:9. I think 16:9 is an odd choice here, since this monitor is clearly intended for productivity rather than media consumption -- and most of Lenovo's own productivity-oriented ThinkPad laptops use 16:10 as well.

text:
owned Thinkvision M14 before: it was good but felt that the resolution was a bit lower and not enough brightness (300 nit).
This Thinkvision M14D is the second generation of Thinkvision M14 but with these improvements:
- up to 375 nit (yes, it looks a bit brighter)
- 4 color modes (Thinkvision M14 is only able to turn on/off blue light suppression by pressing a button at the side)

- resolution up to 2240x1400
