- the cable included sucks because it is not L-shaped. Had to buy an "L”-shaped USB-C cable (Fasgear 100W USB C to Type C 90 Degree Cable 3ft or similar - make sure if it supports video! many do not).
- not convenient to put it vertically because it presses buttons. So if you set it to stand vertically, you may be pressing a button by its weight and turn off the monitor from time to time
- touch screen version costs much more! I would go with a touchscreen version if it was more affordable
- small rubber pad felt off immediately from one corner, exactly as it was with the first generation.
- super portable because it is super thin and weights about a pound

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
As with many who are now in a semi-permanent work at home environment and live in a small apartment, a full home office setup isn't possible. Likewise the space (both workspace and storage) for a full second monitor isn't ideal for me. So, sick of working on the tiny 14" screen of my work laptop, I looked for an alternative. While there are a few portable options available, I decided on this one.

One of the prime drivers behind choosing this monitor was that it doesn't need it's own power supply, it draws power from the attached laptop without too much of a hit to overall battery life. I can also plug the laptops power into the monitor to pass through to the laptop at the same time. This means I can use the monitor anywhere with my laptop without the need for external power, or at worst, a single power brick.

While the monitor doesn't have the RGB range of some in the market, is not 4k and isn't touch, it is perfect for all my work needs. The image is sharp and clear. Colors are perfectly fine. It's as good as my laptop display, only larger. Video also displays fine on it so if I need to go on a work trip (or holiday) I can easily take this with me and watch something on it or hook it up to play a game (I wouldn't suggest it for those wanting to do serious gaming though).

It's super light and comes with a carry pouch. Noting the review where the user reported screen damage, I placed the protective cardboard from the original box in the sleeve and I am now confident I can transport it in my bag with little risk.

The only issue I had was when I initially connected it. I have some ugreen USB C cables and when I used those I got no image on the monitor and the computer didn't detect it. Using the included cable fixed that. It's not a fault of the monitor though and I may need to upgrade some of my other cables to ensure they can carry the appropriate bandwidth.

Overall I am very happy with this monitor. It is light and portable. It has more than doubled my screen workspace, and at the end of the day it is easy to pack away without needing much storage space. The fact I don't need additional power and the laptops power brick is enough for everything is a huge plus as well.

text:
Recently at work I switched from a single monitor setup to a double monitor setup and in doing so realized how much I loved it. At home I don't use a desktop, I use a laptop, so I wasn't sure what the options really were. I ended up originally with a cheaper second monitor, one that needed several cords to work, and while it functioned it was a bit clunky, and it always bothered me that I could never get the angle of the second monitor to line up with my laptop, because it couldn't be completely perpendicular when it needed a separate support to hold it up.

Then my husband's bratty cat (affectionate) decided to jump up on my little table thing and knock over that monitor, breaking half the display. I was very annoyed at the time, but that did ultimately lead to me purchasing this monitor, so maybe that was his secret evil plan along.

This monitor is awesome. I love that it's a single cord plug in (make sure your USB C is Thunderbolt or display capable, there are different versions!), I love that it perfectly lines up with my laptop in both look and size, and I love the base of it, so that I can actually have it at the angle I want it. It also feels a lot sturdier than my other one and is much more difficult to knock over. (The cat has already tried and failed.) One thing to note: I think given that it runs off your laptop, it's best not to leave it plugged in while your laptop is sleeping. I struggled for a bit with my monitor not coming on (keyboard would light up, but just a black screen) and having to restart repeatedly, until I started unplugging the monitor when I closed my laptop. Haven't had the issue since. My best guess is something battery related gets crossed.

All in all, very pleased with this! My husband 3D-printed me a little stand so it can sit right at the height I want it, too. It's exactly what I was looking for initially and works great!

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
TLDR: I'd definitely recommend this monitor for anyone needing a "home base" for a professional laptop setup, but may not meet the needs of a heavy gamer.

I'm gonna be completely upfront: I don't actually *own* this monitor, it was supplied to me from my work (I do analytics for a living) as a WFH supplement. That being said, I LOVE this monitor and I'm going to buy one when my work makes me return the one they loaned me.

Visuals & ports:
The image is crisp and colorful, has plenty of ports, and I could use this for casual gaming if I wanted. The monitor stand rises high enough to allow my laptop underneath without resorting to a VESA mount (I like my screen orientation as one atop the other instead of side-by-side) and connects seamlessly with my work laptop via USB-C to extend my display and charging concurrently. I linked this display to my two ultra-wide (21:9) 30" Sceptre gaming monitors via DP daisy-chaining, which brings my total monitor count to 4 if you include the laptop. I've had no issues with dead pixels, slow charging, or dead ports, either.

Accessibility:
There's a rubber strap on the back of the stand for cable management which is a huge plus for me as I'm a bit of a clean freak when it comes to desk organization. The slot in the monitor base is supposed to be for your phone, but it's not really accessible given my setup (I'd have to reach around my laptop) so I use it to hold a pen or other supplies instead for quick access. I've seen some reviews saying the phone slot is "unusable" but I actually use it a lot to hold paper clips, Post-It note pad, pens or other small office supplies instead. The base is firm enough to stay where you want it, but easy enough to adjust the tilt or height without issue, and is heavy/stable enough to take small bumps without tipping over.

Aesthetics:
This monitor is sleeek; it has ultra-thin bevels, a sturdy base, and overall feel that this monitor is a workhorse. I also like that the company logo is on the base instead of the monitor, which is a nice touch. The main design downside of this monitor is that the bevels are super slim, so I can't stick notes around the edges like my other monitors, and I also have to be careful about adjusting the monitor so no fingerprints are left due to the thin bevel.

Summary:
I'm mainly giving this monitor a 4/5 due to the inaccessibility of the slot in the base, and you can almost get two monitors for the same cost of this unit ($460 at the time of this posting). That being said, you're getting a lot of features for the money, and it's an excellent choice if you want to use this monitor as a sleek, professional main hub of your work/gaming layout.

text:
One usb-c cord to my laptop. Wireless mouse keyboard and Webcam plug into monitor hub. Genius! I don't use the usb-b upstream or the LAN but it's good to see those options in a high end monitor like this.

After one month, this one is going back. Great monitor with few frills but now the brightness swells in and out. Even if I can get that sorted, there are other options to explore at this price point. Without daisy chain I have to run another cable (hub or HDMI) from my laptop. And no PbP/PIP? I'd have to do the math on the bandwidth: seems unlikely we can get 2x4k AND USB 3.0 from a single USB-C connection? So... I may need an external USB hub after all.

1) single cord is EXCELLENT, but not without limitations. Of note, this monitor does NOT support daisy-chaining, so the single cord will only drive a single external monitor. I'm using two monitors (plus my laptop) now but needed to run the second on HDMI. Do I need a hub before the hub?

2) any sound bar with aux (3.5mm) in will work. I didn't find a decent one (yet) that runs off of USB power (from the monitor) so I had to run another power cord. There are pros and cons with that approach, of course - but I have ok(ish) sound now. Good enough for conference calls and background music, to take the headset off for a while!

3) a 32" in portrait is just too tall! I ordered a 24" to serve as a new hub - and to leave in portrait all the time.

I have a Linux desktop that's a bit old, but works well. I got a refurbished Lenovo L13 Yoga laptop which is newer and faster, and came with Windows 10, upgraded to 11. I immediately put in a 2TB internal SSD, installed Linux but kept Windows on half the drive. So... after a short time, I decided that getting a dock would make this all much nicer, and it did. I've been able to reduce cable clutter, have more USB 3 ports, and a wired network connection that doesn't interfere with the USB-C port (Don't know who designed the connectors on my laptop, but they don't both fit at the same time).

Got the refurb model of this dock, connected it up with no directions (there were none) and everything worked right off, with no extra drivers or settings. The audio works just like connecting a line out - all automatic. Even the on/off switch works to turn the laptop on and off. I believe it does not charge when off, which will keep it from overcharging. I'd imagine you could get around this if you needed to charge it while off.

As a bonus, it charges faster than the charger that came with my refurbished Thinkpad, which was not the original Lenovo charger.

By the way, I connected the speakers together with the desktop by using a simple Y-connector for the audio outputs.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I normally don't write reviews, however I had to do quite a bit of research before I landed on this one. Disclaimer towards all my views here, I bought this "Very Good" condition used on Amazon for around 140$ shipped. My attitude and rating reflect that price point.

I am able to connect this to my Macbook, it charges my laptop and I am able to get two DISTINCT external screens. It took some fiddling to do this. I have two external monitors I use, a Samsung Neo G8 32inch 4k 240HZ and LG 27inch 4k 144Hz.

My initial setup was to use this dock to power my mac and run the Neo G8 through the display port with a seperate thunderbolt input for the LG direct into the laptop via DP to TB cable. I was not able to get the Neo G8 to start up with either DP port on the dock. Neither the standalone nor the one that shares its chipset with the HDMI. I tried installing the DisplayLink drivers but it didn't recognize my monitors. I realized it may be my settings and permissions, but I'd have to weaken security too much through the kernel to do this just for DisplayLink. However, I found that the port was able to support DP to my LG monitor. So using DP to the LG, and then connecting my second monitor to the TB4 port on the dock via a DP to TB cable, I was able to get two distinct screens out of this. So before you go thinking that it doesn't work from one of the DP ports, check against another monitor. And use the DP port that's standalone (not stacked with HDMI) for testing, that one runs on a better chipset. Note that I believe that if you want to drive two screens on this, one of them must use the TB4 port. The others will all mirror each other if you're using a Mac.

The Macbook works with this, but it doesn't play well. For my needs it's sufficient after passing the setup headache. Things I still have to watch it for. I use my dock with my laptop in clamshell mode, laptop lid closed. Sometimes it wont wake from sleep using my keyboard, meaning I have to open the laptop, login. Sometimes an additional step of replugging the port in is needed. The audio jack in the front works from single port mic and audio. It's well powered but dont plug your headphones in and out all the time when it's docked. The system has to re-register that there is an audio device present and sometimes it takes a bit.

That all being said, I believe this is one of the better TB4 ports that you can make work with the Mac M1. If I had to spend 300$ on a dock, I'd probably go with Caldigit, more straight forward especially with everything having a thunderbolt converter cable these days. But for that price I could buy two of these at today's price.

Best of luck.

If you’re someone who travels for work and often finds your laptop screen just isn’t enough, this Cevaton 15.6″ portable screen extender is a game-changer. I recently took it on a business trip, and here’s how it held up—and what to consider.

**What I loved:**

* The extra monitor space makes a huge difference when you’re away from your full desktop setup. I could have my email or chat open on the laptop screen while working on a spreadsheet, drafting content, or video-conferencing on the second screen. It turned my laptop into a mini dual-monitor workstation, which is so helpful when you’re “on the go.”
* It’s genuinely portable. At home I might settle for large monitors, but when I’m traveling I’m in hotels, cafés, maybe airports. Having a screen that’s light enough to pack and easy enough to set up means I don’t sacrifice productivity.
* Setup was straightforward. With plug-and-play compatibility, the transition from “just my laptop” to “laptop + second screen” was smooth, which is critical when you’re working under time constraints or in unfamiliar places.
* The screen quality did its part: full HD (1080p) gives me enough clarity for reading documents, managing multiple windows, etc. The viewing angles and brightness were acceptable for hotel lighting and café situations.

**What to watch for:**

* Battery/port considerations: When you add a second screen, you’re adding additional power draw (either from your laptop or from the screen needing its own power/USB feed). On the road that means plugging in sooner rather than later if you’re not at a stable power source.
* Cable/port compatibility: Make sure your laptop supports the necessary connection (USB-C, USB-A + video out, or HDMI) and that you’ve got the right cables with you. Traveling often means you don’t want to be scrambling for adapters.
* Setup space & stability: In hotel rooms or small cafés, finding the perfect angle and stable place for an extra monitor took a moment. The screen is portable, but it still needs a stable stance and slight care.
* Weight/pack size trade-off: It’s far lighter and more practical than a full monitor, but you’ll still want to account for it in your bag and treat it like an added piece of gear, not just a cable.

**My verdict:**

If you’re traveling and you want to do more than just “check in” on email—if you want to work with multiple windows, spreadsheets, presentations, design tools, or video-conferences—this screen extender is absolutely worth packing. It turbocharges your productivity when your laptop’s built-in screen just isn’t enough. For mobile professionals, freelancers, remote workers, or anyone who frequently sets up “office away from the office,” this is a smart investment.

Would I pick it again? Yes—especially given how much more fluidly my travel-work days went once I had it. If you already do heavy multitasking while on the move, this Cevaton screen will feel like a small luxury that seriously pays off.

text:
**Background:** This order will be used with my wife's new work computer, a Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 12. Her old docking station was the kind that you click into the bottom of the laptop, and it is incompatible with this new one. We are on our own for home office setups, so I ordered this for her. She runs two 32” monitors, one portrait and the other landscape.

**Build Quality:** The build quality is good. Although the listing states it's refurbished, it looks brand new.

They provide you with many cords, including a USB C Thunderbolt cable. We had issues when we first set this up, and I started to stress and go down a wormhole. I was worried the doc was defective. My wife heard ones like these were causing issues at the workstation in the office. I was afraid we had to update the firmware of the docking station, and getting company support for your personal accessories can be an issue.
She experienced blurry images on the monitor, and when the laptop went to sleep, it would not turn on some or all of the monitors, even the main screen. Also, the laptop would not charge from the dock.
Well, my wife is more intelligent than I, and she tried different USB-C cords, and all the issues disappeared.

So Tips
-Make sure you plug the power brick into the correct slot. There are two power slots, but since they give you the 135-watt power brick, that is the one you have to find and use.
If you have any issues with connection or stability, don’t use the USB-C Thunderbolt cord they provide. Note that there are many different types of USB-C cords, and you want to make sure the cord you choose is Thunderbolt and quality. I would recommend at least a Thunderbolt 4 since the doc can transfer at 40 Gbps. Thunderbolt cables are very confusing, as there are many generations. I think they're up to Gen 5.

Bottom line: Dock works great with Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 12 with two large 32-inch monitors and super-fast Ethernet. The only issue is that the USB-C Thunderbolt cord they provided did not work well. It looks brandnew and works great once my wife discovers the cord issue.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I was in the market for a screen extender for my husband and me to use while traveling in our travel trailer and for my teaching job the rest of the time, at home. After considering several options, I found this one, and it turned out to be a perfect fit for both a PC and MacBook. It arrived packaged very nicely (think more like the old-school Apple treatment with the protection on the screens and around them, insets for separating the cord configuation options, insets for the 2 basic monitor configuration stabilizers). I've had it a little over a month (using it for long work days) and here's my experience with it, so far:

Pros:
Easy Setup: The extender is super portable and came with everything I needed to get started. It works great with both my MacBook and my husband’s PC. The setup was a breeze—no IT help required! However, I did check out the customer service, and they seemed professional and ready to assist if needed.

Versatile Screen Configurations: Let me just say first, I was pleased with the crispness and color and overall screen quality. The monitors are large enough to allow me to have multiple windows open at once, which is a huge help for virtual classes, grading, Outlook, Microsoft Teams, etc. I was slightly worried when looking at all the options online I wouldn't find a high-quality option and/or I would not find a solution I would find worked great, but I tried a few different configurations over the weeks, including having both monitors vertical, one vertical and one horizontal, and finally settled on having both screens on the right side of my laptop, stacked on top of each other. This is not one that is advertised, but it's what I love most and it does work great. To me, the horizontal setup enables more screen width usage, so everything can be stetched to the largest size and text can be read the easiest without magnifying the screen's contents.

Customization: This kit includes various cables and setup options to give you flexibility. Once set up, it was easy to adjust each screen's resolution and color profile through my Mac’s 'display settings' found under 'system settings'. I was able to fine-tune the settings until I had the perfect balance of dark, mid, and bright shades that worked for me. It's bright and cheery and the ability to look at more screens (instead of needing to cycle through tabs all the time) makes my work days a lot easier to get through and makes work actions faster (reading or copying from one screen to the other).

Cons:
Only really with my laptop setup, as there are Limited Ports on MacBook Pro: My MacBook only has two USB-C ports on the left side, which was a bit of a challenge. However, I'm here to tell you that if you have a macbook pro, it can still work great. I mention this as it might come in handy for some others with the same brand or who also have limited input options for the daisychaining: after some trial and error, we figured out a solution: we plugged the MacBook’s power cord directly into the right-topmost peripheral monitor (the white cord in the image showing the back of the two monitors, one on top of the other), then daisy-chained the two external monitors through the available MacBook ports. This allowed the laptop's regular power supply cord, via the right-side monitor, to supply power to the whole setup, including the laptop. It was a bit of creative thinking, but it works perfectly for me.

Final Thoughts:
Overall, I’m really happy with this purchase. I'm a minimalist and appreciate the simplification this offers for my actual work and also how it looks. The Laptop Screen Extender has been great for work and will also be for travel (there is a carry case that it comes with that I can slip inside my laptop bag). It’s affordable, easy to set up, and provides a flexible, high-quality solution for expanding your laptop’s display. If you're looking for a portable screen extender with two additional monitors, this is an excellent choice, and I’d highly recommend it!

**Laptop:** Lenovo ThinkPad T14

I have been using the FOPO 15" Tri-Screen setup because, a year ago, the largest portable tri-screen option was 14". FOPO was the first brand to offer 15" screens, and the quality at the time was impressive, although it was expensive at $400 last year. I might still be using it, but my new replacement laptop was slimmer in width, which reduced the screen frame by about 0.5 inches while maintaining the actual screen size. As a result, the FOPO mounting system no longer fit, since it requires attachment to your laptop. Even with Velcro and zip ties, it just wouldn’t work. So, I ended up discovering this new system.

One of the best features is that they are not attached to your laptop, making it easy to move your laptop around while the screens stay in place, in addition to the ability to rotate landscape to portrait on the fly or a few other layout options using the additional mounts.

The quality of these screens and the mounting system is far superior; they are constructed from metal and sturdy plastic rather than flimsy plastic like the FOPOs. Admittedly, this does make them heavier, but if you carry your laptop in a roller business bag, it's not an issue.

The first time I set it up, I found it challenging to figure out how to connect everything with the ports available on my laptop. However, if your laptop is relatively new with multiple USB-C ports (at least two), an HDMI port, and a USB-A port, you should be fine (or you can get a mini-hub). Reading the instructions and labels on the wires and monitors is essential, and they will work!

*I use a PC, specifically the ThinkPad T14.*

I highly recommend this Tri-screen setup if you need multiple monitors to work efficiently.

text:
If you are not familiar with Amazon Vine, it is basically Amazon trading free* products for honest reviews. You see a lot of Vine reviews that are cookie cutter and based on templates. I aim to make my reviews honest and non-cookie cutter (other than this intro and disclaimer).

* These items are not actually free as Vine members pay income tax on the items they receive. Therefore, I will never order something from Vine unless I actually intend to use it. I think this is important for readers to understand because it means I will never order an item just to provide a fake five star review to a company. If I review something as good, it means I actually enjoyed using it or it fills its intended purpose correctly. Items that don't meet my expectations will be reviewed accordingly.

Why I ordered this item: I run dual monitors at my desk and was tired of unplugging and replugging cables every time I moved my laptop around. This dock promised to handle 4K displays and come with all the cables I'd need, so I grabbed it.

Likes:

* Setup was straightforward. Plug in the power brick, connect the monitors, plug in the laptop and you're done. No software to fiddle with or drivers to hunt down.

* The dual monitor support is rock solid. I'm running a 4K display and a QHD display side by side and there's no flickering or lag when I'm moving windows around or video conferencing.

* This thing is built well. The metal construction feels substantial without being heavy, and it doesn't wobble around on my desk like some cheaper docks do.

* Port layout makes sense. The DisplayPort and HDMI are on the back where they belong, USB ports are easily accessible, and everything stays organized without cables tangling up.

* It's compact enough that it doesn't take up much space on my desk, which matters when desk real estate is limited.

No likes:

* The power brick is massive and finding a good spot for it was annoying. It takes up a lot of room behind my desk and the cable is just long enough to be frustrating.

* You only get one free USB-C port after you connect your laptop, so if you need multiple USB-C devices this gets tight fast and you will need a USB-C switch.

* The included USB-C cable is pretty short. For my setup, I had to use a longer one to get comfortable spacing.

* The front USB ports are spaced close together. Wide plugs block each other out, so I can't use two of my larger flash drives at the same time.

Would I pay full price for this product: Yes

Final thoughts: This dock does what it's supposed to do without any drama. If you need reliable dual monitor support and don't mind the power brick or higher price, it's a solid choice.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I've been using the Lenovo 40AY0090US docking station with my home office setup with my ThinkPad T14, and it's become an essential part of my daily workflow. I was tired of plugging and unplugging multiple cables every time I needed to take my laptop to a meeting or work from the couch, and this dock has solved that problem completely. One cable connects everything, which was exactly what I needed for a cleaner desk setup and faster transitions between docked and mobile work.

The build quality feels appropriately sturdy for a Lenovo product. It's got some heft to it, which keeps it stable on my desk, and the matte black finish matches my ThinkPad aesthetic nicely. The dock sits vertically with a small footprint, so it doesn't take up much desk real estate. There are status LEDs on the front that indicate power and connection status, which is helpful for quickly confirming everything's working properly. The single USB-C cable that connects to your laptop handles both data and charging, which is the whole point of a dock like this.

The dual monitor support works well. I'm running two 1080p displays through the HDMI and DisplayPort connections, and both monitors are recognized immediately when I dock my laptop. The included HDMI and DisplayPort cables are a nice touch since you don't have to hunt down your own, though they're pretty basic cables without any fancy features. For 4K displays, the dock supports up to 4K@60Hz on a single monitor or dual 1080p displays, which covers most use cases. I haven't tested 4K personally since my monitors are 1080p, but based on specs it should handle it fine as long as your laptop's GPU can drive those resolutions.

The 90W power delivery is adequate for most ThinkPad models. My T14 charges just fine through the dock without any issues, maintaining battery level even under heavy workloads. If you have a larger ThinkPad like a P-series mobile workstation with a more powerful GPU, you might need to check if 90W is sufficient for your specific model, as some of the beefier machines require more wattage. For standard T-series, X-series, and L-series ThinkPads, 90W should be plenty.

The port selection is decent but not exceptional. You get multiple USB-A ports for peripherals like keyboard, mouse, external drives, and other accessories. There's Gigabit Ethernet, which is essential for me since Wi-Fi can be flaky during video calls, and having a wired connection gives me consistent network performance. The audio jack works fine for headphones or external speakers. What's notably missing compared to some competing docks is Thunderbolt support and a wider variety of ports. This is a proprietary Lenovo dock designed specifically for ThinkPads with their docking connector, so it's not a universal USB-C dock that works with any laptop.

Setup was completely plug-and-play. I connected the dock to power, plugged in my monitors and peripherals, then connected the USB-C cable to my ThinkPad, and everything just worked immediately. Windows recognized all the devices, the monitors lit up, and my laptop started charging. No driver installation, no configuration, no troubleshooting. That seamless experience is what you're paying for with a first-party dock versus some cheaper third-party alternatives that can be hit or miss with compatibility.

The USB data transfer speeds are solid. I regularly move large files to and from external SSDs connected through the dock, and I get consistent USB 3.0 speeds without any dropouts or issues. I haven't noticed any bandwidth bottlenecks even when I have multiple devices connected simultaneously. The USB-C cable included for the laptop connection feels reasonably durable, though I'm always a bit paranoid about that single cable since if it fails, the whole dock becomes useless until you replace it.

One nice quality-of-life feature is that the dock supports wake-on-dock, so when I connect my laptop, it wakes from sleep automatically and all my peripherals and monitors come to life. Similarly, when I disconnect, the laptop transitions smoothly to using its built-in display and battery power. These transitions happen quickly and reliably, which makes the daily docking and undocking routine painless.

Now for some limitations and annoyances. The biggest one is that this is a ThinkPad-specific dock. If you have multiple laptops or if you switch between brands, this dock won't work with non-Lenovo machines or even Lenovo laptops that don't have the proprietary docking connector. This lack of universality is a significant drawback compared to generic USB-C docks that work with any laptop. You're locked into the Lenovo ecosystem, which is fine if that's your only work machine but limiting otherwise.

The dock doesn't have any USB-C ports on it for connecting USB-C peripherals, which feels like an oversight in modern docking station design. Everything is USB-A, which works for legacy devices but isn't ideal for newer accessories. There's also no SD card reader, which would've been nice for photographers or anyone who regularly works with camera cards. The lack of these features means I still need to use dongles or adapters for certain tasks.

The included microfiber cleaning cloth mentioned in the product description is such a throwaway inclusion that I barely remember it even came with the package. It's a basic cloth that you could get anywhere, and it feels like padding the feature list rather than adding genuine value. Not a negative, just kind of pointless to even mention.

The power brick for the dock is fairly large and chunky, which is understandable given it needs to provide 90W, but it does add some cable management complexity to your desk setup. The dock itself doesn't get particularly hot during use, which is good, though it does get slightly warm to the touch after several hours of operation.

Pricing is where this dock becomes a tougher sell. It's priced at the higher end compared to generic USB-C docks, and you're paying a premium for the Lenovo branding and guaranteed compatibility with ThinkPads. If you can find it on sale or through corporate purchasing, the value proposition improves significantly. At full retail, it feels a bit expensive for what you're getting, especially given the limitations around port selection and lack of Thunderbolt.

The reliability has been excellent over my four months of daily use. I haven't experienced any dropped connections, failed wake-ups, or other glitches that would disrupt my workflow. Everything just works consistently, which is exactly what you want from a docking solution. I don't think about it, which is the highest compliment I can give to infrastructure-type products.

Overall, the Lenovo 40AY0090US is a solid, reliable docking station that does exactly what ThinkPad users need it to do. It provides clean single-cable connectivity, supports dual monitors well, delivers adequate power, and works flawlessly with compatible ThinkPad models. The build quality is good, setup is effortless, and day-to-day reliability has been perfect. However, the ThinkPad-specific design limits versatility, the port selection could be more comprehensive, and the price is on the higher side. If you're a ThinkPad user looking for a hassle-free docking solution and the price fits your budget, this is a safe, dependable choice. If you need universal compatibility across multiple laptops or want cutting-edge features like Thunderbolt, you'll want to look at other options.

If you have a laptop, tablet, or phone that you want to use more peripherals with or connect to a larger screen, then you already know why you need a USB-c dock. Nothing beats their ease of use and universal fit and compatibility. Some of the main features that set this apart are MAC address pass-through, Wake-on-Lan, automatic firmware updates, and power button mirroring for Lenovo computers that let you turn the computer on using the button on the dock. Most of those features aren't going to matter to the average user, and you should probably save your money if you don't care about any of them. While the ports, stability, and functionality are great, it's important to remember that you may need a Thunderbolt 4 dock instead.

On apple devices, you won't be able to extend your desktop to two monitors. They will just be mirrored. Also, if you're running more than 1 4k display then you're going to need something more powerful unless you want to be at 30hz (ew). Finally, it's only going to provide around 65 watts to your laptop out of the 90 watts provided by the the included power adapter. This is very much meant for stable, efficient, but basic office use.

text:
I bought the 40AF0135US ThinkPad Docking Station Dual Monitor Hybrid USB-C with USB-A because I wanted to streamline my setup and go from laptop to fully docked without plugging in a thousand things like a raccoon in a cable drawer.

I tested this dock with both a MacBook and a Windows laptop, and the experience was very different depending on the machine. On the Windows laptop, it was exactly what you want a dock to be. Plug it in, connect dual large monitors, ethernet, and external speakers, and it just worked. No fuss, no lag, no flickering, no weird resolution issues. Once it was up and running, it quietly did its job and stayed out of the way, which is the highest compliment I can give a docking station.

On the MacBook side, it was not seamless. It required drivers and extra setup, and overall felt like more effort than it was worth. It did work eventually, but it was not plug and play and definitely felt like a pain compared to the Windows experience. This tracks, since this dock is clearly marketed toward Windows and ThinkPad users, and it shows.

Performance wise, once everything was set up, there were no issues at all. Dual monitors ran smoothly, ethernet was solid, and my external Bose speakers worked perfectly through the dock. My keyboard and mouse are Bluetooth so those were not part of the equation, but everything else behaved exactly as expected.

My one real hesitation is the price. It feels a bit high for what it does, especially since I have used other non name brand docks that handle similar setups for less money. That said, this one does its job very well on Windows, which is its intended audience.

If you are a Windows or ThinkPad user who wants a clean, reliable, one cable docking setup, this is a solid choice and does exactly what it promises. If you are primarily on a Mac, you might want to look elsewhere unless you are ready for a little extra setup drama. I did NOT knock down a star for anything mentioned in this review because it is marketed for Windows, and for that, it is effortless.

text:
My laptop is a 2024 Lenovo Legion Pro 7i with a 4080. Monitor is a Dell 1440p 32" 144hz display. This dock was connected to the laptop via an Intel certified Cable Matters TB4 cable (though the TB4 port). All of the Lenovo dock drivers were installed.

The Lenovo dock was intended to replace a TobenOne UDS035 dock which wasn't passing power through the TB4 port. Unless noted, the TobenOne dock didn't display any of the other symptoms noted below.

- The external monitor (plugged into this dock via HDMI) was getting intermittent patchy blurred areas and strange artifacts. Particularly when gaming.
- When changing between the laptop camera and the external Logitech USB camera, the display would momentarily flash off?
- My Logitch wireless gaming mouse plugged into a new powered 7 port Anker USB hub hung off the dock (via USB 3.0) started stuttering. I also tried connecting the hub through USB C and saw the same results.
- Power connector on the included Lenovo combo power/TB4 cord cord wouldn't seat. It almost looks like the connector has heat shrink going too far up the male connector, physically blocking it from seating. According to other reviews and a couple forums, some brave users are having luck trimming this plastic off. I didn't try.
- The TB4 connector on the above Lenovo combo cable barely seated in the laptop as it's physically a very large/long rectangle and it impacted with the triangular corner of the side 7 Pro fan ducting. I believe this problem is only applicable to the 7 Pro (4080/4090) models of the laptop.
- The TB4 portion of the connector was so large it was pulling down on the TB4 port. This alone ruled it out for me.
- The "official" Lenovo dock tool software application said no firmware update was required. Other users reported v3 of the latest firmware resolving similar issues to what I was seeing.
- The standalone Lenovo firmware update tool was repeatedly failing, throwing a vague error. Searches on the error suggest it's a common problem with no known solution that Lenovo has aware of at least since early 2024. Some people claim to be able to still update via Linux. I tried running an Ubuntu Live image but couldn't find the Linux version of the firmware update.
- No power was being passed through the TB4 cable from the dock to the laptop. This was also the case with the TobenOne UDS035 dock (and why I wanted to replace it).
- The 300 watt power brick for the Lenovo dock is huge. Maybe 50% bigger than the OEM 330 watt laptop brick.

Bottom line is this: Either there are compatability issues with my laptop, the firmware on the dock is out of date, I recieved a defective dock, or this dock is just junk. Whatever the case, I'd avoid this dock if you're running a Legion series laptop or wanting to power your laptop via TB4.

If you're looking for an alternative, check out the TobenOne UDS035 dock listed above. It lacks some of the rear 3.2 ports, but is getting the same FPS gaming through it that I see directly connected via HDMI and/or just using the laptop's display.

text:
I've always had a laptop dock at my desk. It just makes connecting the laptop so much easier rather than having to plug in and disconnect multiple cables when going portable. My new Thinkpad Carbon X1 Extreme Gen 2 uses Thunderbolt instead of a proprietary dock, so I picked up this unit.

Yet so far it seems to handle everything I need. I have two monitors connected, Ethernet, audio cable, and all the USB connectors filled, including one going to a filled 10 port USB3 hub.

The big annoyance I have with this dock is that it has trouble syncing two monitors. With my old proprietary docks it was instantaneously synced. With a fresh boot of the computer this dock will first display on one screen, then switch to the second, then switch back to the first, then back to the second, etc., etc. in an eternal loop. To fix it I turn off the second screen, wait for the first to stabilize, and then switch on the second screen and it works fine. This loop doesn't happen if I always use the on/off button on the dock. As long as I use that button to put it to sleep and wake it up the dock only does a single cycle of syncing the monitors and it's fast enough that it's not crazy annoying. So, one star off because dual monitors are not as smooth as proprietary docks.

They came out with new firmware for the dock in January 2020. Prior to the firmware update the hub had trouble syncing, but eventually worked. Now, nothing. Every screen black. Tried all kinds of things including different monitors and cables, etc. I now have to plug one monitor directly into the laptop.

**** UPDATE 02/11/202

Contacted Lenovo support. They over-nighted me a new unit. This new one works. For the first time it boots up with two monitors connected without any sync issues. So, either the first one was bad or they fixed something over the past 6 months.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I believe the other reviewers are not understanding the purpose of the Smart Dock. They should have picked up Lenovo's standard Thunderbolt 4 Universal Dock instead (which has also been perfect operationally for over 100 end users under our management).

We have had zero issues with the Smart Dock while deploying internally or across clients. The Smart Dock is designed to be used with Lenovo's deployment software and Smart Dock Console which ties the devices to Microsoft's IoT solution (which is why they say Microsoft Azure on the front). Not only can we pre-provision docks with misc controls for offices and home users, we can manage each client's dock ecosystem in the cloud as well. This means verifying updates and connectivity checks across all docks at once vs having to manually update each one via a cable connection.

The Smart Dock also has built in WiFi which is a nice addition to make sure the dock can call home. We only use a separate IoT wireless network for these and do not put them on the primary VLAN(s).

Our only concern so far has been the lack of firmware updates being released (the Universal TB4 has had quite a few since release), and the portal went down one time while were in the middle of a deployment. Neither of these have affected the operation of the docks.

For calrity as well, most users run their laptop with two additional screens without issue. Our entire team have 38in ultrawide monitors (3840 x 1600) next to LG Dual Ups (2560 x 2880) without a single video issue. Video calls are also not a problem.

Cannot recommend enough for IT departments or teams looking to centralize docks.

Port selection and thoughtful extras make a difference. Four USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type A ports plus a Type-C port and a Thunderbolt 4 port give me plenty of room for peripherals. text:
The product arrived quickly and in good shape - only a couple of scuffs suggest it was pre-used. The refurbisher included what appears to be a brand new 135 W power supply which is great. Unlike some reviewers, mine came with keys to lock it.

Initially I had some problems with the dock connecting to my laptop (T580). The switch you slide to connect the ports once the laptop is in place was sticking and not connecting properly. I realised that the issue is the notebook needs to be seated *perfectly* in the cradle for it to work as it needs to depress several switches on the dock to allow the switch to unlock and slide. Once I'd practised putting it in and out a number of times it seemed to finally work.

I was still having some video issues at first. I began to notice flickering in dark spaces on my screen that worsened over time. After investigating I found that the problem was the connection again. I have the extended capacity battery for my T580 and this made it sit not quite flush with the dock, even though there is a small divot in the back of the dock that's supposed to accommodate it. I solved this by putting a small cardboard shim under the portion of the dock where it connects to the USB-C ports. This raised it enough that the connection was good and it stopped flickering/disconnecting.

Lastly, I can't seem to get my 4K monitor working at 60 hz. I have a 1440p and 4K monitor attached through DP. I was able to have both running at 60 hz using a DP to USB cable to connect each monitor to the USB C ports on my laptop. One ran through a USB-C hub that allowed me to connect the USB-C charger. But this doesn't work with the dock, which is frustrating because it's supposed to allow 4K/60 hz, but not a deal-breaker.

Overall, I would not even consider paying the original MSRP for this of $400+. But for ~$120 refurbished this is a good deal.

I was really interested in giving this a try. As a remote worker, my laptop has phenomenal security measures when I'm logging in from coffee shops, diner, libraries and just about anywhere else I can think of. Yet all of those security features don't do anything when someone looks at my screen.

To start, the package came with a lint cloth to clean the screen, 1 privacy screen filter, the supplies to attach in two different ways and instructions. The instructions were easy to understand the product was easy to use. Once attached to my laptop screen, there was a difference in the brightness. It wasn't a bad thing and might help with less eye strain. I also ran some tests, looking at my laptop from different angles with the privacy screen filter off and on and and there was a clear difference. From an angle, the privacy was much greater. Straight on, no change but it says that in the product info and if you couldn't see it straight on what use would it be?

Finally, I did some testing because I wanted to see how durable and customizable it was. My laptop screen is less than 20 inches so I cut this privacy screen filter down to size. Because it's a film, I was able to customize it and make it fit perfectly. I used a rotary cutter on a self healing mat and was able to get a clean cut. Cutting it didn't alter the privacy aspects and it still functioned correctly. Another thing to note is if you decide to stick it directly on your screen, it's almost completely un-noticeable as you can see in the corners of the image. The adhesive is 3M and comes off easily if you decide to remove the privacy screen filter or have concerns about it sticking to/damaging your screen,

All in all, I'm really impressed with this privacy screen filter. Well priced, performs as advertised, customizable, easy to install and arrived within just a few days of ordering. If you want extra security, this is the perfect choice.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Worked perfectly on a Lenovo ThinkPad X200 UltraBase (43R8781) with a X200 Tablet converting the "Display Port" output to "Dual Mode" DVI. It appears to be a "Active Device"; some converters are "Passive" and may not have all the pins required or support higher resolutions. I am running dual external monitors at 75Hz.

"DVI-D (Dual Link)" is important because many high-res monitors require almost all of the pins present on the mating connector. You should see 8 long x 3 deep male pins (24) + 1 ~2mm flat pin parallel to the connector = DVI-D (Dual Link)
*The missing 4 pins that go around the flat ~2mm pin are for an analog signal or potentially USB, most monitors/outputs usually do not have these pins but check and see...
**This adapter DOES NOT have the 4 analog pins so make sure to use a DVI-D single or dual link cable.. (This means its a DIGITAL ONLY device...) This is fine because most monitors that have a DVI connector do not have (or utilize) the extra 4 analog pins.

Rules:
1. You cannot run the laptop screen and two external monitors (laptop limitation).
2. You can run an Analog (old school VGA) and a Digital (DVI-D Single or Dual link) monitor at the same time.
3. There are Display Port to VGA converters if you have two "VGA" external monitors; the picture is MUCH better with DVI and the screen scales better with less flicker.
4. Windows 7/8 should remember your "docked" external monitors and when out and about, it will default to the Tablet screen.
5. A cable IS still needed to get from the adapter to the monitor:
5b. Make sure you get a good Male to Male (DVI-D Dual Link) cable...
5c. It should have ALL 25 PINS and be well shielded to take advantage of higher resolutions and refresh rates. (see above)
6 . Good Cable = "9to5Cables Premium DVI to DVI Digital Dual-Link Cable (10 Feet) - w/Aluminum Shell Connectors" on Amazon

This is given as friendly AS-IS advice only, do not rely on it and do your own research on your hardware.. Hope this helps. -R

All my USB devices worked, and both of my HDMI monitors (3440x1440 and 2560x1440) worked fine. But after the computer went to sleep and woke up again, only one of my monitors was active. Windows "Display settings" said there was only one monitor connected. I tried everything I could think of -- rebooting, power cycling, plugging and unplugging every HDMI connector, and the USB-C plug from the docking station to my laptop. I tried several other things, including buying a 100W power supply to replace the 65W one that came with my laptop. No joy. It was time to try a different docking station.

I went back to Amazon and found a Baseus Spacemate docking station that had the functionality that I wanted. It was almost twice the price, but I didn't know what else to try. Amazon offered overnight, early morning delivery, so I bought it. When it arrived I had a very nice out of box experience. Even the cellophane wrapping around the box was done to precision. The box was a work of art, with everything fitting precisely, like a precision machine. It was the same feeling I have when unboxing a new iPhone, where they think of everything, and you want to keep the packaging.

Regarding the docking station itself, It has the feel of a very quality unit -- a good, hefty, solid feel. I liked it before I had connected up a single cable. After connecting everything up, I turned it on (using my 100W power supply), and it just worked -- as advertised. It is only very mildly warm to the touch after running with everything turned on for a couple of hours. There are two downsides compared to the other docking station I had tried. First, the 2X price. Secondly, it's quite a bit bulkier, and I probably wouldn't want to travel with it. But in my case, if I'm traveling, I don't need all the other peripherals, so I don't need the docking station on the road. (OK, one complaint -- the printing in the little user's manual was WAAYYY too small for a person of my age to read.) I'm very happy with the Baseus unit, and I'll soon recover from the higher price. I hope I'll still feel the same way in a year.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I am running a Macbook Pro 2016 with Touchbar. I've been looking for a dock that would ultimately end the "dongle hell" as I've been running off of those dongles for over a year and between them sliding out, poor performance or simply having to disconnect and connect other dongles to accomplish other items, it was a frustrating experience. Enter in when I decided to purchase this item last week, DisplayLink technology which is leveraged in the docking station has had issues with Mac OS 10.13+, however, the latest beta of Mac OS Mojave has re-added support in for DisplayLink allowing these to work properly and I went ahead with the purchase. I have been quite pleased, there is certainly performance differences such that DisplayLink causes some delays and that can be an aggravation factor at times but having the ability to be back to a "normal" setup, I can honestly say, I am more than pleased with the experience thus far. Read below for the full review.

Pros:
* Multiple Displays
* Plethora of Ports
* Built-in Ethernet
* Headphone and Microphone Jack

Cons:
* DisplayLink Software Performance
* Secondary USB-C port limited to 1.5A
* No Memory Card Reader
* Third Monitor Port not HDMI/DP

Initial Setup:
I initially unboxed everything and downloaded the DisplayLink installer, I ended up having to manually configure the DisplayLink agent for the mac as it did not auto-install itself. The installation will require a reboot. After doing this, I then hooked up all of my monitor cables and a couple USB devices. I connected my Mac power adapters USB-C / Thunderbolt cable from the docking station to my Macbook. I could only get a single monitor to display (The 2K one not the 4K which is a direct pass-through). After going through all other options, I used the provided cord instead of the one from my mac power adapter and the 2nd display turned on and ready to use! Therefore, DO NOT use your mac power adapters cord but rather use the provided cord with the unit, otherwise the 4K HDMI/DP WILL NOT WORK.

Up and Running:
The unit is nice and compact, leaving me with being able to hide it behind my monitor and attach it to the laptop. I can easily switch between more of a "desktop" environment and go mobile quickly without worrying about the 5 dongles that used to be thrown about and worrying about connecting each one (or as it happens, searching for said dongle after it falls off of the desk). I am now using 2 HDMI ports, the Ethernet port, all 3 USB ports. The only port I am not using is the headphone port as there is not a need to do so since I work from my home office and noise is not of a concern. The performance has overall been "good" not "great". This is mainly due to the DisplayLink drivers sometimes causing a bit of a visual lag or causing a lag with the Macbook itself. This is not a consistent problem but does happen from time to time. That's not necessarily a hardware issue but rather a software issue with DisplayLink which will slowly be ironed out (they are not known for their quickness in resolving problems).

Future Considerations?
* Having a memory card reader.
* Having a secondary usb-c / thunderbolt port that is not limited to 1.5A.
* Removal of DisplayLink technology
* Change the 3rd display port to be the same as the HDMI/DP

As a guy who works in IT I never would have believed that any laptop in 2023 would ever go back to only working with one monitor after almost any laptop made in the past 5 years would easily work with 2-3 monitors. As I started to support people using M1 and M2 Apple laptops I was baffled to find that they only work with one monitor. My first assumption was that my co-workers didn't know jack diddly squat since obviously I'm the expert here. Imagine my humiliation when I found out they were right. This has kept me up at night, so here I am venting about it to my fellow Amazon explorers.

Apple just keeps making my life harder by convincing people that their bantha poodoo computers with 8GB RAM in 2023 are better than my professional recommendations.

What is DisplayLink? - All you need to know is that it enables laptops that only support one monitor to work with two monitors. It basically works by compressing display data so that there is enough bandwidth to send data to a second monitor on a poopy data pipeline. Magically, it makes a useless Apple laptop a little more tolerable.

There is one downside I've noticed while using this. A lot of my co-workers use this with the laptop display on as well as 2 external 4K monitors. The first external monitor works fine, but the second extra monitor has a noticeably lower frame/refresh rate. It's fine if you aren't watching videos or doing anything graphical. (Not like their laptop could handle that stuff in the first place) Most people just make that their email or spreadsheet monitor. I would assume that this probably only happens with 2 4K displays. I don't have other displays to test unfortunately. People obviously still prefer to have a slower second monitor than no second monitor at all. However, regardless of how annoying that downside might be, I don't blame Plugable. I blame Apple. Plugable is performing miracles by creating something out of nothing. Apple is just creating a demand for miracles.

The last helpful thing you should know is the difference between Plugable's DisplayLink docks vs their Thunderbolt 3 Docks... If your laptop has a Thunderbolt port AND (the important word is 'AND') has a CPU/GPU/APU that supports 2+ external monitors then you definitely want the Thunderbolt dock. You will have plenty of bandwidth to use multiple 4K monitors at the same time at full speed. If you are moneybanks enough to have a high-end Apple laptop with a slightly less poopy CPU that supports 2+ monitors you will also want the Thunderbolt 3 dock instead. It works fine.

DisplayLink Dock - Makes a poopy computer better than it was. If your DisplayLink dock could talk they would tell your lappy, "It's okay little guy, I'll try to translate your sign language so the other monitor can understand what you're trying to say."

Thunderbolt 3 Dock - Makes your monitors treat your laptop like the champ it is. If your Thunderbolt docky could talk this is what it would look like:

Bought these for some users in our office and installed them today. They have good viewing angles for the user (not too precise) but offer good privacy protection at an angle.

The Anti-glare was specifically requested by one of the users, so I'm glad that was included on this.

The multiple mounting options included made it perfect for figuring out the right option for our users. You can either adhere the privacy filter to the screen itself with double-sided adhesive strips, or place clear plastic tabs around the bezel to create a "slot" to hold the filter in like a loose picture frame.

I tried the tabs first, since they would be the easiest to reverse/modify if there was an issue. They worked okay, but one of the keys to getting a good picture for the user is for the filter to be pressed tightly against the screen.

I settled on a compromise, adding a few tabs around the bezel to be safe, and using the smallest adhesives just in the corners so that the screen stays flush. The adhesive isn't as noticeable as I feared (though still slightly visible) so it probable would have been fine to use the larger strips and not use the tabs. Since they include plenty of all mounting options, I can always switch to the larger strips in the future if they don't work (sometimes when the monitor heats up it can reduce adhesion if you don't have enough surface area).

Overall, seems like a good product, does its job (though I haven't done any blue light measurements). I was a little confused over why there was the option to turn it around and have a glossy side instead of a matte (glare reduction) side. Maybe the glossy side is less prone to smudging/scratches? Either way, it serves our purposes, and for less than any of the other reputable options I saw on here.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
tl;dr:
• multimonitor works on Linux
• 75-85% off makes it a hell of a deal
• Lenovo cheaped out on the AC adapter, but it's fine

I picked this thing up because it's compatible with my personal laptop, which despite having a Thunderbolt port, doesn't support my existing TB3 docks. (I think this is for want of PCI-E bandwidth; my TB docks are dual 4k but the laptop's TB3 lane is only 2x.)

My first complaint about this thing is that it didn't actually come with a slim-tip AC adapter. Instead, it came with the old barrel-type and a very short adapter cable. That adapter cable caused problems for me, but I only noticed the problem after I had dropped and stepped on it, so that may not be Lenovo's fault at all. The problem is that due to slight tweaks or a will o' the wisp, the power would get cut to the device, and when it powercycled, my monitors didn't come back. I picked up a very cheap, third-party, aftermarket slim tip adapter with decent reviews, and I've had no problems of that kind since.

LIMITATIONS:

For multi-monitor use, the bandwidth limitations on the two DisplayPort ports on the dock allow only 3840x2160@30Hz each. This can be troublesome if your monitors use more bandwidth than that. Both monitors I have hooked up are that way: one is 3840x2160@60Hz and the other is 2560x1440p@165Hz. This means that with both plugged into the dock, sometimes only one will show up or give any output, but this can be worked around. Additionally, each DisplayPort port is paired with another video port of a different type, and only one of each pair can be used together. So it supports only two monitors. I have had no success daisy-chaining standalone MST hubs to try to add a third monitor, but I have only tried with one so far.

LINUX QUIRKS

You will need a recent Linux kernel for this to work. I'm running Linux 5.3 on NixOS.

Additionally, sometimes a monitor will not show up in the KDE graphical display management tools, even though it is visible in the output of `xrandr -q`. Even when the graphical display is broken, however, VTs pretty much always work. So I have gotten my monitors to behave by instructing xrandr to set the resolutions and refresh rates from the virtual terminal, then quickly switching back. My shell is Fish, so the command in my specific case is this:

sleep 10s; xrandr --output DP2-1 --mode 2560x1440 -r 60; xrandr --output DP2-2 -m 2560x1440 -r 60

and then switching back to the VT of the display server.

OTHER NOTES:

The laptop runs really hot most of the time when it's closed and pushing as many pixels as it can on the two external monitors.

text:
I had previously ordered the Mac version of this doc for my Mac setup, and I was so happy with it, that I ordered ordered this dock for my windows (work) setup. It is every bit as nice as the Mac version, so I’m going to leave this very similar review, at the risk of being redundant.

This is really a beautiful and functional dock. (Unlike my Dell dock, which sat on the floor under my desk, and is now getting thrown away). I'm not going to get into the features, because you can learn about those easily enough from the Amazon description, but rather, I just want to say what really impressed me about the dock. Nor, am I really posting photos of the dock itself, because it's not necessary. It looks just like it does in the amazon photos.

Let's start with first impressions. The box and packaging are very nice, compact and efficient and it feels like quality.  I would compare the packaging to any Apple product I've purchased. This dock did not come in a felt-like bag like the Mac version, but since it cost a lot less, I’m personally totally fine with that. It's not really a big issue for me, because I throw away that stuff after the set up, but if I were buying this dock as a gift for somebody, I'd be happy knowing THEY were gonna be impressed when they opened it up.

If you need them, the instructions are simple and straight forward, but the unit is plug and play, so again, no big deal. I was very happy to NOT have to download display drivers for this unit. (Just one less step.). HOWEVER, I did have an issue setting it up for my 2 4K monitors. (The 1080p monitors were no trouble at all.). To avoid this issue, make sure your laptop supports DSC or Display Stream Compression. Ultimately, mine did but it required me to make a phone call to my IT department to adjust some setting on the lap top.

Which brings me to a comment about TobenOne’s customer support. A simple email to them started the conversation to resolve my monitor issue, and their customer support is fantastic. They are very knowledgeable about their product, prompt, concise, and very polite and helpful. I sent them photos of my setup, and screen shots about the laptop’s capabilities, and they identified the problem immediately. They really were a pleasure to work with. But I digress.

What I really like about this dock, is the weight and the feel of the product.  It feels well made, not flimsy or cheap.  It is a solid anchor for the laptop to sit on top of the unit.  The flip up tabs are substantial, and well built.   The rubber feet on the dock and the tabs keep a firm grip on the Laptop.  The laptop does not move around easily on top of the dock, which is nice and feels solid. The dock is also pretty much completely hidden under the Dell Laptop that I use for work.

The power button on the side, and the card slots on the side are not as easily accessible as front mounted slots.  But since the laptop is sitting on top of the unit, that would not be an option, and since those features are not an everyday utility for me, it's not an issue.  I do like having a power button to turn off the dock, to shut down the peripherals, but the laptop continues to charge. If you are concerned about battery memory, and leaving your laptop plugged in all the time, just unplug the host cable.

I'm also happy about the 3.5mm audio port.  The sound was excellent through a pair of 3.5mm headphones, which I wear during zoom meetings to block out outside noise. Sure I could plug them into the laptop as well, but that is the POINT of having the dock. To be able to pull one plug and run with the laptop.

Two last points. First, I ran a speed test to make sure the ethernet cable was delivering the speed I was paying my ISP for. (if you do this, turn off wifi first). I have a cat 6. Cable plugged into the dock.  Download registered at 738.2mbps and upload registered at 28.4mbps. Obviously, superfast, and very nice. But I am happy to know the dock is not impeding the speed I'm paying for. Secondly, I'm happy it has a security lock option on it. I'm using it at home, for now, but I am going to bring it to my office and I am DEFINITELY locking it up, because I would be very sad if it grew legs.

Final thoughts, This is a beautiful, functional and quality built dock for my Dell Laptop, and much nicer than the brick Dell dock that work gave me.  I feel like the price point is well worth the quality of the build and the function and features. The only suggestion I would make to a buyer considering one, is make a list of what you what to plug into it, to ensure it has enough ports for the devices on your list, and pay attention to the type of port your devices require. If your list matches up with the ports the device offers, buy this thing. It's well worth it.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This 18-in-1 USB-C docking station is a serious desktop hub that turns a single laptop port into a full workstation. I’m using it with a Dell laptop, and setup was straightforward: plug in the included 120W power adapter, connect the USB-C host cable, and everything comes online.
The port selection is excellent. You get two HDMI ports and a DisplayPort, allowing multiple external displays. On a Windows system you can run up to three external monitors plus the laptop display, and the dock even supports high-resolution output up to 8K depending on the configuration. On macOS, you can still connect multiple monitors, but macOS limits them to mirroring the same extended display rather than independent desktops.
Power delivery is another strong point. The dock’s 120W adapter supplies up to 100W to the laptop, keeping it fully powered through the USB-C connection. There’s also a 30W USB-C charging port, which is great for quickly charging an iPhone, iPad, or other device while you’re working.
Beyond displays and power, the connectivity options are extensive:
• USB-A and USB-C ports with both high-speed and standard data options
• Gigabit Ethernet for stable wired networking
• SD and TF card readers for quick media transfers
• 3.5mm audio/mic jack for headsets or speakers
The dock itself is solid metal construction and feels very well made. Everything works reliably and it has enough ports to handle monitors, peripherals, storage, and networking all at once.
The only real drawback is weight. Between the dock and the 120W power adapter, the setup comes in at a little over two pounds, so this isn’t something you’ll want to throw in a travel bag every day. It’s clearly designed to live on a desk as a permanent docking solution, where that weight actually contributes to a stable, high-quality feel.
Overall, this is a very capable and versatile docking station that turns a laptop into a full desktop workstation with a single cable. If you want a powerful multi-monitor dock with lots of connectivity and strong power delivery, this one performs extremely well and earns a full five stars. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I really wanted to give this five stars, but I cannot do in good consious. First - this worked right out of the box. I connected it to my Lenovo laptop fine. Currently, my second monitor is an old VGA monitor which works great so I haven't upgraded it yet. I connected via a VGA-HDMI conversion cable. That worked fine, but I do wish this included a VGA port (but in 2026, I would not knock a star off for that). But it does have a Dislpay Port for another monitor which is good. The number of ports are fine, but I do wish there was another USB Type A port (a much less expensive docking station I have as 5 of those - this only has 4), but two of the four are USB3.1 @ 10 Gbps. There are 3 "usable" Type Cs (the 4th is the Host port for your laptop), with 2 of them at 10Gbps. That is acceptable. The SD/micro SD card slots are necessary as is the RJ45 Ethernet port. The 3.5mm audio jack works fine as well. So it checks a lot of boxes.

What is not very good is the fact that the labels on the ports are barely readable. The color contrast makes it almost impossible to tell what port is what in anything but the best of light - or even using a magnifying glass. What is worse is that the label on the device does not match the label in the manual or product page. The USB C 480 Gbps port is not labeled consistently and is reversed with one of the 10 Gbps ports in the manual and the web page. I don't like that so I have to knock off a star. I even produced my own labels so I know what is what.

Know aslo that this is not a true Thunderbolt dock. It states that it is compatible with a Thunderbolt port, but it does not provide the bandwidth of a Thunderbolt dock. Now those are usually more expensive, and the word "Thunderbolt" does not appear in the title of the product item, but they do use Thunderbolt in the detaisl. Just know what you are getting. I believe the product description is a bit misleading.

text:
Excellent Dual Monitor Docking Station with Smart Display

This TobeOne ONE USB-C docking station has been a solid addition to a home office setup. It has been in continuous use with a Windows laptop for about a week.

Smart Display Feature:
One standout feature is the built-in smart display on the front of the dock. It shows which HDMI ports are active and the resolution they’re running at (for example, “HDMI 0: 3840×2160 60Hz”). This is very helpful for confirming monitor settings or troubleshooting display issues without needing to dig through system menus.

Display Performance:
The dual HDMI ports work reliably with two monitors on Windows. One monitor is running at 4K@60Hz and the other at 2K@144Hz with no noticeable issues. Image quality is clear and stable, which is important for daily work like video calls and multitasking across screens. It also supports 1080p@144Hz for higher refresh rate setups.

Heat Management:
After about 7 days of continuous use with multiple devices connected, the dock remains cool to the touch. Compared to other docks I’ve used, heat output has been noticeably lower during extended operation.

Charging Capabilities:
The 100W USB-C Power Delivery port charges the laptop during use, and additional USB ports allow simultaneous charging of smaller devices like a phone. Power distribution has been stable with everything connected.

Connectivity Options:
The port selection covers most everyday needs:
• 2× HDMI ports
• Multiple USB 3.0 ports
• USB 2.0 port for peripherals
• USB-C ports
• Gigabit Ethernet
• USB-C Power Delivery input
• Button to check display resolution status

Compatibility:
Tested on a Windows USB-C laptop, where it worked as expected without requiring any drivers. Setup was straightforward and plug-and-play.

Build Quality & Design:
The dock feels sturdy and well built, with a compact, modern design that fits neatly on a desk and helps reduce cable clutter. The included QR code for warranty support is a nice addition.

Minor Wish:
A DisplayPort option would add flexibility for certain monitor setups, but the dual HDMI ports meet current needs.

Bottom Line:
This docking station provides reliable dual-monitor support, stable charging, and a useful smart display feature in a compact design. It has performed consistently during daily Windows use and has been a practical single-cable solution.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Updating review after further investigation of the buggy behavior I experienced.

The unit has high build quality. The braid-wrapped cable is robust and stiff which makes me think it's not going to fray easily. It's also compact and simple, your HDMI cable is going to be more cumbersome by itself.

Video output has zero lag and no noticeable CPU impact (this is the idea behind DisplayPort over USB/Thunderbolt; it doesn't impact performance because it's rerouting the built-in graphics chip's output rather than acting as another graphics chip like adapters built for USB 2.0 and 3.0 type A).

Overall this is a great value for the price.

On the other hand, I have experienced issues on a Lenovo Yoga 730. When configuring the output from the adapter as a 2nd display, the Windows shell wedges itself (can't start new processes, start menu won't come up, etc. but you can very slowly interact with apps that are already running and in focus), and the bottom of both displays flickers (looks like a strobing task bar). However, if configured as a mirrored display (or only displaying video on the external monitor) everything works fine. This implies a software issue, and since this adapter has no software (it's handled entirely by the system's already existing graphics driver), it has to be a bug in the Intel 620 graphics driver or in Windows 10 (desktop window manager or something).

Lenovo customized the graphics driver for this system and it's 5 months older than Intel's version, but Intel won't allow installation of their base version ("This driver is not compatible with this hardware, contact your computer manufacturer"). I'm holding out until Lenovo/Intel/Microsoft release more patches and will update this review if it changes. In the meantime I'm using the adapter in single display mode to utilize the larger external display when at my desk.

Configuration: Lenovo Yoga 730 (USB-C 3.1/Thunderbolt 3 ports) with latest available drivers and firmware as of June 14 2018. Windows 10 1803 17134.112 (2018 Creators Update).

text:
Overall at about $49.99 this is a good value and getting close to a great value if it drops into the low-$40s for a 13-in-1 USB-C laptop docking station with dual HDMI, DisplayPort, Ethernet, and 100W PD passthrough.

Setup was easy – I plugged the USB-C cable into a Windows laptop with a full-feature USB-C port, connected my monitors and peripherals, and it showed up without needing any drivers. Functionality and compatibility have been good for me: I can run two external monitors (or three total including the laptop screen) with a mouse, keyboard, Ethernet, and a couple of USB devices all off this one dock. The 2x HDMI plus DisplayPort layout is handy since it covers most of my monitors, and once everything is connected the displays stay stable with no random flicker or disconnects. The SD/TF card slots and extra USB ports are nice to have for quickly grabbing files from a card or plugging in a flash drive or webcam. I also like that it supports power delivery – with the right 100W USB-C charger, it’ll pass through up to about 85W to the laptop so I can use a single brick instead of the original charger plus a separate dock.

There are a few trade-offs to keep in mind. This type of dock really needs a USB-C port that supports DisplayPort Alt Mode and PD; on systems that only do basic data over USB-C it won’t drive the screens. On macOS it’s also limited to mirrored displays rather than full triple extended, so it’s much better suited to Windows machines if you want multi-monitor setups. The dock gets a bit warm when you’re powering a laptop and running multiple displays, and it doesn’t include a USB-C power adapter, so you have to provide your own 100W charger to get the most out of the PD feature. But overall, for a compact dock with 2 HDMI, DP, Ethernet, SD/TF, audio, and a mix of USB 3.0/2.0 ports that has worked reliably and cleaned up my cable clutter, I’m happy with it around $49.99 and would call it an even better value when it’s on sale.

text:
Pros:
- Ethernet port gives stable upload and download speeds
- HDMI x2 works well for UHD at 60Hz
- Build quality feels solid

Cons:
- USB3.0 read and write speeds only 40MB/s and 30MB/s, closer to USB 2.0 (spec not met)
- DisplayPort does not work with a DP-capable monitor, Windows 11 detects no external display
- PD port is more picky than other docks on USB-C power sources

The WAVLINK USB-C Docking Station has decent build quality with a solid metal construction.

The Ethernet port was tested to have an upload speed of 58.8MB/s and a download speed of 278MB/s. These results are lower compared to other docks I have tested. The HDMI ports both work well at UHD resolution with a 60Hz refresh rate. This makes them suitable for dual monitor setups.

The USB3.0 ports only reach 40MB/s read and 30MB/s write, which is closer to USB 2.0 speed. These two USB 3.0 ports do not meet the specifications. The DP port does not work when directly connected to a DP-capable monitor. Windows 11 fails to detect any external display. This makes the DP port unusable. The PD port is more picky than other docks when tested with USB-C power sources. The reason is unclear, but it reduces flexibility.
