title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I've owned several budget smartwatches before, so I had a good baseline for comparison when testing this Momax. After using it for a few weeks, I can confirm it handles the basics well—step counting, heart rate monitoring, and the 100+ sports modes all work as advertised. The 1.85" AMOLED display is crisp and the setup process was genuinely painless. The companion app connected via Bluetooth immediately, and anyone who's used an Amazfit GTS will navigate this interface without any learning curve. The battery life is okay depending on what features you turn on. Features that continuously run in the background will obviously drain the battery more. I got about three days of wear before I had to charge it again.
Here's where it gets tricky though: I've found similar watches with identical features for about half this price point, which makes the value proposition harder to justify. The bigger issue for me is ecosystem compatibility. While it technically works with both Android and iPhone, it doesn't sync with popular third party apps like MyFitnessPal or Strava, so you're stuck manually transferring data if you track fitness elsewhere. I also spent more time than I'd like to admit searching for screen protectors and cases with the right dimensions, which suggests this model doesn't have the accessory support of more established brands. If you want a standalone fitness tracker and don't need integration with other apps, this delivers. But if you're building a connected health tracking system, the limited compatibility might frustrate you. I don't think it's worth the price despite being well made.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
For some reason, I couldn't get it to work with my Surface Book laptop. I plugged it in using a simple USB-C cable and the screen would turn on but neither my computer nor my monitor would detect a connection. I was able to navigate the controls on the side such as brightness, contrast, input selection etc.
I'm not sure if it was an issue with the laptop or an issue with the monitor. After searching a number of forums, the solution was to undock the keyboard, shut down the laptop, unplug any remaining peripherals then hold the power button for a minimum of 20 seconds. Then start everything back up normally. For me, this initially didn't work, but I was able to take it home and connect it using an HDMI adapter (one of those 5-in-1 devices that plugs into my USB-C port). The monitor isn't powered through the HDMI connection so I had to supply an additional power source using the USB-C ports. This worked and the monitor powered up and displayed the screen. It automatically detected the HDMI connection. This was really disappointing because I didn't want to have to carry around an additional HDMI cable everywhere. I then switched everything back to a single USB-C connection, even unplugging the power source, and it worked. Note that I only had it plugged into the USB-C ports and never touched any of the USB-A ports. I'm pretty sure that would never work except to provide power.
The monitor itself is pretty big compared to most laptop screens and is incredibly light.
The back is thicker for the lower 25% of the monitor about the width of a travel battery while notebook thin for the upper half. The borders of the monitor are about 4mm along the top and sides and 10mm for the bottom. The screen itself is recessed just a bit. It will not fit into a 15-inch laptop case, you're going to need something larger.
I had recently ordered a Laptop Sleeve Case for 16-inch laptops and it fits this monitor like a glove.
The monitor is powered by a simple USB-C connection and contains no battery. A single USB-C cable from a laptop that supports USB-C monitors is enough. If you have to use the HDMI connection, you'll have to supply power.
The monitor has rubber contacts for feet and a kickstand in back plus two VESA screws if you want to mount it to something. It has built in speakers which at best, do their job. They receive the audio feed both through HDMI and the USB-C connection. It also has an analog 3.5mm headphone jack.
I want to note that I had a little more time to play with the connections and found that you really need to use a high capacity USB-C cable. I was pulling my hair out trying to figure out how I got it working with the USB-C cable once and realized that it only worked with my really thick USB-C cables of which I only have two. The one that came in the package works for this. I also had one of those magnetic tips that also block the functionality of the USB-C monitor. It doesn't even work when I have it connected to my USB-C to dual HDMI adapter.
I need to point out that it works fine using the HDMI port on the adapter but I need to supply a separate power source this way. Once I removed the tips, adapter and only connected with the supplied USB-C cable it worked fine.
TLDR:
HDMI requires an additional power cable.
USB-C requires a high capacity USB-C cable, PC compatibility and no other connections between.

text:
This has been an absolutely beautiful, crisp, and wonderful upgraded monitor for me. It hits all the good boxes: clean and crisp picture, no noticeable screen lags, many nice features. But it has a few considerations that may be deal breakers.
Pros:
- The display is crisp and bright, and had no dead pixels or any issue on arrival. It doesn't have any screen ghosting or any refresh issues readily noticeable, even under heavy load.
- The multiple inputs feature is easy to use and a nice addition, and all inputs test with the same quality.
- The fine-tuning options of the display seem robust (but that may just be advances in general monitor technology).

"Cons:"
- The mounting area for this monitor is recessed into the body, and since my current monitor mount has been with me for 2 moves and a decade of time, I don't have the hardware to add it to my existing monitor mount, as the mounting area isn't flat on the back of the monitor. I suspect a newer mount would support it, but I don't know. (I expected this possibility when ordering so it's more just annoying than it is a problem)
- The built in speakers aren't the best, and are limited in volume and their ability to not sound like they've been run through a 6" tin pipe. That said, if you're not aiming to run high-end media with the audio through the monitor (such as streaming, gaming, or music) most audio "issues" are passible. The main issue is convincing Windows which speaker set to use for which application, but that's not the monitor's fault.
- Lateral mouse movements are considerably quicker (more responsive) than vertical movements in a Windows environment for this display, and will feel more responsive on the x-axis and sluggish against the y-axis for similar mouse movements. In most gaming environments I've tested with, they allow scaling to x and y sensitivity that can help mitigate the issue, but it might just be best to learn a new movement feel.

Overall, it's a fantastic piece of hardware, but you should be aware of possible drawbacks just in case.

GRV Smart Watch Review – A Budget-Friendly Fitness Companion

I’ve been using the GRV Smart Watch for iOS and Android for a while now, and overall, it’s a solid budget-friendly option for anyone looking for basic smartwatch features without breaking the bank.

Pros:

✔️ Easy to Set Up & Use – Pairing with my phone was quick and straightforward, and the interface is user-friendly.
✔️ Good Fitness Tracking – It does a decent job tracking steps, heart rate, sleep, and various sports modes.
✔️ Battery Life – Lasts several days on a single charge, which is great for a smartwatch at this price point.
✔️ Notifications & Calls – Displays messages and call alerts, which is handy when my phone isn’t nearby.
✔️ Lightweight & Comfortable – The watch is lightweight and fits well for all-day wear.

Cons:

➖ Limited App Integration – It works well for basic tracking, but it doesn’t sync with all third-party fitness apps.
➖ Basic Display & Customization – The screen is clear, but the watch faces and customization options are somewhat limited.
➖ No Built-in GPS – It relies on your phone for location tracking, which might not be ideal for runners or cyclists.

Final Thoughts:

For the price, the GRV Smart Watch is a great entry-level smartwatch, especially for those who want essential health and fitness tracking without spending too much. It’s not as advanced as premium smartwatches, but it delivers well on its core functions. If you’re looking for affordability and simplicity, this is a great option!

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought a name brand fitness watch years ago, mainly used it for steps, heartbeat, and seeing text messages without getting out my phone(No phone calls though). I had one BIG issue with it. I could never read it outside when it was sunny. Then never wanted to get another because of how much they cost.

That all changed when I found this watch and gave it a try. First, at $40 it doesn't break the bank. It's amazing what this watch does for that price. It does steps and distance (you can even program your stride length). It does your oxygen level and heartbeat accurately. It does blood pressure, but that is not so accurate. The top number can be low 10-20, and bottom number off about 5-10. I have never found a non pressure cup device to be accurate on that though. But I can use this as a gauge to see what my BP is doing, so it is helpful.

What makes me the happiest with this watch is that you can easily read it outdoors in the sun. You can adjust the brightness, and also pick what watch face you want. I had to download one that I liked. At half brightness it is very easy to read outdoors in the sun. You do need to download an app to make this work at first and program things, but that is easy. I've haven't used much of the fitness trackers on this watch because there are so many, but I will learn them over time.

As for Bluetooth connection, download app first, follow directions, then look for ZL80B on your phone to connect to, pretty simple. For messages it notifies you and you can read them. Phone calls can be made directly from watch, dial and also program in a few contacts. There is a speaker and microphone that work well, but I did notice you may have to speak on the left side of watch for others to hear you better.

This watch will be great for what I do outdoors, not having to get phone out of pocket. Being water resistant, I can go kayaking and put my phone in a dry bag or box, and then use this watch to not miss a call or message that might be important. All in all, for how cheap price this watch is, it is very much worth it to me.

LIGE Smart Watch for Men - GPS/Barometer/Altimeter/Compass, Make/Answer Call, LED Flashlight, 530mAh, 100+ Sports Modes Fitness Tracker, 1.43" Amoled Smartwatch for iOS Android, Black Silicone

At the time of this review this watch was ~$50, so I set my expectations pretty low. I have to say my expectations were far exceeded!

The watch is good quality and well made. It has a lot of functionality for such an inexpensive watch. It's hefty and feels robust.
You can receive notifications from various apps, although not all, the app presents you with a limited list of apps that you can select to receive notifications from.

You can password protect the watch which I think is a good idea but the execution is poor. It doesn't seem to lock automatically when the display turns off. I actually can't figure out exactly when it decides to lock.

The display is crisp and sharp and colourful. The watch faces are limited but there's plenty of good options.

The battery life is pretty good. I last charged it five (4) days ago and it is currently at 75% so that looks very promising, I use it very regularly including GPS but I turned off the 'raise to wake' feature that turns on the display when you raise your wrist. That helps prolong battery life but can be annoying to have to hit a button to see the display. I do find that 'raise to wake' seems to turn back on by itself; I have 'do not disturb' scheduled to end at 7am and everyday at 7am 'raise to wake' is back on, I think this is a software glitch that needs to be addressed.

The 'always on' display is OK, defaulting to a simple time, date display with low back light but it really takes a toll on the battery so I don't use it.

I put my watch at the bottom of a full five (5) gallon bucket of water and there doesn't seem to be any problems with water ingress, it does appear well sealed but, of course, this isn't a very good test but I am confident the watch will survive splashes of water or heavy rain.

The watch can also measure blood pressure and compared to a cuff style one I have it was a bit high. I didn't think it was possible to measure blood pressure without a cuff but they have figured it out!

The call quality is pretty good. The caller heard me fine but even on high volume the caller sounded quiet, it is still usable. It is a nice feature to have.

The GPS works great but there is no transfer to the app so all you see is a path on the watch itself as to where you traveled. It would be nice if the data imported to the app and then overlaid on a map.

The watch comes with two different strap options which is great to have a spare or different style depending on your taste.

The LED flashlight is neat and works well enough, it's just a splash of light but could be really handy in the dark.

Here are some less than stellar things I encountered:

-The notification font is not very good and can't be changed.
-Only so many characters are received from notifications and then they are cut off, which is common on most watches I believe.
-You can't respond to text messages through the watch even though customized responses can be setup in the app.
-The app is pretty limited, although, of course that could change as time goes on.
-The app was a bit involved to setup, I had to manually add Android permissions so that the app could read notifications and grant it permissions for various other things.
-In the app I tried to sync my contacts to the watch but not all my contacts show up in the app, only about half do, I have no idea why.
-The watch / app only reports the active calories you burned and doesn't include your BMR or RMR so it's hard to judge how many Calories one should eat in a day to maintain or lose weight.
-The watch does not seem to be able to receive RCS messages only SMS come through, that's disappointing as most phones are switching to RCS, I hope there is a fix soon for this.

Overall, if you just want to try out a smart watch without paying a bundle, I think this watch is great, don't expect too much but you should still be pleasantly surprised like I am.

text:
I really like having several types of watches depending on the occasion and needs. Some have more battery life, others more features and in short, there's a bit of everything.

I decided to test this LIGE model mainly to try out the watch's built-in GPS. Here are my impressions below.

Pros:

- The frame appears to be made of very good quality solid metal.

- I like the fact that the dial isn't too big, as some smartwatches have very large dials. When going on expeditions, I hope to stay lightweight and minimize the risk of snagging on watches, etc.

- The functions I tested seem to do a good job, whether it's measuring heart rate per minute, stress testing, or oxygen levels. It seems to be credible data.

- There's a function for briefly assessing blood pressure. It's simply an additional indicator that shouldn't be taken literally. A real test with a machine is always more reliable like explained in the application, but the measurements I obtain are credible and consistent with my usual practice.

- The integrated GPS is very useful for nature walks. It shows us our route so we can retrace our steps. Super smart.

- It's nice to be able to change the dial design for people who like to customize the look according to their clothing colors of the day for example or to see the numbers better.

- It's sturdy but not too heavy, so I find it ideal for traveling. I often want to limit the weight of my gear but still have access to a GPS, etc.

- I love the way the menu is designed on the watch. It's easy to understand what each icon means, but at worst, you can use a text version of the menu, which is very useful at first to familiarize yourself with the icons.

- It comes with a 2 years warranty which seems very decent to me considering it's price range.

- I like having two different straps that come with the watch. One has a slightly more leathery texture and the other has a rubber touch.

Cons :

- The exercise mode called "indoor walking" is not detecting my steps correctly. I see really big differences between my steps and the indicator, which also seems to be suffering from slowness. However, I gave all the exact information requested when setting up the watch. With the outdoor walking mode using GPS, distances and everything else seem more reliable and consistent, that said.

- I think the phone app used to configure the watch could be improved. You should be able to choose the timeframes for each test, but some are not available on the watch or the phone. They are therefore carried out when the watch decides, maybe for power limitation purposes. It's a bit the same for the weather. I can't find an UPDATE button to request a quick update via my watch. Sometimes the update takes a while to come.

- I really feel like the battery and/or processor on this watch are too weak for what it's asked to do, or too limited. Even the slightest activity, like using GPS, drains the battery very, very quickly, and the display can be a bit sluggish. If I'm walking outside and forget to turn the activity off at the end, the battery can drain very quickly. I once left the watch in outdoor walking mode for 6 hours while I slept at home, and it lost over a third of its charge. Constantly searching for the GPS signal probably uses a lot of battery, so it's best to remember to turn off GPS activities when you get home or while you're indoors.

- It seems to me that the accuracy of the motion detection was sometimes strange despite the calibration. I recalibrated after a reset and it worked. Now the watch reacts every time I raise my hand.. although a little bit late sometimes.

Conclusion :

I feel like this watch is great but needs a boost in terms of battery life and maybe a little boost in terms of processor. Everything else is very good and even impressive for most of all features. It's still a good budget choice if you're patient because sometimes, I feel that the delay to see some changes is long in the heartbeat section and some others. It's not so annoying but it's a thing to know. It's not the fastest.

Yet, it still has over 500 mAh, but if the processor puts too much strain on the battery, it can drain faster than normally. In standby mode, it can last for long days, even more than a week, but as soon as I start an activity, it can drain quickly.

The contradiction I see here is that normally, for an expedition watch with a compass and built-in GPS, I would expect a battery life compatible with a long wilderness expedition, like more than a week of battery life despite slightly more active use. I don't always have a charger with me on an expedition, and well, for a watch with such great features (even approximate full blood pressure), I would have expected a longer battery life per charge.

I still recommend it as a budget choice for hikers and it's even better if you have a power delivery charger when you go out for long days.

text:
Ero titubante e temevo che mi sarei ritrovato un semplice orologio digitale ma mi sono dovuto ricredere.
Non elencherò tutte le sue caratteristiche dato che è possibile leggerle in descrizione, ma elencherò quello che mi ha più colpito e quello che mi ha deluso.
PRO
- Display enorme. E' paragonabile a quello della nota marca con la mela e ha anche la rotellina...
- Display luminoso. Avevo deciso di cambiare il mio vecchio Xiaomi 2 perchè avevo difficoltà a leggere il display sotto il sole al mare durante le sessioni di windsurf. Con questo ci riesco anche se non porto la luminosità al 100%. La luminosità si regola velocemente tirando giù lo schermo in modo da avere le opzioni rapide, quindi la possiamo adattare alle nostre esigenze. NOTA: se la lasciamo al 100% il consumo ne risentirà parecchio e la batteria durerà anche qualche giorno in meno.
- Compatibile con Alexa. Con un comando veloce è possibile inviare comandi al nostro Alexa anche se non siamo a portata di voce. NOTA: su questa funzione non sono ancora del tutto convinto perchè alcune volte mi risulta disconnesso dall'applicazione. Non so se è una questione di software del telefono o dell'orologio. Per il momento non mi funziona tutte le volte, quindi merita un 5 su 10. Però c'è e quando funziona è grandioso
- Comandi vocali. Puoi inviare i comandi vocali al tuo assistente vocale del telefono. Nel mio caso uso google e con un click sull'orologi puoi fare le richieste senza toccare il telefono.
- Ovviamente ci sono tutti i vari contatori per gli sport con cui misurare le prestazioni, il tempo ecc. Questo non è una novità e funziona come ci si aspetta
- I quadranti ovviamente sono personalizzabili tra un'infinità di inutili opzioni ma è divertente poter scegliere. Per finire è possibile anche costruirlo con una fotografia che avrà una bella grafica nitida. NOTA: la cosa strana è che mi fa tenere in memoria solo 5 quadranti. Ogni volta che ne voglio uno nuovo devo rimuoverne uno vecchio
- Durata. La prima carica mi è durata quasi una settimana (perchè non avevo scoperto che potevo anche aumentare la luminosità). Giocando con la luminosità e dimenticandola al 100% anche quando non serviva la carica è scesa ma parlamo di giornate intere di utilizzo
- CHIAMATE! E' possibile rispondere alle chiamate direttamente dall'orologio e funziona sul serio. La prima chiamata era stata un pò deludente perchè sentivo poco. Poi ho scoperto che in chiamata c'è il simbolo dell'altoparlante con cui si può aumentare il volume. Sono riuscito a parlare anche stando in mare sul windsurf (con il cellulare riposto in una sacca impermeabile)
- Notifiche. Naturalmente tutte le notifiche che ci servono (è una cosa personalizzabile) arrivano sul cellulare, compresi i messaggi di Whatsapp. NOTA: non legge le emoticons e non legge i vocali
- cinturini a sgancio rapido da 22mm. In un'altra recensione avevo letto che si potevano mettere i cinturini da 20mm ma in realtà bisogna prendere quelli da 22mm. Ne ho già provati diversi e mi sto divertendo a cambiare stile tutte le volte che voglio. Basta scegliere cinturini da 22mm con sgancio rapido
- tante misurazioni come battiti cardiaci, Ossigeno...
- funzioni utili come meteo...

CONTRO
- come ho scritto sopra, ho qualche difficoltà con Alexa ma non tolgo punti per questo motivo dato che è un plus e potrebbe dipendere dal mio telefono
- solo 5 quadranti in memoria. Non tolgo punti per questa caratteristica

In definitiva per il prezzo a cui viene proposto fa tante cose (non le ho elencate tutte perchè alcune non le uso neanche) e le fa anche bene.
Le notifiche, l'orario, le chiamate, la sveglia, i promemoria.... insomma non credo possiamo chiedere molto di più. APPROVATO

text:
AMAZON REVIEW - WMK White Smart Watch (ID208 Plus)

Worth Every Penny for Basic Fitness Tracking

I wasn't sure what to expect at this price point, but this watch has been a pleasant surprise. Setup was straightforward - downloaded VeryFit, paired it within minutes, and everything synced without issues. The display is bright enough to read outdoors, which matters more than I thought it would.

The band is surprisingly comfortable. It's light enough that I forget I'm wearing it, but the clasp feels secure. I've worn it for three days straight now and no irritation on my wrist, which is saying something because I usually can't stand watch bands for long periods.

Battery life seems solid so far. I charged it to 98% two days ago and it's still at 67%. If you're someone who forgets to charge things overnight (guilty), the multi-day battery is clutch.

The fitness tracking does what I need - steps, heart rate checks throughout the day, and sleep data that's interesting even if I'm not sure how accurate it is. I'm not a serious athlete, just someone trying to move more and be aware of activity levels. For that purpose, it's perfect.

One thing to know: it's water RESISTANT, not waterproof. The manual is clear about this - fine for washing hands or getting caught in rain, but don't swim with it or shower with it. I appreciate that they're upfront about the limitation rather than overselling it.

The app connects consistently, notifications come through reliably, and the UI is simple enough that I didn't need to dig through the manual much. Sometimes basic is better, you know?

If you need swim tracking or super precise athletic metrics, look elsewhere and spend more. But if you want a reliable daily tracker that doesn't require a second mortgage, this is a solid pick.

text:
Honestly you get what you pay for. This is a very simple fitness watch that does have the capability to show notifications from your phone (like calls and texts). The battery life is great, it consistently lasts for about a week between charges.

However, there is very limited functionality, especially as someone who previously had a name brand Fitbit. I wanted something cheaper after being frustrated that my fitbits were only lasting 2 years before bricking out.

The Pros:
*Battery life is great
*Shows ALL of my notifications, whereas Fitbit only let me choose either SMS or FB Messenger and not both
*Seems durable but the screen protector slid right off of it within the first week (I do a lot of manual labor and the protector was purchased from a 3rd party, so this isn't necessarily the fault of this watch)
*Cute customizable face screen backgrounds

The Cons:
*The instruction booklet and the directions in the app are very badly translated English.
*There is very little that you can do to adjust settings; for example I can't turn off the ringtone without also turning off the vibrate notification, which means I have to have both on all the time and it dinging from my notifications can be distracting in meetings.
*I don't have the ability to say "I'm going to start exercising now" and have it track that activity live.
*When I answer calls on the watch, the audio is SO quiet, even at max volume.
*And it keeps inexplicably disconnecting from my Bluetooth unless I go into the app to pair it at least once a day.

Overall it's fine, but once this one dies, I'm going back to name brand. I can't speak to how accurate the tracking is because honestly all trackers are pretty inaccurate so I don't use it for that other than a rough ballpark for step counts.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I’ve been using this monitor light, for several weeks, on an Acer display for daily work, and overall it’s been a really solid addition to my desk setup. Installation was straightforward — it mounted easily and felt secure once positioned. No complicated setup or tools required, which I always appreciate.

The lighting itself is where this really shines (no pun intended). The adjustable color temperature range from warm to cool is useful depending on what you’re doing. It can give you more of a relaxed desk lamp vibe in warmer tones or a bright, focused work light when you need better visibility for detailed tasks. There’s also an auto-dimming feature, but I personally prefer setting a static brightness level once and leaving it there. The included remote control is a nice touch and honestly makes the product feel more premium than the price point would suggest.

Build quality feels better than expected — not cheap or flimsy. I use this every day for work, and it’s especially helpful during gloomy weather or late afternoons when natural light drops off. It reduces the need for overhead lighting and keeps the workspace evenly illuminated without glare on the screen.

My only real complaint is the articulation adjustment. The mounting design doesn’t provide quite enough tension, so adjusting the angle sometimes requires two hands to keep everything aligned. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it’s an area that could be improved in a future version.

Overall, this has been a great upgrade for my workspace and something I didn’t realize I needed until I started using it consistently.

text:
A light bar, particularly a monitor light bar for a workspace, has completely transformed my desk setup and reduced eye strain in a way I didn't expect. Its asymmetrical design is its killer feature; mounted atop my computer monitor, it focuses bright, glare-free light down onto my keyboard and documents, but never onto the screen itself. This eliminates the frustrating glare and reflections I used to get from traditional desk lamps, which is crucial for long hours in front of a display. It's essentially a dedicated task light that saves significant desk real estate, providing a clean, organized, and perfectly illuminated work zone while simultaneously enhancing the contrast and comfort of my screen viewing.
Beyond just the work benefits, a versatile LED light bar offers fantastic opportunities for accent and functional lighting throughout my home. I've used smaller, strip-style bars to add sleek, modern under-cabinet lighting in the kitchen, instantly brightening the counter space for cooking and giving the whole area a high-end look. They are also brilliant for adding indirect bias lighting behind a TV or monitor, which helps to reduce the harsh contrast between a bright screen and a dark room, making late-night viewing much more comfortable. Whether for focused work or creating a better ambiance, the light bar is a simple, effective upgrade for any modern space.

text:
RECOMENDO a lightbar PRO+ da Quntis!
O produto é excelente, encaixou perfeitamente no meu monitor curvo de 34' (Husky Tempest).
O controle remoto é excelente, tanto a rotação superior para ajuste da temperatura da luz quanto a rotação lateral para ajustar a intensidade do brilho, possuem diversos níveis de graduação de intensidade, acredito que suba de 5% em 5%, e possui feedback tátil ao girar.
Ou seja, existem diversos níveis de ajuste de intensidade, é possível personalizar da melhor forma que desejar.
Testei o modo de ajuste automático de brilho e funciona perfeitamente.
Testei o modo de desligamento automático de 2 horas, funciona perfeitamente.
O controle remoto é muito bonito, elegante, chega a ser prazeroso mecher nele, ele funciona com 2 pilhas palito (AAA).
O único ponto negativo desta lightbar é que ela não possui nenhum botão touch, ou seja, o ajuste é totalmente dependente do controle remoto, se ele estiver sem bateria será necessário retirar da tomada para desligar.
Nas minhas fotos tiradas a noite, a primeira mostra somente a luz da lightbar com o brilho no mínimo e a temperatura totalmente quente, e a segunda com a mesma temperatura porém com o brilho no máximo.
Vale comentar que a construção da lightbar é toda em metal, o que torna o produto premium.
Deixei ela ligada por algumas horas, e ela não esquenta.
Eu só tenho elogios a falar deste produto, deixa o setup muito mais confortável e aconchegante.
Recomendo a marca QUNTIS e o produto Lightbar PRO+.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I was initially concerned about buying a Philips monitor because I assumed the quality would not be on par with other well-known brands. The reasonable price, 4 year warranty, and good reviews are what led me to settle on this monitor.

PANEL
The screen itself is bright. I tend to keep the brightness level around 85-90.

1. Text looks clear both in the middle and the sides
2. Contrast is good
3. Images look great
4. Colors are quite accurate
- I have not made any changes to customize the colors of the panel. Out of the box the colors looked good to me. I am not planning on using this monitor for editing photos. I have another monitor that is more geared towards creative work.

AESTHETICS
The whole monitor looks great. Even the back has sort of a brushed look. I love it!

CURVE
I really enjoy the curve. I have heard some people say that the curve takes time to get used to, but getting used to it seemed easy to me. I don't think I would want a monitor wider than this. The size is perfect.

Thankfully the monitor I received was in perfect condition. No dead pixels. Philips dead pixel policy is not clear at all. I hope that this will never be an issue. The 4 year warranty seems pretty awesome. Seems like Philips will stand behind their product.

GAMES
I have not yet tested any serious games on this monitor, but I will soon and post an update here. I did play some Roblox and the game filled the whole screen. Any content that fills the whole screen is really awesome.

USB-C
My work laptop is a Lenovo ThinkPad. The USB-C port on the laptop where I plug the power adapter did nothing when I connected the monitor using the supplied USB-C cable. This is probably a misunderstanding on my part. There is a secondary USB-C port on the laptop that has an energy bolt next to it. When I plugged the monitor into that USB-C port, the laptop displayed on the monitor in 1440p, and the laptop was receiving a charge from the monitor. Pretty amazing.

STAND
The stand is very sturdy. The screen can tilt up & down, twist left and right, and can raise up & down. Very happy with this.

SPEAKERS
The speakers are great if you consider they are built-in speakers, not dedicated reference monitors. It's a very welcomed addition, and they do the job.

PURPOSE
People may settle on this monitor for different reasons. For me the biggest reason was work. Having this monitor for work is a total dream. I am an IT engineer, so being able to have Visual Studio Code, PowerShell, Outlook, and the Azure portal all open at the same time (I have a 2nd monitor) really helps with productivity.

A creative professional may want to avoid the curve and go for a panel with even higher color accuracy. A gamer might want more than 100hz to keep gameplay as smooth as possible.

If you are looking for more screen real estate and you want to be more productive, then this monitor is for you.

Side note: Amazon's characteristics for this item don't make any sense. They asked me to give a rating for the "sheerness" and "thickness" of the monitor.

Envia OLED 34”: Let me start by saying I wanted to love this monitor, but I absolutely cannot recommend it.

The good: the price is highly competitive. The OLED panel is glossy so colors are vibrant. I play in a fairly dark room with backlighting and did not have any glare issues. Out of the box color and uniformity was excellent.

The mid: Ambiglow backlighting is a nice-to-have if you don’t have other backlights, but it’s not the brightest. This is a problem with many of Philips screen backlight products…I’m not sure why they choose not to light the bottom of a screen.

The Bad: The menu system while useable, isn’t great. The toggle makes a cheap plastic echo sound whenever it’s pressed. Changing settings can be cumbersome compared to others and if you have pixel refresh turned on, you can’t easily turn off the monitor. The unacceptable: The first monitor arrived with a dead pixel near the center of the screen, making it hard to ignore. I contacted Philips warranty support and was told that they won’t replace it unless it’s more damaged. They said 1-3 dead pixels is acceptable in their eyes and would only consider replacement if more failed. On a $650 product, I beg to differ. Amazon helped me get a quick replacement thankfully. Unfortunately, this one had a broken mount clip. I had not sent the other one back so I swapped out the clips and thought I’d be fine. title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
If you want an *HDR, 1440p, OLED* monitor, I believe this is it.
Color-sensitive work on a budget? This is it. Gaming? This is it.
I have scouted and rejected many monitors to find the best within my budget, and here I am staying for good.

It has anything you'd want in a color-sensitive, professional setting as well as in a gaming context. I use this monitor more as a 'pro budget' choice for color-based work which requires specific color gamuts, and the monitor can switch between them (DCI-P3, Adobe RGB, and sRGB) well with no fuss. The colors have been pre-calibrated at the factory (I received a calibration report in-box), and the brightness is great too-- I am completely content in using this for any editing or viewing purpose.

The very high refresh rate of 360hz isn't something I take advantage of most of the time, but definitely is wild to see. If you're into ultra-competitive games, this may be key for you, especially as anecdotal BlurBusters/UFOTest viewings did show that 360hz was in fact clearer than 180hz for fast motion. But for most modern games, you'll need a fairly decent GPU to even reach 360fps at 1440p. VRR tech like FreeSync and G-Sync will be your friend.

I don't care about border space on monitors, but if you do, then this monitor isn't going to soothe that. The panel itself is actually higher than 1440p, but the monitor staggers the display image around as to reduce burn-in from static UI elements like your taskbar, which I do not notice at all. Even set it to its fastest shifting, I just couldn't notice the single-pixel adjustments in image, and I'm sitting fairly close to it. I doubt you could either.

Despite being classified as a 'gaming monitor', there are no unsightly 'gamer aesthetics' to it; It's completely professional looking, and behaving. It's nice, and stays out of the way.

Philips' Ambiglow (LED backlighting reactant on video) is actually great for using the monitor in dark rooms, as the surrounding glow off the wall helps to adjust your eyes to the image in focus. It's less 'sting' on the eyes for the same image. I usually *hate* RGB/light-up effects usually, but these will stay on because these RGB's have genuine utility to them. text:
Edit May 2023: still loving it months later. Some minor edits below.
-----------------
I'm just a few days into using the monitor, but zero complaints so far. I'll run down different aspects I considered when deciding on this monitor vs the many competing options. First & foremost, the 5 stars reflects getting a quality monitor, mostly as advertised, for a very solid price. Some competing monitors are more than 2x the price, so that factors into the rating.

--General screen impressions: It's crisp, wide, and the curve is pleasing. I use this monitor for work, with occasional light video watching (eg youtube). The 1500R curve is great for sitting at desk distance. The picture quality for that is more than enough and I see no issues. If, like me, you're not a total connoisseur of screens, then you'll be in good shape and things like a lack of HDR aren't a big deal. I wouldn't likely even notice the difference vs the highest priced screens. It works very well for professional (non-creative) uses where I frequently take advantage of the large real estate to view multiple windows simultaneously.

One note - the monitor is actually 60hz native, not the 100hz highlighted on the amazon page. You can get to 100hz via certain setting modifications, but it seems there are some tradeoffs.

--Connectors: this was a key attraction for me, and it's working. You need to download a driver update for the ethernet port, but once I did then it is working to pass along reliable hardline internet to my machine (Thinkpad X1) via the USB C connection. That USB C is also handling the AV connection itself, and regular USB inputs like my keyboard and webcam (the monitor does not have a built in camera, which I knew, and that's fine). I was able to also have the USB C pass power, but - one small knock - that seemed to create overload on the connection. The screen would randomly recycle, and at one point my machine put itself to sleep cause I guess it thought it was on battery mode. So, I'm keeping the laptop plugged in with its own charging port, and then it works really smooth. Still a big gain in clutter reduction & easier dock/undock for the machine. (Edit: new ASUS machine in 2023 and it works cleanly on one plug for everything, including power)

The extra usb ports on the side are definitely going to be useful, compared to some monitors that have only one or two. And of course it has standard DP and HDMI ports on the back, which I'm not gonna use.

--Speakers: this was a minor but important consideration for me and they seem solid for their purpose. Just like with the USB C connector, I want less clutter. So, I don't want to have to use extra speakers. And the sound I need is for video conferences (google & zoom) plus occasional casual video/music. For that, the speakers work well and are powerful enough to hear fine & clear. Music is a bit...mushy is maybe the word. They aren't producing great sound quality, but if you buy a monitor for that then idk what you're thinking.

-- Features & options: this isn't the most feature rich monitor, but it has a list of "modes" you can choose from, plus a menu accessed via the bevel buttons which is easy enough to navigate. Plus you can move where it appears, which is helpful on such a big screen.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Overall it's a great monitor for productivity work and occasional gaming where you can easily switch between 2 inputs pretty quickly. It's not exactly a great gaming monitor with only 100 Hz refresh rate but better than most others at this price range that only offer 60Hz. The 5ms panel refresh rate is a little slow, you can notice some blurring and ghosting on fast moving games but it's acceptable to someone like me.
This is a pretty good monitor for working from home, I wanted a monitor that supports 2 inputs and can do picture by picture and has a refresh rate more than 60 hz, this one does both. I previously had 2 different 1080 monitors and switching to one ultrawide 1440 monitor has been a great experience, so much better than 2 separate monitors. I am impressed with the image quality of the monitor. The color and contrast quality is pretty good, although it is a VA panel, there is a little bit of color shifting when looking at the corners or off center but the black level is better than my old IPS monitor. The curve took a little getting used to but once adjusted it seems pretty natural and I like being able to set up multiple windows across the space based on the work I'm doing. There isn't very much light bleed, can really only see it in complete darkness. It is plenty bright, not the brightest and most color accurate monitor but it is good enough unless you're strictly doing digital graphics, I dont. The monitor has inputs for HDMI and DisplayPort as well as USB-C. I have not gotten USB-C video input to work, you supposedly need a video card than can do DisplayPort ALT mode. I don't think mine do. The input switching works well and can be controlled from the buttons on the front of the monitor but it does cause my computers to think the monitor is disconnected for a second before it comes back, which is slightly annoying. It has built in speakers that aren't very good, but most monitors don't have good speakers it's slightly better than my business Dell laptop. However one big downside is you can switch between the audio from HDMI and Display Port but only if they are both being displayed at the same time with PIP or PBP, you can't full screen one port and play audio through the other which is one thing I wanted to do with a work PC and a media PC hooked up to this monitor. The KVM functionality of the monitor is a bit misleading. It's more of a USB hub switch, where you can connect the "hub" to 2 PCs and switch back and forth but it will completely disconnect anything connected to the monitor from the other PC which may not be what you want.
All in all it's a pretty good less expensive ultrawide monitor from others I've seen out there that checks all the boxes for features I was looking for. Not the best but I'm pretty happy with it and not going back to 2 separate monitors.

I'm so glad that I put aside the idea that I thought Philips was probably a Walmart quality monitor and that collectively the reviews on this weren't the best (because, as I said they aren't review of THIS monitor). title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
The monitor is nice and bright. It is also quite clear. Even if you come from better than Full-HD to 4K, you'll like the crispness -- at least once you get used to figuring how to make your fonts bigger. Haven't used all the features, yet. Will enjoy having two computers hooked up side-by-side on the same monitor, when I do. But hey, a 4K monitor for $280, its almost a winner. This monitor is bright and pretty. Of course, one will have to debate whether a 4K TV with some terrible AI installed is what you'd rather have -- those are cheaper for VESA mountable larger screens.

It is quite stylish with its non-VESA base. Yet, that is its major problem. It was designed so that you buy this one, and later, when you find you really want it mounted, you buy another. VESA is the standard for mounts that manufactures tend to use if they want to allow their monitors to sell well in the corporate or in-the-know home market.

There does not seem to be any lag on how well it shows images. There is no blurring or ghosting with normal office work or simple games. I've not tried it with real games requiring a GPU other than what Intel does on the CPU.

There is the nice feature that it warns the user that burn in may occur if the same image is displayed for long periods of time. It actually mentions 30 minutes as the time. It gives that warning almost as soon as it detects a video mode about to cause burn in. Its kind of a disembodied floating text box.

I've used it with both Mac OS X and with Pop!_OS. The picture shown is that of a game, Bomber, played on Pop!_OS. If using a Gnome based User Interface, I suggest that you use Backslide with only a five minute change of the background picture to help avoid burn in. When the Pop!_OS login screen shows up for X-Windows it tends to make the monitor go black if there is no user interaction.

When using a Macbook Pro, or likely any other modern Mac, you'll need to have a HDMI 2 to Thunderbolt converter. There are a ton of those around. So, if you don't like having a converter, then, you'll likely not want this monitor.

If you are anywhere near two meters tall, then, you'll want to have something to raise up the monitor so to keep good posture. Cause, you'll not be happy with the non-adjustable mount for the monitor.

At the time of this review, I have used the monitor for about 13 hours. Most of them doing textual work.

I bought it just before the next wave of trade-war with China tariffs hit and as it was first offered on Amazon.

The following are the features I've not tried yet:
1.) LowBlue
2.) MultiView
3.) DisplayPort
4.) More than one HDMI

Nothing to complain about with the panel. Colours are good. Brightness is good. Wish the description said how many Nits it is. I’d like to know to find other monitors as bright as this one.

The matte finish is as it should be. So I can see the image on screen without annoying reflections. Same location with a glossy screen and I couldn’t see anything except reflections.

IMPORTANT:

There are two power switches on it. The front one, in the lower right corner, wakes it from sleep. title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Pros:

- Stunning monitor, bright, crystal clear, works just like any other monitor attached to a Windows machine
- For laptop users with a USB C connector and power source, this will act like a hub, charge your laptop and transmit video/ethernet/USB via your single USB C cable (you'll need to supply a quality cable, not just a charge cable)
- Sound built in

Cons:
- Like multiple reviewers the camera doesn't seem to operate well. It will come on and then it freezes and you can never get it going again without at least a reboot. Unusable.
- Heavy

This is a big monitor, four feet of solid screen in front on any desk really fills your field of view. I can't say I feel "immersed", it might be because I have the monitor pushed back or it might be because the curve while useful, is pretty gentle.

Relatively easy to connect to my laptop; a couple of gotcha's; the USB default setting is to power down the USB ports when the monitor goes into power save mode (you can override that in the monitor settings), also the USB ports are set to USB 2.0 by default. The result was at USB 2.0 it didn't recognize my wireless keyboard, and then once I fixed that it disconnected the keyboard when the monitor went to sleep. Both quick fixes.

Unless you want a ridiculously HUGE monitor stand on your desk you might want to look at a monitor arm -- there are very few that are rated to handle the weight of this monitor. WALI Single Monitor Gas Spring Desk Mount Heavy Duty worked fine for me; I had to crank the gas arm adjustment quite a few turns but it stiffened up nicely and now the monitor can be adjusted with a single touch of a finger.

Sound is acceptable, and the software you can download from Philips gives you at least basic ability to modfy the brightness through an on screen control rather than endless monitor menus. It's likely you'll want to adjust the brightness down, this is just a bright monitor, but I was able to get it to an acceptable level (though I reduced it almost all the way to the minimum).

With a USB C cable this is a one connection to your laptop (or PC) monitor, you have a limited number of ports on the monitor (to make it more aesthetically pleasing you might want to get a hub at (or below) desktop level to hide cords -- this could look silly having 3 or 5 cords hanging from the bottom of the monitor. I find that the USB C cable can be a little too easily pulled out, so the less hanging cables the better.

Video playback (like youtube) seems problematic, at least when I have the monitor set to it's maximum resolution. I had to turn off HDR playback and go down to 480p (which still, however, looked stunningly like high def). This is likely due to my video card in my laptop not being very high grade -- frankly, I'm happy enough that it runs this monitor without any noticeable delays or artifacts (Intel UHD 620 with some memory on board).

Totally satisfied with this purchase and the price, hopefully they'll fix the camera drivers (in the meantime I used a plug-into-the-usb-hub fingerprint reader for Windows Hello).

text:
Don't get me wrong... This is a gorgeous super ultra wide 49" monitor with all the bells and whistles you could possibly get on a monitor: decent speakers, built-in webcam (decent quality though working on and off), HDR 400, and a very curved display (1800mm radius of curvature) that wraps around you nicely.

First things first, I never managed to get the advertised 60Hz refresh rate out of this monitor. It's hooked up to a Lenovo P1 workstation laptop with NVIDIA Quadro P2000. This VGA in theory is capable of handling four 5120x2880 displays @ 60Hz according to the datasheet. I have this and a Dell U4919DW attached to the Lenovo (using the 2 Thunderbolt ports on the laptop) simultaneously and no issues other than the Philips can't do any better than 30Hz.

I have tried the Philips alone and with HDMI as well as the USB C cable (both original cables that came in the box) and yet nothing better than a 30Hz refresh rate.

I have been trying the Philips monitor customer service through emails and phone for the past week having always been promised to be called back by their technician(s) and here I am still waiting for that one call on a Friday evening! before a long weekend.

Radius of Curvature
This might be a personal preference and only applies if you are thinking of doing office tasks like using spreadsheets or a design software like AutoCad. This monitor has an 1800mm radius of curvature (i.e. it's very curved) and even though the curve looks very nice to the eyes if watching a video or surfing the web, once you get to the productivity side of the business (like using AutoCad) all the horizontal lines appear so curved to the eye that it becomes a constant mental challenge to convince yourself that those are in fact, straight lines.

Another issue that I noticed and were not able to see mentioned elsewhere in reviews, is the fact that the curve is not a continuous simple curve but rather a deep curve in the center (3/4 of the screen width) and becomes a tangent on both sides towards the edges. This adds to the annoyance imposed to the eyes and mind since horizontal lines (if long enough to go across the screen) are seen/ as very curved in the center and almost flat towards the edges of the display. I don't know about reasons (or manufacturing limitations) behind this, but believe this type of curvature is better to be left to gaming monitors if not avoided all in all.

The camera worked perfectly fine the first time I connected the monitor to the computer but has been working on and off since and does not get detected by Windows after a boot for most of the times. The quality of the camera is mediocre at best and you are probably better off with most other stand alone webcams or in my case the built-in laptop camera.

The speakers are of decent quality but nothing special about them other than the convenience of having an extra set of speakers on your desk.

Right now I'm waiting on the seller to issue a return approval to send this back. You might be able to get the 60Hz refresh rate out of this depending on what machine and VGA you are hooking this up to but the fact about the nonuniform curvature is there to stay after you've noticed it for the first time.

Review:
I purchased two of the Koorui 34‑inch curved ultrawide monitors for a dual‑monitor setup, and so far I’m very pleased with them. The picture quality is sharp, the brightness is solid, and the “Normal” color preset looks natural without any adjustments. For the price, these 34‑inch panels deliver very good performance.

That said, there are a few important details the product listing and reviews don’t mention — and knowing them ahead of time would have saved me some stress during installation.

1. YES, the 34‑inch model DOES include stand‑offs (spacers)
This is not mentioned anywhere in the listing, and even Amazon’s Rufus incorrectly says they are *not* included. They actually come in the small accessory packet with the manual.

If you’re mounting these monitors, you will need those stand‑offs because of the recessed VESA pattern. They are already in the box — just not advertised. I rushed to order a separate spacer kit because the listing didn’t mention it, so I’m putting this here to help the next person avoid that.

2. One of my monitors flashed briefly until I disabled FreeSync
On one of the two monitors, I noticed a quick bright “flash” when moving the mouse. Turning off Adaptive Sync / FreeSync in the monitor’s menu fixed it instantly. The other monitor didn’t have this issue, so it seems to vary by panel.
Not a defect — just something to be aware of if you see flicker or brightness pops.

3. Color and brightness match well once set manually
After setting both monitors to the same brightness, contrast, and color mode, they match very well side‑by‑side. The “Normal” color preset looks the most accurate on these VA panels.

4. Build quality and packaging are solid
Both monitors arrived well‑protected, and the included cables work fine. The stand is basic, but I’m using monitor arms, so that wasn’t a factor for me.

5. Too early to comment on long‑term support or durability
I’ve only had these monitors set up for a few hours, so I can’t speak yet to long‑term reliability or how responsive Koorui’s support is. I’ll update this review if anything changes over time.

Bottom line:
These 34‑inch Koorui ultrawides are excellent for the price, especially for gaming or a dual‑monitor setup. Just be aware that:

- Stand‑offs ARE included (despite the listing not saying so)
- FreeSync may need to be turned off on some units
- Picture quality is great once you match settings manually
- Long‑term support is still unknown

If the listing had mentioned the included spacers, it would have saved me a last‑minute order — so I hope this review helps the next person.

text:
Today I set up my dual KOORUI 27" model N07 monitors. I was somewhat worried by multiple reviewers reporting that this model isn't really a 4K screen. So while I don't usually write reviews, I'm here to assure you the N07 is in fact a 4K screen with resolution of 3840x2160 and refresh rate of 60hz.

And I know why some people got this wrong. When I unplugged my old 1920x1080 monitors and tried to use the same HDMI cables, Windows identified the monitor as having a 1920x1080 native resolution. But my cables were very old. I plugged both my new monitors in using DisplayPort cables and they were instantly reporting 3840x2160. My monitors did not come with DP cables, just new HDMI cables. But my office had extra DP cables laying around.

If you're still having trouble getting 4K on one of these, be wary of adapters, such as DP-to-HDMI, DVI-to-HDMI, etc. Also try shorter or newer cables. You CAN get 4K out of HDMI cables, but remember that HDMI has been around since 2002 and that standard has gone through many versions with new capabilities over the years.

As for reviewing the other aspect of these monitors... they look great to me! Neither of mine had dead or stuck pixels. the colors look good and image is sharp. I'm not a professional monitor reviewer, but these seem like perfectly good office monitors for a fantastic price compared to big brand names. I took a chance on some of their smaller screens several months back and was blown away at the quality and low price. I'm glad this higher end model hasn't let me down!

UPDATE: My original review was written 10/13/2023 and now it's 5/16/2025. I have never had a single issue with these monitors in the 1 year 7 months I've been using them. In fact I stumbled across my own review after looking to purchase a 3rd matching one... because a triple-monitor setup with these bad boys would be awesome! title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This review is for the SB220Q series (1920x1080) 75Hz monitor variant. At a $90 price point as of July 2020, all of the praise this monitor has gotten and continues to get is pretty well deserved. Right out of the box the factory calibration is pretty awful as with most TVs and monitors (I’ll never understand why that is), but Acer’s built-in menu gives you a wide range of control to tweak the image quality to your liking. Here are some of the most noticeable Pros & Cons after using this monitor daily for the past three weeks:

PROS:
- The colors can be very vibrant and the sharpness makes everything nice and crisp both up close and from a distance without going overboard. Although the spec sheet does not specify the exact Adobe or sRGB color gamut range, it does have a stated 72% NTSC coverage (keep in mind that the NTSC color gamut has the highest level of color reproduction), which would imply that it should have close to 100% sRGB coverage. This is pretty standard for most sub $200 monitors (note: the unit that TechSpot tested came in at around 93% of sRGB coverage mostly losing detail in the green range so your unit’s reproduction may vary). The 6-bits + FRC (equal to 8-bits) color depth is also an industry standard for entry level monitors and is completely fine for casual use.

- This montior’s “100,000,000:1” Dynamic Contrast Ratio (DCR) (non-standardized measure of contrast for videos) definitely seems to outperform my other slightly more expensive budget IPS monitors (the HP VH240a and ViewSonic VS2412-H) that only have 20,000,000:1 and 50,000,000:1 contrast ratios respectively. However, note that it still has an industry standard 1000:1 Static Contrast Ratio (measure for non-moving images) which isn’t great but is perfectly acceptable for casual viewing since only the highest tiered ($400+) IPS panels exceed that point with 1,500:1 being the maximum native contrast typically achievable with an IPS.
~ A quick side note about that “100,000,000:1” DCR number: there is no industry standard methodology for this particular measurement so the number itself is mostly useless marketing fluff. But as I noted, compared to the two other monitors with the same industry standard SCR, this monitor did seem to outperform them both in that area.

- Its 102 PPI pixel density actually makes a subtle difference in image quality when viewing up close compared to my 24 inch 1080p monitors that have a 92 PPI. Text seems to be a bit smoother in comparison. This is purely an advantage of having the smaller 21.5 inch screen.

- The Color Adjustment Menu allows you to adjust both the RGB and CMY gains, bias, hues, and saturation levels to get a better color balance.

- The Picture Menu lets you adjust the screen’s brightness, contrast, gamma, and blackness (“black boost”) levels while also providing a ‘blue light’, ‘adaptive constrast’ (ACM), and a ‘Super Sharpness’ on/off switch.

- The Game Menu has FreeSync (for AMD GPUs) and Overdrive options

CONS:
- The bezels are a bit thicker than I woud’ve liked (they’re about 1 cm on the top, left, and right sides) making the frameless design nothing more than a gimmick.

- The top-down viewing angle is noticeably darker compared to looking at the screen head on.

- Despite having a good DCR of 100M:1, the blacks are still a bit too bright for watching anything with heavy dark scenes since the display itself does not have any HDR capabilities with high contrast control zones aka local dimming (to be fair, this is completely expected at this $90 price point and is only being mentioned as reference for those that may be thinking of using this monitor to watch TV/movies).

- The Picture Menu’s ‘Super Sharpness’ option is just an on/off switch; it does not give you a more granular adjustment control over the amount of sharpness to apply.

- Even with all of the image quality adjustment options available in the settings, the whites remain on the slightly warmer side of the color temperature chart. It’s not that noticeable when viewing on this monitor alone, but the difference can be seen if you have another slightly cooler display adjacent to it. This is most likely just an issue with my particular unit since other reviews have noted their unit had a more neutral or “near perfect” white temp.

- It only has a paltry 15° degree back tilt compared to most other budget monitors being able to tilt closer to 30° degrees (this is super nitpicky as compromises are to be expected at a sub $100 price point).

- The Power button is completely indistinguishable from the rest of the menu buttons (both in shape and spacing).

Overall, if you’re looking for a nice quality budget monitor to look at spreadsheets, word documents, and do some internet browsing or even some light casual gaming, then this is a great choice. If you are a competitive gamer, photographer, professional editor, or a content creator then you’ll obviously need to invest in a higher spec monitor.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I purchased this monitor for my wife to use with her Alienware R17X4 laptop. She had broken a key on her keyboard but also wanted a little larger screen. So, I purchased a wireless keyboard and this monitor. She now uses the powerful Alienware laptop as a desktop with a larger display and a wireless, movable keyboard. She is a very happy camper.

Others have commented on the great graphics, thin design, and good quality build for a great price, so I won't repeat those details here. I will however point out a few tips:

1. At first, it seems the stand will not tilt. But it does! Grasp the stand firmly and then tilt the monitor back to the desired position. Note it does not tilt forward or side to side, but does tilt back (facing more upwards towards your eyes) which really helps in most settings.
2. If you don't get a signal, make sure you plugs the HDMI cable into the "HDMI out" port on your PC, not the "HDMI in" port. Duh. I had mine plugged into the wrong port until I found my reading glasses and saw the problem.
3. We changed three settings which you may want to also do if you have a laptop. First, we changed the display settings to choose between "Second screen only", "Duplicate", or "Extend". We chose "Extend" so she can have two documents open at once on the two monitors, her laptop screen and the new monitor. You just drag one document off the edge of the monitor to move it to the other screen.
4. Next, we found that closing the laptop, when she only needed one screen, put it into hibernation and shut everything down. We went into Control Panel and changed Power Settings under "What happens when you close the lid". We changed it from "Hibernate" to "Do nothing". Now the laptop keeps running even when the laptop is closed.
5. Third, most Windows laptops are configured so you have to drag things off the right edge of your new remote monitor to get them onto the laptop screen. However we wanted her laptop setting to the left of her new monitor, so it was confusing to have to drag something off the right-hand edge of the monitor to get it onto the left-hand screen on the laptop. We went back into display settings, where you can drag the two monitors in the settings to reverse them. Now, she can drag items from the left-hand screen to the right-hand screen by dragging them in that direction, and vice versa. Much more intuitive to use that way.

With those changes to the settings, she can open the laptop and use it as two monitors, dragging and dropping documents and apps from one screen to another. When she closes the laptop lid, it reverts to a single monitor (the new Acer) but does not go to sleep. This is perfect for what she needs. She can still power off the monitor when not needed for an extended period. Also, the laptop speakers still work when she turns on the sound even when the laptop is closed.

I highly recommend this monitor for anyone wanting a very good quality, cost-effective solution.

Needed a bracket that would work with the swing arm TV mount in my RV. The original 40" Insignia (Best Buy Brand) TV mounted way low on the back of the TV and was a VESA 200X200. There is an opening in the entertainment center the TV fits into so it can be strapped down and secured when traveling. I went to install a new ROKU 40" TV which has a VESA 200X100 mount which was higher up on the back of the TV which meant the TV hung down farther than the old one and wouldn't set in the opening. I couldn't move the swing arm up to bring the TV up, so I had to use a fixed wall mount and bolt it to the mounting bracket on the swing arm.

This wall mount worked great, the holes for mounting it to the wall lined up with the mounting holes that were already on the swing arm mounting bracket so all I had to do was use the longer 6M bolts that came with this bracket and buy 4 nylon locknuts to bolt it in place. My only complaint was I need to use the top holes on the brackets that bolt to the back of the TV to mount to fit it in the center of the opening so it can be locked in when traveling. Since the TV was a VESA 200X100 mount the slots in the bottom of the TV brackets were not slotted high enough to be able to put the screws through to secure the brackets to the lower nut-plates on the back of the TV. What I ended up doing was drilling a 6.5M hole, 100mm below the top-hole center and the TV mounting screws went right in and tightened up.

Now the TV is centered in the opening and it moves just like the old TV did. I can lock it in place with the strap when traveling and no one can tell the TV was ever swapped out! And I can use the mount if I ever need to swap out this TV because I can use the different mounting holes in the TV brackets to move a new TV up or down and I can move the new TV left and right on the wall mount to center it.

This wired Philips Hue Secure Doorbell works as expected, and the hardware delivers on the basic premise of a doorbell camera. The 2K video looks sharp, the field of view is wide, and notifications arrive reliably through the app. If your goal is a doorbell camera that can trigger Hue lighting scenes or tie into your existing Hue automations, it performs very well in that role. I question whether I need Hue triggers though for actions through the camera or doorbell. With nearly any camera that feeds motion sensor triggers I can create an automation to turn on the parch lights. Which in my case are controlled by a Leviton HomeKit compatible switch to normal LED lights.

The drawbacks show up when you try to use it outside the Hue environment. It technically supports HomeKit with live views, but it does not integrate as smoothly as devices that are built specifically for Apple’s platform. You do not get HomeKit secure video so you’ll only see a live view in Home. To access the full range of security features, the Hue app becomes necessary, including its notification permissions and all the devices you would need like sensors. That adds another app to manage unless you plan to treat Hue as your complete security setup. I already have tons of Hue bulbs and an Ecobee smart thermostat and other HomeKit devices. This is yet another thing which kinda works together.

I have tried a variety of security systems including Abode and Ecobee, and none of them have been ideal, especially because HomeKit has limited RBAC access controls for cameras and settings. Do you want kids to have access to the lights, the garage door, locks, cameras, thermostat schedules, or automations? Maybe some subset of that, but not all of them. I do not blame Hue entirely for this since the ecosystem itself creates some of the friction. This doorbell clearly caters to homes that are already centered around Hue products.

If you want a straightforward wired doorbell camera that works cleanly with your Hue lights, this is a solid choice. If you want something that integrates well with HomeKit as part of a larger smart home strategy, this is not the best fit.

text:
I have 2 sets of HUE play, it’s great.

For many of you wondering how to get the HUE SYNC (pc and mac) to work with things like ROKU (Netflix), gaming consoles (PS4, Xbox, Switch)...etc etc, let me walk you through this extensive process of making it happen along with the devices you’ll need:

******5/2/2019 UPDATE******
(If you get confused, grab a piece of paper and draw it out lol)

1) HDCP2.2 HDMI Splitter with at least 2 Outputs
(Look for splitter that has auto step down to 1080 from 4K for second output)

If your TV is 4k, then make sure the Splitter you get is 4k and HDCP2.2 ready. It must say HDCP 2.2 and not just 4K or HDCP1.4 in the description of the splitter! As For input side, you only need the amount of devices that you have (no you shouldn’t run multiple splitters into one splitter). For me, I have all of my devices going into my AVR, so I just need 1 input with 2 outputs HDMI Splitter (1x2). If you have just a ROKU, then that’s what you need. If you have ROKU and a XBOX/PS4, then you’ll need a HDMI switch that has 2 inputs and 2 outputs (2x2). No matter how many input you need, you must have 2 outputs and the second output has the feature to convert 4K to 1080. This is not a feature you need if your TV is 1080p, but very important for the 4K people because it’ll save you a lot of headache in adjustments.

2) HDMI to USB Video Capture Device
Most HDMI video capture only captures 1080p, there’s absolutely no reason for 4K just for HUE Sync if you are simply trying to pick up the color from the video capture. Connect the video capture device to the Output 2 of the HDMI splitter on one side via HDMI cable, and the USB side connect it to your PC/Mac.

3b) STOP!
Before doing anything else, download the Philips Hue smartphone app, and connect the lights you want to sync with your TV to the Hue Bridge first. Update everything and make sure it’s ready BEFORE you setup with the HUE Sync software on the PC/MAC.
3c) On your PC/MAC, download “OBS Studio”, install the driver/software. I’m running Windows 10 here, so I don’t know if it will work with Chromebook or any other OS. With the OBS Studio software, what I did in the setting is to make sure the canvas screen is set to 1080 so the screen ratio of the video capture is correct. You don’t need high frame rates and you don’t need high resolution here! Lower left side of the OBS Software you’ll see the sources box, select + and select OEM Video capture. Set the PREVIEW screen to full screen, and make sure there’s no black cutoff portions.

4) HUE SYNC
Install HUE Sync, there’s plenty of YouTube video telling you how to setup the HUE Sync on your computer, so just go ahead and do that and you’re good to go. What I did do is turn off music sync, intensity to subtle. NOTE: Under Settings/General-Preference/Background-lightning: Turn off background lighting. It messes with the HUE Sync with this low white light when the same section of the display is showing black.

Optional: I bought a mini windows PC to run as a dedicated TV PC. Please install a CCleaner and run it automatically at start up so you won’t ever see the infamous Windows “slowing down” issues. In the HUE SYNC PC software, you can set specific buttons on the keyboard to start Syncing. I have to say, that I did end up buying 3 different mini PC and returned two of them because they simply can’t power 4K without freezing. I ended up getting a MSI cube n with a 5000N processor with 8GB ddr4 ram. I changed resolution down from 4K to 2048x1152, and refresh rate to 60Hz. It runs very smoothly all day without issue.

If you do all of this correctly, you now can watch or play everything on your TV and enjoy HUE Play, regardless of the source.

Remember to check your 4k setting in your Xbox/PS4 pro/ROKU to make sure it’s able to output 4K on your 4K tv. If the splitter you use or any parts you use besides the video capture is NOT HDCP2.2, you will not be able to watch 4K. If you force 4K output on your ROKU, it may work but the video capture will show a black screen. Make sure your HDMI are at least 2.0, amazon’s cable works fine, there’s no benefit with more expensive HDMI cables.

I’ll take my 2 cents, thanks.

text:
When creating a review for this, there's a metric offered of "value for money" I am inclined to just avoid that metric, because you're buying a philips hue product: you know that this isn't cheap. By no means is it a Nanoleaf product, but Philips Hue isn't cheap. What you get in turn though is a highly integrated ecosystem that utilizes a Zigbee backhaul to make sure that it can communicate to the devices even absent a WiFi network (assuming you can send the commands, like from other Zigbee devices), solid quality control, and HomeKit integrations.

Its not to say that they're necessarily a perfect product for you: Until the Ambient they didn't offer individually addressable LED's, and even that I'm pretty sure is zone based.

As for the Playbar's specifically? I love them: They're great, but they still have a few downsides. This kit isn't cheap (at time of writing, around $70-80 per bar), but doesn't give you the Bridge (which is mandatory for these; no bluetooth mode). You likely have a bridge already if you're looking at investing, so that does help. The lights do not have a built in battery, and personally what I found most disappointing is the lack of adjustability for their physical stands. You have a few mounting options, but they're all fixed mounts: they don't allow you to tilt or adjust them. You decide a particular orientation and you're stuck with it unless you disassemble their mounts, which considering you're using 3M pads isn't really ideal. If you're wanting to do a set-and-forget layout it is fine, but be aware it's not like you can tilt them or anything.

The plug that comes with these lights supports up to three lights being plugged into it: so if you get a third play bar, you can just plug it into the same plug. Alternatively (and what is neat to me): If you get the Philips Hue Sync, you can also plug it into this 3rd port: it utilizes the same style. I think that's a relatively clever idea to minimize socket use, especially because its quite likely that you are going to be utilizing play bars with the Sync. The trade off, of course, is that a lot of people run three or more playbars for a sync - one to the left, one to the right, and one on top. If you have an orientation like that, the third plug point is going to be taken up by default.

All in all though, I recommend these: They're bright. They're easily controlled via all major assistants, and there is some absolutely *great* Zigbee accessories that can be utilized. Outside of Philips Hue range itself, I really love the Lutreon Caseta control, and recommend people look into something like that to make your space more accessible to the folk in your life who are less tech-y.

Flipping breaker in our house:
Unfortunately after I bought this light strip, the breaker in our townhouse mysteriously started tripping every other day. We couldn’t figure out what the problem was. An electrician that we called asked us if we had any LED lights in the house. Surprised, we said yeah. He told us to unplug them. I unplugged this light strip and suddenly our breakers stopped flipping. Coincident? Unlikely.

Prob almost burned our house down:
A few weeks later I plugged the light strip back in for a day and within 30 minutes of me doing so the breaker flipped THREE TIMES in a span of like 8 minutes.

Got a used product apparently:
I saw in quite a few other reviews that people said they received used units despite them being advertised as new. Funny enough, when I opened mine up, the adhesive was completely detached from the strip in one spot towards the end of the strip. I didn’t give it much thought until now but why would my “brand new” light strip be in that condition?

Hue customer service:
By the time I realized this light strip was causing major electrical problems in our brand new townhouse I was outside the return window and had to go through Hues customer service. To their credit they did let me send the product back. They were supposed to send me another one but it was backordered for literally months but weirdly was in stock on Amazon? I guess because they’re secretly selling used units on here that others have returned for defects. Summary:
